This document explores the process of moving data into Google Cloud, from planning a data transfer to using best practices in implementing a plan.

### Storage Transfer Service overview

Access guides, references, and resources for learning more about Storage Transfer Service.

### Managing transfers for on-premises jobs

This document describes how to create your transfer job, install transfer agents, and how to manage your transfer jobs.

### Metadata preservation in Storage Transfer Service

This document describes metadata that is preserved when you use Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data to transfer data to Cloud Storage.

### Performance, scaling and requirements for transfers

Understand the requirements for object size, object naming, and other scale and performance guidelines.

### Not seeing what you’re looking for?

Use cases

#### Explore common use cases for Storage Transfer Service

###### Data center migration

Move from your existing infrastructure to the cloud. The data you create and store on-premises demands time and significant resources to manage cost-effectively, securely, and reliably. Utilize our Storage Transfer Service solutions to migrate your workloads and datasets quickly to Google Cloud and start saving. Learn about all of Google Cloud’s [migration services and solutions](https://cloud.google.com/products/cloud-migration).

###### Content storage and delivery

Storage Transfer Service enables you to push your media assets from other clouds or your private data center into [multi-regional setups](/storage/docs/storage-classes#multi-regional/), designed for video streaming and frequently accessed content like websites and images. Moving data can enable more efficient content distribution and simpler publishing operations, with the help of products such as [Cloud CDN](/cdn).

###### Disaster recovery, backup, and archival

With our data transfer services, you can schedule incremental syncs to enable disaster recovery for apps running in other clouds and on-premises, to meet your recovery goals. Learn about all of our backup and disaster recovery options, or read about how to use Cloud Storage for [archiving your data](https://cloud.google.com/storage).

###### Analytics and machine learning

Once transferred to [Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage), your data is enabled for analytics or machine learning projects, via data pipelines that are hybrid or run across multiple clouds or cloud regions. Wherever your data is, you can take advantage of Google Cloud’s [analytics](https://cloud.google.com/solutions/smart-analytics) and machine learning suite. Learn more about our innovative [machine learning products and services](https://cloud.google.com/products/ai).

All features

### Learn more about Storage Transfer Service features

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Monitoring and logging | Transfer service for on-premises data produces transfer logs so that you can verify the results of your transfer jobs and offers an option to monitor progress of transfer jobs via Cloud Monitoring. Storage Transfer Service could be configured to deliver Pub/Sub notification on transfer completion. |
| Data integrity | Storage Transfer Service uses metadata available from the source storage system, such as checksums and file sizes, to ensure that data written to Cloud Storage is the same data read from the source. In addition to data integrity provided by the TLS protocol, the Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data calculates a [CRC32C](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/hashes-etags) checksum over each file that it copies as the file is being read. |
| Security and encryption | We use TLS encryption for HTTPs connections, through the public internet and private connections, and support transfers to Cloud Storage buckets protected by VPC Service Controls. The only exception to TLS encryption is if you specify an HTTP URL for a URL list transfer. If you are using interconnect, you can get another layer of security by [accessing a private API endpoint](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/on-prem-vpc-sc). |
| Data transfer scheduling | You can schedule one-time transfer operations or recurring transfer operations. When transferring data from other cloud providers, you can schedule periodic synchronization with advanced filters based on file creation dates, file-names, and the times of day you prefer to import data. There is no manual intervention needed, and the results are recorded in the Cloud Console. |
| Bandwidth throttling | We’ve incorporated controls into Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data to avoid disruption of your day-to-day business operations. Configure a bandwidth limit for your Google Cloud project to limit the rate at which on-premises agents will copy files. The bandwidth limit is shared across all transfer jobs in your project. |
| Incremental transfer | By default all transfers begin by evaluating the data present at the source and destination. This process determines which source objects are new, updated, or deleted since the last transfer. With this initial step, you are able to minimize the amount of data that needs to be sent, use bandwidth effectively, and ensure transfers run quickly. |
| Flexibility, filtering, and controls | You can use includePrefix and excludePrefix when [creating transfers](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/create-manage-transfer-program) to limit what objects Storage Transfer Service operates on. We also support modification-time-based data filtering options. |
| Dynamic scale out | When transferring data from on-premises locations, getting better performance is as easy as bringing up more Storage Transfer Service agents. No transfer config changes or re-submissions required. As soon as the agents are up, they will start performing transfer work. |
| Reliability and fault tolerance | We make reliability work out of the box. If some of your agents fail, the remaining ones will pick up their work. If all of your agents fail, no problem—as soon as you bring them back up, transfers will pick up where they had left off. No special recovery or retry logic required. |
| Simple pricing | When using Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data, we charge at a per-GB rate. When transferring data from other cloud providers, Storage Transfer Service is free of charge. After transferring data, you are charged for data stored on Cloud Storage as documented in Cloud Storage pricing, and external cloud providers' costs may also apply while you use Storage Transfer Service. |
| Transfer from a URL list | You can use Storage Transfer Service to transfer data from a list of public data locations to a Cloud Storage bucket. |

Transfer service for on-premises data produces transfer logs so that you can verify the results of your transfer jobs and offers an option to monitor progress of transfer jobs via Cloud Monitoring. Storage Transfer Service could be configured to deliver Pub/Sub notification on transfer completion.

Storage Transfer Service uses metadata available from the source storage system, such as checksums and file sizes, to ensure that data written to Cloud Storage is the same data read from the source. In addition to data integrity provided by the TLS protocol, the Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data calculates a [CRC32C](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/hashes-etags) checksum over each file that it copies as the file is being read.

We use TLS encryption for HTTPs connections, through the public internet and private connections, and support transfers to Cloud Storage buckets protected by VPC Service Controls. The only exception to TLS encryption is if you specify an HTTP URL for a URL list transfer. If you are using interconnect, you can get another layer of security by [accessing a private API endpoint](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/on-prem-vpc-sc).

You can schedule one-time transfer operations or recurring transfer operations. When transferring data from other cloud providers, you can schedule periodic synchronization with advanced filters based on file creation dates, file-names, and the times of day you prefer to import data. There is no manual intervention needed, and the results are recorded in the Cloud Console.

We’ve incorporated controls into Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data to avoid disruption of your day-to-day business operations. Configure a bandwidth limit for your Google Cloud project to limit the rate at which on-premises agents will copy files. The bandwidth limit is shared across all transfer jobs in your project.

By default all transfers begin by evaluating the data present at the source and destination. This process determines which source objects are new, updated, or deleted since the last transfer. With this initial step, you are able to minimize the amount of data that needs to be sent, use bandwidth effectively, and ensure transfers run quickly.

You can use includePrefix and excludePrefix when [creating transfers](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/create-manage-transfer-program) to limit what objects Storage Transfer Service operates on. We also support modification-time-based data filtering options.

When transferring data from on-premises locations, getting better performance is as easy as bringing up more Storage Transfer Service agents. No transfer config changes or re-submissions required. As soon as the agents are up, they will start performing transfer work.

We make reliability work out of the box. If some of your agents fail, the remaining ones will pick up their work. If all of your agents fail, no problem—as soon as you bring them back up, transfers will pick up where they had left off. No special recovery or retry logic required.

When using Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data, we charge at a per-GB rate. When transferring data from other cloud providers, Storage Transfer Service is free of charge. After transferring data, you are charged for data stored on Cloud Storage as documented in Cloud Storage pricing, and external cloud providers' costs may also apply while you use Storage Transfer Service.

You can use Storage Transfer Service to transfer data from a list of public data locations to a Cloud Storage bucket.

Google Cloud Storage Transfer Service is a managed data transfer solution that moves data quickly and securely between object and file storage across Google Cloud, Amazon (AWS), Azure, on-premises data centers, and other locations. It enables cloud-to-cloud, on-prem-to-cloud, and bucket-to-bucket transfers without requiring any code, offering centralized job management for monitoring transfer status.

**Key Benefits:**
- Enables hybrid- and multicloud strategies by moving data from private data centers, AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud through a single interface
- Optimizes infrastructure management and reduces costs by moving storage/application infrastructure to Google Cloud with minimal downtime
- Handles large-scale transfers of petabytes of data, billions of files, and 10s of Gbps throughput over online networks

**Core Features:**
- Data encryption in transit with TLS, VPC Service Controls support, and checksum-based data integrity validation (including CRC32C checksums)
- Incremental transfers that only move new, updated, or deleted files since the last transfer
- Metadata preservation controls during transfer
- Scheduling for one-time or recurring transfers with filters based on creation dates, filenames, and preferred times
- Bandwidth throttling controls for on-premises agents (shared limit across project jobs)
- Prefix-based filtering (includePrefix/excludePrefix) and modification-time-based filtering
- Dynamic scale-out by adding more transfer agents (no reconfiguration needed)
- Built-in reliability and fault tolerance—failed agents' work is picked up by remaining agents; transfers resume automatically when agents come back online
- Monitoring and logging via Cloud Monitoring, transfer logs, and Pub/Sub notifications on completion
- URL list transfers from public data locations to Cloud Storage buckets

**Pricing:**
- Transfers using on-premises agents: $0.0125/GB
- All other sources/sinks: Free
- Post-transfer Cloud Storage storage costs apply per standard pricing

**Use Cases:**
- Data center migration to Google Cloud
- Content storage and delivery (media assets to multi-regional setups, with Cloud CDN)
- Disaster recovery, backup, and archival via scheduled incremental syncs
- Analytics and machine learning by moving data into Cloud Storage for pipelines

**Partners:** Cloud FastPath, Komprise, Server General, and Signiant offer advanced network-level optimization and ongoing data transfer workflows.

**Documentation resources** cover topics including large dataset migration, transfer job management, metadata preservation, and performance/scaling requirements.

# Data transfer options Stay organized with collections Save and categorize content based on your preferences.

 

Google offers multiple solutions for transferring your data to or from Cloud Storage, or between file systems.

| Transfer scenario | Recommendation |
| --- | --- |
| Transferring from another cloud storage provider | Use Storage Transfer Service. |
| Transferring less than 1 TB from on-premises | Use [`gcloud storage`](/sdk/gcloud/reference/storage). |
| Transferring more than 1 TB from on-premises | Use [Storage Transfer Service](/storage-transfer/docs/create-transfers) or [Transfer Appliance](/transfer-appliance/docs/4.0/overview). |
| Transferring less than 1 TB from another Cloud Storage region | Use [gcloud storage](/sdk/gcloud/reference/storage). |
| Transferring more than 1 TB from another Cloud Storage region | Use Storage Transfer Service. |

Use this guidance as a starting point. The specific details of your transfer scenario will also help you determine which tool is more appropriate.

## Move or back up data from another cloud provider to Cloud Storage

We recommend using [Storage Transfer Service](/storage-transfer/docs/overview) to move or back up your data from other cloud storage providers to Cloud Storage.

We support transfers from the following cloud storage providers:

* Amazon S3
* Microsoft Azure Blob Storage

To get started, see [Create transfers](/storage-transfer/docs/create-transfers).

## Move data between Cloud Storage buckets

We recommend using Storage Transfer Service to move large amounts of data between Cloud Storage buckets.

You can alternatively use the Google Cloud CLI to transfer between Cloud Storage buckets. This can be helpful for moving data between bucket locations.

To get started, see:

* [Transfer between Cloud Storage buckets with Storage Transfer Service](/storage-transfer/docs/cloud-storage-to-cloud-storage).
* [Move data from one bucket to another](/storage/docs/moving-buckets#move-buckets) using the command line (`gcloud storage`).

## Move or back up data from on-premises storage

We offer several solutions for moving or backing up on-premises data, depending on your specific situation:

### Locations with good internet connectivity

We offer the following solutions for on-premises data:

* You can use Storage Transfer Service. For file system transfers, you install a small piece of software, called an agent, on a machine with access to your file system. The agent runs within a Docker container and has access to your locally-mounted NFS data. We upload the data you specify to Cloud Storage.

  To get started, see [Manage agent pools](/storage-transfer/docs/on-prem-agent-pools).
* You can use a Transfer Appliance with online mode enabled. You connect the Transfer Appliance to your network, and copy data directly to it. The appliance transfers the data you copy to it to Cloud Storage.

  To get started, see the [Transfer Appliance documentation](/transfer-appliance/docs/4.0/procedure-guide).

### Locations with poor or no internet connectivity

We recommend using Transfer Appliance to move or back up your on-premises data if you have poor or no internet connectivity. You connect Transfer Appliance to your network, and copy data directly to it. When the appliance is full, you send it back to us to copy to Cloud Storage. When we finish copying your data, we wipe the device for its next use.

To get started, see the [Transfer Appliance documentation](/transfer-appliance/docs/4.0/procedure-guide).

## Transfer from Cloud to a file system

We recommend using Storage Transfer Service to move data from Cloud Storage to your file system storage. With this method, you install a small piece of software, called an agent, in your private data center. The agent runs within a Docker container and has access to your locally mounted NFS data. We download the data you specify from Cloud Storage.

To get started, see [Requirements for file system transfers](/storage-transfer/docs/on-prem-set-up).

For small data sets you can use [`gcloud storage rsync`](/sdk/gcloud/reference/storage/rsync). Use `gcloud storage rsync` to transfer data between Cloud Storage and other cloud storage providers, or between Cloud Storage and your file system data.

- Transferring less than 1 TB from on-premises: Use `gcloud storage`
- Transferring more than 1 TB from on-premises: Use Storage Transfer Service or Transfer Appliance
- Transferring less than 1 TB from another Cloud Storage region: Use `gcloud storage`
- Transferring more than 1 TB from another Cloud Storage region: Use Storage Transfer Service

**Specific Scenarios Covered:**

1. **Move/back up from other cloud providers**: Storage Transfer Service is recommended, supporting transfers from Amazon S3 and Microsoft Azure Blob Storage.

2. **Move data between Cloud Storage buckets**: Storage Transfer Service is recommended for large amounts of data; alternatively, Google Cloud CLI (`gcloud storage`) can be used, which is helpful for moving data between bucket locations.

3. **Move/back up from on-premises storage**: Two approaches depending on connectivity:
   - With good internet connectivity: Storage Transfer Service (using an agent software running in a Docker container with access to locally-mounted NFS data) OR Transfer Appliance with online mode enabled.
   - With poor or no internet connectivity: Transfer Appliance is recommended — data is copied directly to the device, which is then shipped back to Google to copy to Cloud Storage, after which the device is wiped for reuse.

4. **Transfer from Cloud to a file system**: Storage Transfer Service is recommended using an agent in the private data center that downloads data from Cloud Storage to locally-mounted NFS storage. For small data sets, `gcloud storage rsync` can be used to transfer between Cloud Storage and other providers or file systems.

# How Google Cloud Storage Transfer Service Works & When to Consider an Alternative

![Eleanor Parker](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='0'%20height='0'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

#### Eleanor Parker

[Back to Resilio Blog Homepage](https://www.resilio.com/blog/)

Google Storage Transfer Service (GSTS) is Google’s solution for transferring files from on-premise file systems to cloud storage or from cloud to cloud.

It’s a pay-as-you-go product suitable for transferring data in one direction across Google Cloud Platform (GCP), Amazon Web Services (AWS), Azure, and on-premise environments (including from on-prem file systems).

This makes GSTS a solid choice for transfer scenarios like:

* Migrating data from file systems into GCP.
* Migrating on-premise data from a source bucket to GCP.
* Moving data in one direction between storage buckets, whether inside GCP or across cloud providers.

However, **GSTS also has downsides. Mainly, it can be very difficult to deploy and manage.**In situations where you’ll be movingor syncing large files, larger file systems, or multiple file systems in multiple directions — for example, two-way, one-to-many, many-to-one, or many-to-many — you may want to consider alternatives.

*In these cases, a solution like Resilio Platform is well suited to moving and syncing data in any direction, across any cloud**provider**— using any type of device and network. To learn more about Resilio Platform or see it live in action,*[*please schedule a demo*](https://www.resilio.com/schedule-demo/)*.*

Specifically, limitations with GSTS include:

* **Complex deployment options.**GSTS’s agents require you to have Docker installed and running on Linux servers or VMs. This can make the deployment difficult (or even impossible) for companies that rely mainly on Windows or other non-Linux technologies in their stack. It’s not like most Google services due to the complexity associated with setting up containerized instances, permissions, and other manual configuration steps.

* **Time-consuming to set up and manage in larger projects.**If you want to speed up transfers when moving lots of files, you’ll have to manually partition up your dataset and set up parallel transfers. While useful, this capability takes effort to set up and creates complex management demands down the line.

* **Limited one-way transfer.**This means you can only transfer data from a single source to a single destination. GSTS isn’t a good choice if you have a subset of data that needs to be continuously synced with data in other locations.

In the second part of this guide, we’ll discuss how [Resilio Connect](https://www.resilio.com/connect/) — our WAN-optimized data replication, sync, and file gateway solution — can help you overcome these downsides.

Resilio Platform enables **omnidirectional, real-time sync**across cloud regions, cloud providers, on-prem environments, and hybrid cloud infrastructure. Our solution offers:

* **Versatile, hassle-free deployment options.**Resilio Platform works with any device — including servers, desktops, laptops, edge devices, and more — and popular operating systems, including Linux, Windows, Android, Mac, FreeBSD, and more. There’s no limitation to using Docker, Linux, or any other combination of technologies.

* **The ability to transfer and sync files in any direction.**With Resilio, you can transfer files from endpoints collecting data at the remote edge, push updates to thousands of locations globally, let users in different regions continuously sync files in real time, and much more. There’s also no need to manually partition your dataset to increase your bandwidth, regardless of the number of files or endpoints.

* **Reliability for all transfer, sync, and replication use cases.**Resilio Platform uses a unique P2P architecture that doesn’t have a single point of failure. If any endpoint in your environment goes down, you can still access your data from another one. Plus, Resilio can also fully utilize any network (even if it’s unreliable), including VSAT, Wi-Fi, 3G/4G/5G cell networks, or any IP network.

* **A single point of management for your data.**You can control transfer, sync, and replication jobs from a Central Management Console. Plus, with our agents installed, you get a centralized view of all your data, regardless of whether it is in a Windows, Linux, Mac, Android, NAS system, or any other endpoint.

* **Blazing-fast transfer speeds.**Resilio Connect’s P2P architecture and proprietary, UDP-based WAN optimization deliver the fastest transfer speeds in the industry. We’ve [achieved transfer throughput speeds of over 100 Gbps](https://www.resilio.com/blog/introducing-scale-out-file-replication-and-sync) and have transferred 500 GB of data in GCP from London to Australia in 50 seconds.

*Brands like Exxon Mobil, 2K Games, Warner Brothers, Cisco, and KFC use Resilio Platform to achieve fast and reliable data transfer, sync, and replication. To see Resilio in action for yourself,*[*schedule a demo with our team*](https://www.resilio.com/schedule-demo/)*.*

## Google Storage Transfer Service: How It Works, Pricing, & Limitations

GSTS is a software-based solution (SaaS) that can transfer data from various sources to destinations in Google Cloud Storage (unlike Google’s Transfer Appliance which is a hardware-based transfer solution).

At the time of this writing, the supported sources are:

* Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3).
* S3-compatible storage.
* Google Cloud Storage.
* Azure Blob Storage.
* File systems.
* Publicly accessible or signed HTTP and HTTPs URLs.

You can also use GSTS to transfer data from Google Storage to file systems or between two file systems. Make sure to refer to [Google’s documentation on sources and links](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/sources-and-sinks) for the most up-to-date info on this topic.

Regardless of the source and destination, GSTS:

* Reduces the amount of data that needs to be transferred by only moving files or objects that have been changed since the last transfer.

* Encrypts data in transit automatically and performs data integrity checks to ensure it arrives intact.

* Can be configured to deliver Pub/Sub notifications on transfer completion.

* Enables you to choose to preserve your files’ or objects’ metadata.

Depending on the use case, you can get started in different ways, including the Google Cloud console, REST APIs, the Gcloud command-line tool, and Java or Python client libraries.

In terms of the setup, transfers where the source and/or destination is a file system or S3-compatible storage require agents and agent pools, while transfers from other sources don’t. For more details about each use case and transfer option, check out Google’s documentation on [agent-based transfers](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/file-system-permissions) and [agentless transfers](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/iam-cloud).

GSTS also uses a parallelized architecture to accelerate transfer speeds. You can create multiple parallel transfers, which is especially useful (but also time-consuming and difficult to do) when transferring a large number of relatively small files.

Besides simply transferring data to the cloud, you can also use GSTS for:

* **Data archival** by moving cold data to Cloud Storage from on-premise storage systems.

* **Data backup**by replicating your data to Google Cloud or creating a copy of a Cloud Storage bucket in another region.

* **Data processing pipelines** by moving data generated on data centers or other clouds to Google Cloud for analytics using BigQuery.

In terms of pricing,**GSTS charges $0.0125 per GB transferred to the destination**successfully for agent-based transfers to or from file systems. The service is free for agentless transfers or for agent-based transfers from S3-compatible storage.

However, remember that you’ll also incur regular storage charges, as well as charges for moving data from one storage bucket to another. There are also other factors that can contribute to your charges and you can [learn more about them here](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/pricing).

### Downside #1: Limited Deployment Options

If your transfer operation involves a file system or S3-compatible storage, you’ll need to set up GSTS agents. These agents are apps that can only run on Linux servers and VMs inside a Docker container.

There are no other deployment options here, which can **overcomplicate your****workflow****and cost you lots of time** if Linux and Docker aren’t part of your regular tech stack.

For example, say you’ve got a NAS system with Windows systems connected to it. In order to use GSTS, you first have to set up the Linux VMs and Docker containers. Then, you have to mount the storage and copy it into the Linux VM, after which it can get transferred. This whole process can take a lot of engineering hours.

Not to mention, IT teams that use Windows (or other non-Linux technologies) likely won’t be comfortable with their data running through Linux.

### Downside #2: Time-Consuming Setup and Management for Large Projects

GSTS can be easy to use for simpler projects, like one-time transfers or cloud migrations from one site to GCP. However, things get **exponentially more difficult if you want to maximize transfer speeds in a larger project.**

For example, say you have to transfer a few hundred million files. GSTS has a maximum number of allowed queries per second (QPS) per transfer job. Since transferring data can trigger list, read, and write operations, you can easily hit this limit. Theoretically, you could overcome this by partitioning up your dataset and having multiple parallel transfers running concurrently.

In reality, this can be a very cumbersome process. First, you have to do the math on exactly how many Linux VMs you’ll need on the source site (or sites) to handle each part of the load based on the throughput you need to achieve. And that’s before you start setting them up.

The bigger issue is that you’re actually**creating multiple points of management.** For instance, if you need five Linux instances, you now have five points of management. You also have to get the data from your source servers into these instances at scale, which can be very difficult.

### Downside #3: Differences in Transfer Features Depending on the Data Source and Destination

GSTS’s features don’t work the same way when it comes to cloud object storage vs. Cloud Storage transfers vs. file system transfers. For example:

* You can adjust transfer bandwidth when dealing with file system transfers but not when moving data from cloud object storage to cloud storage.

* There’s no overwrite option for file system transfers. This means that when GSTS detects a new or changed object on the file system, it copies the complete object to Cloud Storage (and you can’t change that behavior).

* Name-based source data filtering and modified-time source-data filtering are not supported for file system transfers.

You can learn more about these differences in [Google’s documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/transfer-differences).

## How Resilio Platform Delivers Fast and Reliable Transfer and Sync in Any Direction

Resilio Platform is a software-only, agent-based file transfer, sync, and replication solution that delivers the fastest transfer speeds across multiple locations over any distance.

You can **deploy Resilio directly on your endpoint devices** — from mobile phones to desktops, servers, cloud instances, and many more. There’s no need to buy new hardware or work with a particular set of technologies (like Linux and Docker).

Our solution also lets you manage on-premise and cloud data from one unified management view, from any location. You can set up, manage, and monitor data transfer, sync, and replication jobs from one central place, without needing to partition your dataset to increase throughput (like with GSTS). Plus, all jobs can be automated via the graphical management console, scripts, or APIs.

Brands like [Mercedes-Benz](https://www.resilio.com/casestudies/mercedesbenz/), [Deutsche Aircraft](https://www.resilio.com/casestudies/deutsche-aircraft/), and [Northern Marine Group](https://www.resilio.com/casestudies/nmg-stena/) use Resilio Platform to:

* Achieve near-instant transfer speeds across any cloud region, on-prem storage, and hybrid cloud setups.

* Handle massive data workloads and sync large volumes of data over many endpoints.

* Distribute updates and time-sensitive operational data in predictable timeframes across the globe.

* Collect data from geographically dispersed sites, machines, and vehicles.

* Deploy updates and security patches to vehicles, vessels, and other machines operating at the edge.

* Sync branch offices to ensure good remote work collaboration (even if they’re located in areas with poor or unreliable connectivity).

### Flexible Deployment Options — No Technology Limitations

As we said, GSTS’ transfer agents run only on Linux servers or VMs and require having Docker installed. This means you’ll often be forced to use Linux and Docker even if they’re not part of your usual technology stack, which can overcomplicate your workflow.

In contrast, Resilio Platform offers much simpler and more flexible deployment options. **Resilio is an agent-based, cross-platform solution that runs on your choice of physical or virtual machines**. Agents run on Windows, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, and some NAS systems.Deployment options include:

* Industry-standard desktops, servers, storage, edge devices, networks, and much more. Plus, Resilio is compatible with all popular operating systems, including Windows, Linux, FreeBSD, Open BSD, Mac, and Android. Open source or closed source, you can choose the OS that works for you.

* DAS, SAN, and NAS, including OSNexus, Synology, TrueNAS, QNAP, and more. This means you can continue using your current storage, without needing to purchase new hardware.

* Any hypervisor on any hardware running popular operating systems — VMware, Citrix, Hyper-v, and other hypervisors can be used for hosting virtual machines. Docker can be used for containers. There are no dependencies on having to run in a specific type of OS (e.g., Linux in Docker) like with GSTS.

**Resilio is also a cloud-agnostic solution that can be deployed on any infrastructure** — single-cloud, multi-cloud, hybrid cloud, on-premises, and so on.

For example, Resilio Platform lets you:

* Transfer and sync data across GCP regions and services.

* Use a variety of file storage solutions and cloud storage services simultaneously, including GCP, AWS, Azure, Wasabi, Backblaze, and more.

* Use any persistent or ephemeral compute engine hosted on any cloud. For example, some workloads may perform better on GCP while others perform better on AWS. Resilio makes it easy to move and sync cloud data between cloud providers automatically and transparently.

* Browse and sync files on file, block, or object storage via popular tools on operating systems like Mac and Windows.

* Blend storage capacity from any type of storage — hard drives, SSDs, storage systems, and so on.

Put simply, Resilio lets you continue using your current solutions and gives you the freedom to move data across any number of storage systems and cloud service providers without restricting you to Docker, Linux, or any other technology.

### Fast, Reliable, and Predictable Transfer Speeds across Any Network

Conventional transfer solutions like GSTS are limited by “point-to-point” architectures. These architectures usually come in one of two topologies — client-server or “follow-the-sun”.

* **In the client-server model**, one device is designated as a hub server, while the others are clients. The hub can transfer and receive objects from any device but clients can only share data with the hub server. For example, if Client 1 wants to sync data through the other servers in your environment, it must first send them to the hub, which then replicates them to the other clients.

* **In the “follow-the-sun” method**, transfers can only happen sequentially, from one device to the next. So, if Device 1 wants to sync data across the environment, it must first replicate them across Device 2, which will then replicate Device 2 to Device 3, and so on.

Both of these topologies create bottlenecks by limiting data transfers or syncs to only two devices at a time (be it from hub to client or from one device to another). This leads to slower transfer speeds and creates single points of failure in your environment.

To overcome this issue, Resilio Platform uses a unique P2P (peer-to-peer) architecture. With this architecture, **every device in your environment can transfer data across other devices**. As a result, you can leverage the full bandwidth of your environment, leading to much faster transfer, sync, and replication speeds.

Resilio Platform also uses file chunking to turn files into several chunks when sharing them. Each one can be transferred independently from the others.

For example, say Device A wants to sync data to Devices B, C, D, and E. Device A can transfer the first block to Device B. Once it receives the block, Device B can share it with any other device in the network while Device A sends the remaining blocks. This mechanism **results in transfer speeds that are 3-10x faster than traditional solutions.**

These capabilities work automatically, regardless of the size and number of files you need to transfer or sync. **There’s no need to manually partition your data** in order to get fast, reliable, and efficient data transfers every time.

In short, our solution is ideal for transferring or syncing lots of files to locations all over the world, regardless of the network, number of endpoints, regions, and cloud providers.

For example, [VoiceBase uses Resilio Platform to distribute 50 GB of files to 400 servers](https://www.resilio.com/casestudies/voicebase/) quickly and reliably. They were able to achieve an 88% drop in software distribution time thanks to Resilio.

Besides contributing to our industry-leading speeds, **the P2P architecture makes Resilio an organically scalable solution**.

This means that adding more endpoints only speeds up transfers and increases available bandwidth. As a result, you can use the full bandwidth of your environment to sync thousands of systems and millions of files quickly, reliably, and efficiently. Resilio can sync data 50% faster than point-to-point solutions in a 1:2 scenario and 500% faster in a 1:10 scenario.

**The P2P architecture also doesn’t have a single point of failure**. If one endpoint goes down, Resilio Platform can simply retrieve data from the nearest available endpoint by automatically routing around the outage.

Plus, in the event of a server failure or another disaster, Resilio can utilize all of your servers to achieve sub-five-second RPOs (Recovery Point Objectives) and RTOs (Recovery Time Objectives) within minutes of an outage.

This makes Resilio an [ideal disaster recovery software](https://www.resilio.com/blog/hot-site-disaster-recovery-solution) for use cases like:

* Hot-site DR
* Warm-site DR
* Offsite copy
* Cold DR

### Transfer, Sync, and Replicate in Any Direction

Unlike GSTS, and other typical [file transfer](https://www.resilio.com/blog/secure-large-file-transfer) and [replication solutions](https://www.resilio.com/blog/real-time-replication-software), Resilio Platform can sync all data — including cloud data — in any direction: one-way, two-way, one-to-many, many-to-one, and N-way (full mesh).

This versatility makes Resilio Platform perfect for lots of use cases.

Let’s take n-way synchronization as an example. Say you have a workforce that’s distributed across the globe. With n-way sync, everyone can make changes to files and have those changes immediately distributed to every other office, regardless of where they’re working from. As a result, everyone can be sure they’re working on the same file versions.

The same goes for syncing a large environment of servers. With Resilio’s P2P architecture and n-way sync, every server in the environment can sync across the others in real-time, without having to rely on a hub server. This makes the whole process much faster and more efficient, as you can utilize the environment’s full bandwidth.

### Centralized Granular Control over All Ingest, Replication, and Sync Tasks

With GSTS, you may need to partition your dataset manually in order to achieve maximum transfer speeds in some cases. Besides being time-consuming, this process creates multiple points of management (i.e., servers or VMs running Docker and Linux).

Resilio Platform avoids that complexity by **giving you a single point of management for all data transfer, replication, and sync jobs** in the form of a Central Management Console.

Here are some examples of things you can do with the Console:

* Create new replication, transfer, and sync jobs. You can have Resilio run across as many agents as necessary with only a single job set up to move the data that can be controlled from the Central Management Console.

* Create automated policies that govern bandwidth allocation for each endpoint.

* Monitor the progress of each job and set up real-time notifications that can be sent via email or webhooks.

* Script any type of functionality your job requires with Resilio’s REST API.

* Adjust key parameters like buffer size, bandwidth usage policies, and disk I/O threads.

* Manage files (or objects) stored in Google Storage, S3, Azure, or another cloud storage provider.

* Configure permissions for who can access, view, and edit your data.

The Management Console also shows you all key metrics for tracking each job’s progress, including duration, number of Resilio agents, number of agents, total bytes to transfer, maximum speed, ETAs, and more.

Lastly, you can store the console pretty much anywhere, including:

* In any virtual or physical Windows or Linux instance.
* In your on-prem environment.
* In a VM instance in a cloud computing provider.

And, because you can easily control every data movement aspect, **you don’t need to manage NFS mounts or manage data across remote devices.**

For a real-life example of the power of Resilio’s Central Management Console, check out [our case study with MixHits Radio](https://www.resilio.com/casestudies/mixhits-radio/). They were able to massively reduce their troubleshooting times thanks to the Management Console.

***“We have gone from spending 15 hours on average per week troubleshooting conflicts in the prior solution to spending no time at all with Resilio. We configure jobs once in the Resilio Platform Management Console and never have to look at it again.”***

*— Gary Hanna, CEO of Mixhits Radio*

### High-Speed WAN Transfers and Full Utilization of Any Network

Most file transfer solutions use the TCP protocol for transfers over wide area networks (WANs). This can be a big issue because latency and packet loss (which are defining characteristics of WANs) disrupt TCP’s performance.

TCP treats packet loss as a network congestion issue and reduces the transfer speed in response. However, packet loss is not a network congestion issue in WANs, so you end up getting data transfer speeds that are significantly lower than the available bandwidth of your internet provider. This prevents you from fully utilizing expressive WAN connections and synchronizing data across multiple sites and cloud providers.

That’s why **Resilio Platform uses a proprietary, UDP-based transfer protocol called Zero Gravity Transport™ (ZGT).**ZGT intelligently analyzes the underlying network by measuring packet loss, latency, and throughput over time, allowing it to:

* Adjust and maintain consistent speed.

* Adapt to changing conditions in real time.

* Maximize network performance and the utilization of any connection, including broadband, VSAT, Wi-Fi, cell, and more.

This technology is **designed for unreliable networks**, so you can always rely on it to ingest, sync, and replicate terabytes of data from the edge of a network to a centralized location in predictable timeframes. If you want more details on how ZGT works, check out our detailed [WAN Optimization Whitepaper](https://www.resilio.com/resources/assets/resilio-connect-wan-optimization-white-paper.pdf).

In the event of an outage, network failure, or another similar issue, Resilio Platform can also perform checksum restarts. This allows failed transfers to continue where they left off, which reduces the strain on your network since you’re not transferring the same more than once.

Lastly, we have a free [speed calculator on our website](https://www.resilio.com/speed-calculator/), which you can use to see how much time Resilio Platform can save your business, depending on your use case (server sync, file send, remote work, and so on).

Overall, the combination of P2P architecture, [WAN acceleration](https://www.resilio.com/blog/wan-acceleration), and file chunking enables Resilio to **deliver the fastest transfer speeds in the industry**. For example:

* We have [achieved transfer throughput speeds of over 100 Gbps](https://www.resilio.com/blog/introducing-scale-out-file-replication-and-sync).

* In early tests of a next-generation release, we’ve seen speeds of 200 Gbps across Azure regions.

* We’ve transferred 500 GB of data in the Google Cloud Platform from London to Australia in 50 seconds.

### Efficient File Transfer and Access

Resilio Platform is a flexible [object storage gateway](https://www.resilio.com/blog/object-storage-gateway-solution) solution that lets you ingest, sync, and access files across any cloud storage provider (including GCP, AWS, Azure, Backblaze, and more).

Additionally, our solution operates in a very efficient way to keep your cloud costs as low as possible. Here’s how:

* **Resilio detects and transfers or syncs only the changed portion of your files**. That way, there’s no unnecessary data being moved across the network.

* **Our solution lets you choose the optimal network for your traffic.** This feature is called Smart Routing and it enables you to move traffic (or just parts of it) to a LAN, instead of keeping it on an expensive WAN.

* **You can download and sync files on demand with Transparent Selective Sync (TSS)**. TSS lets you browse objects stored in Google Storage or any S3-compatible storage as files, select individual files, and download, partially download, or sync them. This granular control is crucial for minimizing unnecessary data transfers.

* **Resilio also lets you store frequently used files locally and keep infrequently used files in long-term cloud file storage.** That way, you don’t have to download frequently accessed files from the cloud every time, which helps you [reduce egress fees](https://www.resilio.com/blog/aws-egress-costs). Files that are not fully downloaded remain in the cloud but still appear local, which saves local storage capacity.

Lastly, Resilio is also a great solution if you want to provide people in your organization with low-latency access to the data they need. This is done through a very simple interface that operates similarly to Microsoft OneDrive, as you can see below.

Using this interface, people in your organization can **access the data they need quickly and efficiently, regardless of where it’s stored**.

For example, say you have key operational data stores in different environments, including on-prem servers and cloud storage services like Azure Blobs, Amazon S3, and Google Storage. Resilio Platform gives your teams a unified view of all that data, while TSS lets them browse, sync, or download the files they want to on-prem devices where they can be cached locally.

### State-of-the-Art Security by Default

Our solution provides end-to-end data protection and encryption for data at rest and in transit. This means there’s no reliance on 3rd-party security tools or services when working with Resilio Connect.

Some of the most essential security features of Resilio include:

* **AES 256 encryption** for data at rest and in transit.

* **Cryptographic data integrity validation** to ensure files arrive uncorrupted and intact.

* **Mutually authenticated endpoints**, meaning endpoints must be pre-approved in order to receive data. That way, data arrives only at its intended destination.

* **Data immutability**, which protects you from ransomware and data loss by storing immutable copies of data in the public cloud.

* **Access management**, so you can set granular permissions that govern who can access, view, edit, and copy your files.

* And much more.

These and all other security features have been reviewed by 3rd-party security experts to ensure their reliability and data protection capabilities.

## Achieve Fast, Reliable, Efficient Transfer and Sync in Any Direction

Resilio Connect’s unique P2P architecture and proprietary WAN optimization technology remove single points of failure, speed up transfers, and overcome latency and packet loss across any network, regardless of distance.

Plus, our solution is installed directly on endpoints, like Windows, Mac, Linux, and Android devices, NAS systems, and more. This makes its deployment much easier compared to GSTS’ method, as you’re not required to use Docker or Linux and can continue working with your existing infrastructure.

Additionally, our solution is:

* **Able to transfer and sync data in any direction,** including one-way, two-way, one-to-many, many-to-one, and n-way.

* **Easy to manage**, because you can control all aspects of data transfer, sync, and access from a single interface. You also get a single point of management and don’t need to manually partition your data, which saves a ton of time and effort.

* **Efficient**, as it only transfers or syncs the changed portion of files, so no unnecessary data gets moved across the network. Plus, you can use features like TSS, Smart Routing, and local storage to make each transfer or sync even more efficient.

* **Flexible**, as you can use it with various storage types, cloud providers, on-prem infrastructures, and hybrid cloud environments. You’re not restricted to any vendor’s ecosystem.

* **Secure**, thanks to AES 256 encryption and other security features that have been verified by 3rd-party security experts.

* **Organically scalable** because it performs better as you add more endpoints.

This is a Resilio blog article by Eleanor Parker comparing Google Cloud Storage Transfer Service (GSTS) with Resilio Platform as an alternative. The article explains how GSTS works (a pay-as-you-go SaaS for transferring files from on-premise to cloud or cloud-to-cloud across GCP, AWS, Azure, and file systems) and details its three main downsides: (1) limited deployment options (agents require Docker on Linux servers/VMs only), (2) time-consuming setup and management for large projects (requires manually partitioning datasets and managing multiple parallel transfers/Linux instances), and (3) differences in transfer features depending on data source/destination (no overwrite option for file system transfers, no name-based/modified-time filtering for file systems, no bandwidth adjustment for cloud-to-cloud transfers).

GSTS supports transfers from Amazon S3, S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, file systems, and public/signed HTTP URLs. It costs $0.0125 per GB transferred for agent-based transfers to/from file systems; agentless transfers and S3-compatible transfers are free. GSTS reduces data transferred by only moving changed files, encrypts data in transit, supports Pub/Sub notifications, and can preserve metadata.

The article then positions Resilio Platform as a superior alternative, highlighting its key advantages: P2P architecture (no single point of failure), cross-platform agent deployment (Windows, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, Android, NAS systems), omnidirectional sync (one-way, two-way, one-to-many, many-to-one, n-way), proprietary UDP-based Zero Gravity Transport (ZGT) WAN optimization protocol, file chunking, Central Management Console for unified job management, and speeds of over 100 Gbps (200 Gbps in early Azure tests; 500 GB transferred from London to Australia in 50 seconds). Resilio's P2P architecture delivers 3-10x faster transfer speeds than traditional solutions, syncs 50% faster than point-to-point in 1:2 scenarios and 500% faster in 1:10 scenarios. Security features include AES 256 encryption, cryptographic integrity validation, mutually authenticated endpoints, data immutability, and granular access management.

Resilio also offers efficient features like detecting/transferring only changed file portions, Smart Routing, Transparent Selective Sync (TSS) for on-demand downloads, local caching, and supports DR use cases with sub-five-second RPOs. Notable customers include Exxon Mobil, 2K Games, Warner Brothers, Cisco, KFC, Mercedes-Benz, Deutsche Aircraft, Northern Marine Group, and MixHits Radio. The page notes Resilio has been acquired by Nasuni.

--- SOURCE 2: Medium ---
URL: https://medium.com/@CloudifyOps/the-7-rs-of-cloud-migration-explained-which-strategy-is-right-for-you-ad2dd90beb7c

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by CloudifyOps (a Cloud & DevOps technology company) provides a comprehensive guide to the "7 Rs of Cloud Migration" — a decision-making framework for categorizing, prioritizing, and executing application migrations to the cloud. The framework evolved from Gartner's original 5 Rs to AWS's 6 Rs, and now includes a 7th strategy called Relocate.

The seven strategies are:
1. **Rehost (Lift and Shift)** — Fastest route; move infrastructure to cloud with minimal changes. Example: financial services firm migrating 200 VMs to AWS EC2 ahead of data centre lease expiry.
2. **Replatform (Lift and Reshape)** — Targeted cloud optimizations without redesigning core architecture. Example: migrating on-premises PostgreSQL to Amazon Aurora.
3. **Refactor/Re-Architect** — Cloud-native rebuild with microservices, stateless architecture, managed services, and CI/CD. Example: logistics platform achieving 10x deployment velocity and 99.99% uptime on Amazon EKS.
4. **Repurchase (Drop and Shop)** — Replace legacy apps with SaaS alternatives (Salesforce for CRM, Workday for HR, ServiceNow for ITSM). Example: manufacturing company replacing 15-year-old CRM with Salesforce.
5. **Retire** — Decommission systems no longer needed. Example: healthcare organization retiring 30 underused applications.
6. **Retain (Revisit Later)** — Keep applications on-premises when compliance constraints or risk outweigh near-term benefits, particularly for government/classified data.
7. **Relocate (Hypervisor Lift, the 7th R)** — Move entire VMware virtualization estates to cloud-hosted environments (VMware Cloud on AWS, Azure VMware Solution) without changing hypervisor, applications, or tooling. Differs from Rehost (which moves VMs to native cloud infrastructure); Relocate moves "the data centre virtually." Example: insurance company migrating 400 VMs with zero changes and zero retraining.

The article provides a four-step framework for choosing strategies: (1) portfolio discovery and assessment, (2) score each application across business criticality, technical complexity, compliance requirements, and cloud/AI readiness, (3) map applications to the 7 Rs, and (4) plan and execute in waves.

It advocates for an industrialized, AI-driven migration platform approach, claiming benefits including: accelerated timelines by 30–50%, reduced modernization rework by 25–40%, and reduced planning effort by 40–60% for refactoring. The article emphasizes AI readiness (API enablement, event-driven compatibility, data extraction capability, architecture modernity) as a migration-time criterion, and presents a four-stage legacy-to-AI-ready journey: Stabilize (Rehost/Relocate), Optimise (Replatform/Repurchase), Modernize (Refactor), and AI-Enable.

Key takeaways: Rehost/Relocate are best for speed and low disruption; Refactor delivers maximum long-term value; Replatform balances effort and benefit; Repurchase accelerates modernization via SaaS; Retire and Retain reduce scope/cost/risk; most enterprises use all seven strategies; and AI-driven platforms bring intelligence and automation to every migration stage.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Azure Migration Strategy: The 6 Rs Explained (Rehost, Replatform, Refactor) ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Apps4Rent (published July 31, 2026) provides a comprehensive guide to Azure migration strategies based on the "6 Rs" framework of cloud migration, which originated from Gartner and was popularized across the industry. The framework consists of six strategies ordered from least to most transformation: Rehost (lift and shift to Azure VMs with no changes), Replatform (move with targeted upgrades to managed services), Refactor/Rearchitect (restructure applications to be cloud-native), Repurchase (replace with SaaS products), Retire (decommission unused workloads), and Retain (keep on-premises for now).

Key highlights include:
- Rehosting involves discovery/dependency mapping, right-sizing via Azure Migrate, replication/test failover, and wave-based cutover. It's best for deadline-driven moves, datacenter exits, or vendor-constrained apps. Azure Hybrid Benefit allows applying existing Windows Server/SQL Server licenses to reduce VM costs.
- Replatforming swaps components for managed services without code rewrites (e.g., SQL Server on VM to Azure SQL Managed Instance, IIS web apps to Azure App Service, file servers to Azure Files, or apps to containers). It delivers the best return per engineering hour.
- A practical rule: "rehost by default when the calendar is the constraint, replatform by default when operations are the constraint." A hybrid pattern (rehost app servers, replatform databases) is often optimal.
- Refactoring is justified only for core business applications with real scaling/deployment needs; Microsoft's guidance is to modernize during migration only when the team has the skills and time, otherwise defer. A plan marking half the portfolio as "refactor" is usually wrong.
- Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework uses 8 strategies (adds rebuild and splits refactor into refactor, rearchitect, and rebuild; renames repurchase to replace), but the underlying per-workload decisions are identical.

The article also outlines a 5-step migration process: (1) inventory everything with Azure Migrate discovery, (2) eliminate retire/repurchase candidates first, (3) assign an R per workload scored on business value and technical fitness, (4) prepare the foundation via Azure landing zone, and (5) migrate in dependency-complete waves with post-migration optimization.

Common mistakes to avoid include blanket rehosting or refactoring, one-to-one sizing, ignoring licensing strategy (Hybrid Benefit, reserved instances), migrating dependencies apart, and having no day-2 plan. --- SOURCE 4: The 7 R's of Cloud Migration | IBM ---
URL: https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/7-rs-cloud-migration

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IBM Think article, published 13 October 2025 by Stephanie Susnjara and Ian Smalley, explains the 7 R's of cloud migration—a framework of seven strategic approaches (rehost, relocate, replatform, refactor, repurchase, retire, retain) for moving applications and workloads to the cloud. Each application has unique architecture, dependencies, and business needs, so the framework helps organizations evaluate each situation and select a migration path balancing speed, cost-efficiency, and long-term value.

**Origin of the 7 R's:** The framework evolved from the initial 5 R's (rehost, refactor, revise, rebuild, replace) introduced by Gartner in 2010. AWS expanded it to 6 R's in 2016 by adding "Retire," then added "Retain" in 2017 to complete the 7 R's. Today most enterprises use hybrid and multicloud strategies.

**Cloud migration overview:** Cloud migration is the process of moving applications, data, workloads, and IT infrastructure from on-premises data centers to cloud-based infrastructure. Benefits include cost optimization, scalability, disaster recovery, business continuity, and access to AI/ML technologies. The global cloud market was valued at USD 752.44 million in 2024 and projected to grow to USD 2,390.19 billion by 2030.

**Types of cloud migration:** data center migration, hybrid cloud migration (which can achieve 2.5 times more value than single public cloud, per IBM IBV report "Mastering Hybrid Cloud"), cloud-to-cloud migration, multicloud migration, and workload-specific migration.

**Challenges:** undocumented dependencies in legacy systems, performance issues, network latency, security and compliance concerns, and skills gaps (approximately 58% of global decision-makers report cloud skills remain a considerable challenge, per an IBM IBV 2023 report). Cloud costs can spiral without proper governance.

**The 7 R's explained:**
1. **Rehost (lift-and-shift):** Moves applications as-is without changing code or architecture, typically via VMs. Best for quick migrations or when lacking resources to rearchitect.
2. **Relocate:** Moves virtual machines directly between environments without modifying applications, typically VMware-based workloads.
3. **Replatform:** Makes targeted optimizations during migration (e.g., migrating SQL databases to managed services like Amazon RDS, or containerizing apps) without changing core architecture.
4. **Refactor (rearchitect):** Completely rearchitects applications into cloud-native solutions, typically breaking monoliths into microservices or adopting serverless computing, working with DevOps practices.
5. **Repurchase (drop-and-shop):** Replaces existing applications with cloud-based SaaS alternatives.
6. **Retire:** Identifies and decommissions applications no longer needed, eliminating unnecessary costs.
7. **Retain (revisit):** Keeps applications on-premises for now, with plans to revisit migration later—applies to recently upgraded/stable apps, apps with compliance issues, or complex dependencies.

**Strategy guidance:** Effective migration starts with comprehensive discovery and assessment. Organizations typically begin with low-risk, quick-win applications to build momentum, then migrate complex apps later. Plans should include success criteria, rollback procedures, data migration planning, and stakeholder coordination. Governance and cost management frameworks (resource tagging, budget alerts, regular cost reviews) should be established before migration begins.

**Tools and partners:** Cloud providers offer tools like AWS Application Migration Service, IBM Cloud migration services, and Azure Migrate. Ecosystem partners (IBM, Microsoft, managed service providers, system integrators) extend capabilities with specialized expertise.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: The 7 Rs of Cloud Migration: 7 Strategies Explained |  NetApp ---
URL: https://www.netapp.com/blog/aws-cvo-blg-strategies-for-aws-migration-the-new-7th-r-explained

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from NetApp (authored by Sudip Sengupta) explains the "7 Rs of Cloud Migration" — a framework of strategies for moving applications and data from on-premises infrastructure to the cloud. The 7 strategies are: rehost, relocate, replatform, refactor, repurchase, retire, and retain.

The framework has evolved over time: Gartner first introduced the 5 Rs model in the early days of cloud computing. AWS expanded it to a 6 Rs model by adding "Retire," then introduced the 7 Rs model by adding "Retain" (recognizing that not all workloads should move to the cloud).

The seven strategies in detail:
1. **Rehost ("Lift and Shift")** — Move on-prem applications and dependencies as-is to cloud IaaS without changing core infrastructure; easy for enterprises lacking cloud-native expertise.
2. **Relocate ("Hypervisor-Level Lift and Shift")** — Migrate server collections (e.g., VMware or Kubernetes) to cloud versions of the same platform (e.g., GKE, EKS) with minimal downtime and no source code rewrites.
3. **Replatform ("Lift and Reshape")** — Move applications to cloud with some platform optimization while keeping source code and core architecture unchanged; enables cloud-native capabilities like automation.
4. **Refactor ("Re-architect")** — Re-architect workloads from the ground up for cloud-native capabilities (serverless, autoscaling, distributed load balancing); most complex and costly but most future-proof; often breaks monoliths into microservices.
5. **Repurchase ("Drop and Shop")** — Swap internally administered systems for third-party managed SaaS services from the cloud provider; reduces operational overhead and ties IT costs to revenue.
6. **Retire** — Terminate or downsize applications no longer useful in production; first step toward modern cloud-native adoption.
7. **Retain ("Revisit")** — Keep workloads on-premises when they cannot be retired or migrated (due to dependencies, compliance, security, or lack of immediate business value).

The article includes a detailed comparison table covering use-cases, pros, and cons of each strategy. Key considerations include: Retire is cheapest but risks incompatibility with interconnected stacks; Relocate is quickest but limits cloud-native capabilities; Refactor is best for high-usability complex applications but requires extensive planning, training, and monitoring.

The article concludes by highlighting NetApp's solutions for supporting AWS cloud migration and provides links to NetApp's guide to migrating enterprise workloads and cloud migration case studies.
</summary>

The 7 Rs of cloud migration are a set of strategies designed to help organizations plan, execute, and optimize their migration projects. The 7 cloud migration strategies are: rehost, relocate, replatform, refactor, repurchase, retire, and retain.

--- SOURCE 6: Lift and Shift vs. Re-architect: Cloud Migration Guide ---
URL: https://thecompetenza.com/blog/lift-and-shift-vs-rearchitect-cloud-migration-strategy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a detailed blog article from The Competenza (a software development and cloud migration services company with offices in the USA, UAE, Australia, and India) published June 25, 2026, by Nishant Agrawal. The article provides a comprehensive comparison of two cloud migration strategies: Lift and Shift (rehosting) vs. Re-architecting (refactoring).

**Key Content:**

**Lift and Shift (Rehosting):**
- Definition: Transferring applications to the cloud with minimal or no code changes
- Cost range: $40,000–$150,000+ (small business apps $40K-75K, mid-sized enterprise $75K-120K, large enterprise workloads $120K-150K+)
- Benefits: Rapid migration, lower development costs, reduced business risk, rapid payback, enables data center exits
- Disadvantages: Technical debt carries over, limited cloud optimization, greater long-term costs, scalability limitations, reduced innovation potential
- Best for: data center consolidation, M&A integrations, time-sensitive projects, tight budgets, cloud-first initiatives, stable/low-change applications

**Re-architecting (Refactoring):**
- Definition: Redesigning applications to fully leverage cloud-native technologies, microservices, containers, and serverless computing
- Cost range: $200,000–$600,000+ (small modernization $200K-300K, mid-sized $300K-500K, large complex systems $600K+)
- Benefits: Cloud-native scalability, better performance, reduced long-term costs, improved security, AI/automation readiness, reduced technical debt
- Disadvantages: Higher initial capital, extended timeframes (months to years), increased complexity, change management requirements
- Best for: growth-focused organizations, legacy systems with high technical debt, SaaS product development, digital transformation projects

**Comparison Highlights:**
- Lift and shift: faster migration (weeks vs. months), lower upfront cost, but higher long-term operating costs and limited cloud-native capability
- Re-architect: slower, higher initial investment, but superior long-term ROI, scalability, performance, security, and AI-readiness
- Re-architect is the better option for nearly all long-term factors (infrastructure, maintenance, operational, scalability, security, technical debt, long-term ROI); lift and shift wins on initial migration costs and short-term ROI

**Security Considerations:**
- Lift and shift risks: legacy security gaps, excessive user permissions, poor cloud configurations (misconfigured storage buckets, firewalls, unsecured APIs), limited cloud-native security features
- Re-architecting enables zero-trust access, encryption, automated checks, microservices isolation, and DevSecOps (automated security testing, continuous compliance monitoring, secure CI/CD pipelines)
- HIPAA (PHI protection, encryption, audit logs, access controls) and GDPR (data privacy, consent management, breach notifications, data residency) compliance must be planned from the start

**Cloud Provider Perspectives:**
- AWS: best for fastest lift and shift migration, legacy app migration, enterprise digital transformation, cloud-native development (EKS, Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, Aurora)
- Azure: best for Microsoft-centric infrastructure, hybrid cloud, .NET modernization, regulated industries (Azure Migrate, Site Recovery, AKS, Functions, Cosmos DB)
- Google Cloud: best for AI/ML projects, Kubernetes/microservices, data-intensive workloads (Migrate to VMs, GKE, Cloud Run, Vertex AI, BigQuery)

**Recommendation Framework:**
- Choose lift and shift for speedy cloud adoption, reduced initial expenses, minimal business impact
- Choose re-architect for digital transformation, cloud-native innovation, AI-readiness, scalability, long-term value
- Choose a hybrid approach (recommended for most enterprises) to move stable workloads quickly via lift and shift while re-architecting mission-critical applications

The article includes 7 questions for business leaders and 7 questions for IT teams to consider when choosing a migration strategy, plus a per-workload framework. The company notes it has delivered 300+ solutions for 150+ global businesses across fintech, education, eCommerce, healthcare, and logistics industries.
</summary>

- Lift & Shift: Lower upfront cost (~$30k/year maintenance due to legacy system inefficiencies) but higher ongoing costs.

1. Audit current systems (performance, cost, scalability, compatibility)
2. Set clear goals (e.g., reduce IT costs by 20-30%, improve flexibility)
3. Compare both options against goals (Lift & Shift = fast/low risk; Re-architecture = long-term efficiency)
4. Pilot with a low-risk component (test with sample data before full migration)
5. Choose based on pilot results—Lift & Shift for short-term needs, Re-architecture for long-term goals

--- SOURCE 8: Lift and shift vs re-platform vs re-architect: choosing the right cloud migration strategy | Sequentur ---
URL: https://www.sequentur.com/lift-and-shift-vs-re-platform-vs-re-architect-choosing-the-right-cloud-migration-strategy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Sequentur blog article (an IT managed services provider) providing a detailed guide on cloud migration strategies for small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs). The core thesis is that migration strategy must be decided per-workload, not per-project, and that the "cheapest strategy that delivers what the business needs" is the right approach.

The article covers five migration strategies that matter for SMBs (drawn from the cloud industry's "6 R's" framework):
1. **Retire** - turn the workload off entirely (lowest cost, highest ROI per dollar)
2. **Retain** - leave the workload on-prem (for latency, compliance, or cost reasons)
3. **Repurchase** - replace with a SaaS equivalent (often the most underrated strategy)
4. **Lift-and-shift (rehost)** - move unchanged to a cloud VM (fastest, lowest risk, but no operational savings)
5. **Re-platform** - move with some cloud-native features adopted (moderate effort, the "sweet spot" for most SMB workloads)
6. **Re-architect (refactor)** - rebuild cloud-native (highest cost, only for core business apps with 5-10 year horizons)

A sixth "R" (Relocate - moving VMware to managed VMware-on-cloud) is noted but dismissed as overkill for SMBs in the 15-250 employee range.

Key data points include:
- Lift-and-shift: $3,000-$15,000 per single Windows Server migration; often costs slightly MORE per year than on-prem due to ongoing cloud bills with no operational changes; 1-4 weeks per workload
- Re-platform: 30-80% more project effort than lift-and-shift; $10,000-$40,000 for SQL workloads; operational savings recoup the higher one-time cost in 12-24 months; 4-16 weeks per workload
- Re-architect: 5-20 times the cost of lift-and-shift; typically $150,000-$750,000 for a line-of-business app at a 40-person business; 6-24 months timeline
- Typical full SMB migration combining multiple strategies lands in the 3-to-9-month range

The article provides a per-workload decision tree: (1) does anyone use it? No → Retire; (2) should it be in cloud at all? No → Retain; (3) does a mature SaaS exist? Yes → Repurchase; (4) critical, 5+ years, architecturally limited? Yes → Re-architect; (5) can it run on managed service? Yes → Re-platform; (6) default → Lift-and-shift.

A worked example uses a 40-person law firm with 11 workloads showing a realistic mix: 4 retire/retain, 4 repurchases (email→M365, file server→SharePoint/OneDrive, document management→NetDocuments/iManage, time/billing→Clio/Centerbase), 2 re-platforms (SQL→Azure SQL DB, Active Directory→hybrid Entra), 1 lift-and-shift (practice management app), and 1 retain (specialty discovery review tool).

The article lists 10 common migration mistakes, including picking one strategy for the whole project, lift-and-shifting everything, re-architecting the wrong workload, skipping repurchase evaluation, forgetting retire/retain, and letting the platform (Azure vs AWS) pick the strategy. The piece concludes with Sequentur's promotional content, client testimonials, and FAQs about their managed IT services.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The right migration is the one that uses the cheapest strategy that delivers what the business needs for that specific workload, not the most ambitious strategy applied across the board."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an informational guide from vFunction (a cloud and application modernization company) titled "Migration Strategies Basics: Lift and Shift, Refactor, or Replace?" It serves as a comprehensive resource for organizations considering application modernization and cloud migration strategies.

**Key context:** The article notes that industry analyst IDG reports "Application/legacy system modernization" has risen to become a top priority for CIOs in 2022, driven by the pace of technology innovation and accelerated by the pandemic. Gartner defines application modernization services as addressing "the migration of legacy to new applications or platforms," including re-platforming, re-hosting, recoding, rearchitecting, re-engineering, interoperability, replacement, and retirement.

**Why modernize:** The article explains that monolithic applications (defined as apps with all or most functionality within a single process or container) often represent core business functionality and significant revenue. Companies modernize to enhance user experience, keep employees productive, protect sensitive data, and gain cloud benefits like scaling and security.

**Assessing legacy applications:** Gartner recommends evaluating six factors:
- Business fit (competitors modernizing and gaining market share)
- Business value (modular architectures allow faster value delivery)
- Agility (accelerated development and time-to-market)
- Cost (pay-as-you-go model lowers operating costs)
- Complexity (tight coupling in monoliths makes changes difficult)
- Risk (changes to monoliths can have unpredictable downstream effects)

**Migration/modernization strategies covered:**
1. **Encapsulation** – Makes application features accessible as APIs without modernizing the underlying system; a stop-gap approach that accrues technical debt.
2. **Lift and Shift** (includes rehost and replatform) – Moving apps to the cloud; the article cautions this "genuinely does not modernize anything" and can simply move technical debt to the cloud.
3. **Rehost** – Migrating without modifying code, data, or functionality; quick but risks disruption and poor early user experiences.
4. **Replatform** – Minimal code changes to run on a new platform (e.g., newer OS); cheaper and lower-risk but requires automation and careful scope control.
5. **Refactor** – Reorganizing and optimizing existing code to reduce technical debt and improve performance, security, and usability; provides long-term cost savings and ROI but requires advanced skills and carries risk of errors.
6. **Rearchitect** – Breaking applications into microservices for individual cloud migration; offers flexibility and scaling but requires significant investment and automation tools.
7. **Rewrite** – Rebuilding applications while retaining intellectual property and unique selling propositions; substantial time and expense investment.
8. **Replace** – Swapping to a new SaaS or software solution; reduces maintenance burden but may face user adoption challenges and loss of customization.

**Company positioning:** The article concludes by promoting vFunction's AI-driven platform and "factory model purpose-built for cloud-native modernization," which helps software architects incrementally modernize legacy application portfolios. The page also links to vFunction resources including a 2025 report on "Architecture in Software Development: Rethinking the Role of Architecture in the Age of AI" and case studies on modernizing Fortune 500 applications.

--- SOURCE 2: Azure Hybrid Benefit - Azure SQL Database & SQL Managed Instance | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/azure-hybrid-benefit?view=azuresql

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Learn documentation page about the Azure Hybrid Benefit for Azure SQL Database and SQL Managed Instance. The Azure Hybrid Benefit allows customers to allocate their SQL Server licenses (with Software Assurance) to Azure SQL Database and SQL Managed Instance, saving up to 30 percent or more on these services. Enabling the benefit requires no downtime.

**Key details:**
- Azure Hybrid Benefit is only available for the provisioned compute tier of the vCore-based purchasing model for Azure SQL Database. It does not apply to the DTU-based purchasing model or the serverless compute tier.
- Enabling the benefit for Azure SQL Database can be done via Azure portal (select "Save money" option), PowerShell (New-AzSqlDatabase/Set-AzSqlDatabase with -LicenseType), Azure CLI (az sql db create with --license-type), or REST API (properties.licenseType parameter).
- Enabling the benefit for Azure SQL Managed Instance can be done via Azure portal (select "Azure Hybrid Benefit" option), PowerShell (New-AzSqlInstance/Set-AzSqlInstance with -LicenseType), Azure CLI (az sql mi create/update with --license-type), or REST API (properties.licenseType parameter).

**FAQ highlights:**
- There is a 180-day migration allowance for licenses; after that period, the SQL Server license can only be used on Azure.
- Azure Hybrid Benefit differs from license mobility in two ways: it provides economic benefits for moving highly virtualized workloads to Azure (Enterprise Edition customers get 4 cores in Azure General Purpose SKU for every core owned on-premises for highly virtualized applications), and it provides a PaaS destination (SQL Managed Instance) highly compatible with SQL Server.
