# Control Tower and Security Hub

In a large environment that is highly secure, how do you deal with Control Tower and Security Hub for the Security OU accounts. ( audit and log archive) In many environments Risk teams require compliance to a particular framework (NIST 800.53 or others) in ALL accounts and not just the workloads. The problem is Control Tower does not manage and cant turn on controls in the management or Security OU by design. So my thought was to centralize Security Hub for the org and delegate to the audit account. This means Control Tower cant manage any SH controls because it cant create the standard in a given account since it enables each account individually.

I have engaged support and the are pushing towards letting Control Tower manage and enable Security Hub manually in each account that it cant. This is problematic because you must enable the entire standard and no option to limit controls, so lots of noise and no central management. How do others manage this in secure environments? I want to hear how others deal with this.

[User-4258384](/community/users/US217UTmFNR-G-_xuG0ZHBzg)

asked a year ago946 views

Hello,

For environments where Security Hub compliance is required across ALL accounts (including management and security accounts), AWS Support confirms:

Key Issue:

Two Supported Solutions:

Important: Security Hub central configuration should NOT be used with Control Tower as they are incompatible and work against best practices.

![AWS](/static/icons/common/aws_logo_rgb_squid.svg)

[Harika](/community/users/USqI_zwAwNQaOiQjNyCyf_Lw)

answered a year ago

Thank you for your response. I had heard a similar response as I discussed with colleagues but it just seemed counter-intuitive to have to turn on Security Hub in each of these accounts (management, audit, and logarchive) individually. I am already using CfCT for bootstrap but have the landing zone in terraform. I can use either for this purpose. I don't want to do anything against practice hence why I was going to lengths to get definitive answers. I am having a call with the aws Control Tower team next week and no doubt I will hear the same answer.

Regards,
Andy

I’d like to expand on my previous comment after speaking with the AWS Control Tower team. The solution really depends on your specific use case.

In highly secure environments where Control Tower's native controls are not sufficient, it is absolutely valid to manage AWS Security Hub centrally and independently of Control Tower, as I previously described. There is no technical conflict as long as you have no intention of using Control Tower to enable and manage Security Hub controls.

By default, Control Tower enables a standard in Security Hub that includes only a subset of the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. In environments that require strict adherence to frameworks like NIST 800-53, this is often inadequate. Furthermore, Control Tower does not currently offer the flexibility to automate or suppress findings at scale within Security Hub, nor can you enable Security Hub controls in the Security OU through Control Tower. These limitations can make it impractical for certain organizations with more advanced compliance needs. As a result, managing the NIST standard directly within Security Hub—outside of Control Tower—is often the more viable approach.

A few caveats to be aware of:

Once you choose to manage Security Hub independently, you won’t be able to re-enable its controls through Control Tower. That said, this is generally acceptable if you’ve made an intentional decision to operate outside the Control Tower framework for any non-mandatory controls.

If you are using the Landing Zone Accelerator, it will attempt to manage Security Hub through Control Tower by default. However, this can be overridden by implementing your own custom stacks.

AWS Support does not typically provide detailed guidance on this topic, other than what I was told by them initially and what the answer was here. I understand why but sometimes you need to dig deeper. I had to speak directly with someone on the Control Tower team to gain deeper insights. Ultimately, the answer is not straightforward—it really depends on the environment and specific compliance or security posture required. The main point in all this is that it is fine to use Security Hub independently in an environment with Control Tower as long as you are aware of the tradeoffs.

Side Note:
There are also recurring issues with Control Tower not fully complying with certain frameworks in the resources it provisions, particularly in the Security and Management accounts. For example, the default S3 buckets or SNS topics may lack customer-managed keys (CMKs), which often raises concerns with internal risk and security teams. While there are compensating controls in place, these gaps can be frustrating to explain and justify.

I hope this helps others who are navigating similar questions. It's been a bit of a journey to uncover these details, especially since much of this information isn’t well-documented. As always, you learn the most by building, experimenting, and observing how different architectural patterns behave in real-world environments. As a consultant, I get to see a wide range of use cases and approaches, which helps shape this perspective.

Best regards,
Andy

# Set up multi-account management with AWS Control Tower

#### Set up a Landing Zone with AWS Control Tower

Using [AWS Control Tower](https://aws.amazon.com/controltower/features) you can implement a multi-account scheme, as recommended by best practices, where you can centrally enforce policies (guardrails) while you centralize and protect AWS Cloudtrail logs in a designated logging account.

#### Multi-Account / Organizational Structure

Make sure your workloads are dividen into multiple accounts leaving a set of core accounts (logging, audit, backups, networking, etc.) that will provide support for all accounts, and a set of (dev-test-prod) per business unit, or workload. If you have “THE production account” start working towards moving workloads to separate accounts to reduce the blast radius on potential security incidents.

#### Delegated Administration - Services integrated to AWS Organizations

The following services are integrated to AWS Organizations (AWS Control Tower uses AWS Organizations) and support delegated administration, therefore, the security team can have visibility about the security and compliance of the whole organization from the security account:

* AWS Security Hub
* Amazon GuardDuty
* Amazon Macie
* Amazon Detective
* AWS Firewall Manager
* IAM Access Analyzer
* Amazon Inspector
* AWS Audit Manager

#### AWS Control Tower deployment in existing organization

If you have an existing organization you can still enable AWS Control Tower.

#### One account to an Organization with Control Tower

If you have all in one account, set up control tower in a new account, and add the account to the organization. It’s not advisable to configure AWS Control Tower on an account that has workloads, as the management account (org-root) is not affected by SCPs, and should not be accessed all the time.

* If workloads are not separated into a multi-account structure the blast radius grows.

* Have you implemented AWS Control Tower ?
* Are you isolating your workloads in multiple accounts ?
* Is there a particular account in your organization that has most of the workloads of the organization ?

#### Pricing

Note: if you can’t enable AWS Control Tower as you need additional Flexibility / Personaliation of the account, then you can leverage the following solution: [Landing Zone Accelerator on AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/implementations/landing-zone-accelerator-on-aws/)

## [AWS Cloud Operations Blog](/blogs/mt/)

# AWS offerings available to support your cloud migration

With over a million active customers, AWS has experience helping organizations of all sizes migrate workloads to the cloud. A common theme is that selecting the right tools is crucial for reducing risk and enabling a reliable migration. In this blog post, I will select some of the most popular AWS migration tools and outline how they can be used to support your cloud migration. It’s worth noting that it’s common for a single application to utilize multiple tools during a migration. I fully encourage you to review what might apply to your scenario. This blog post will introduce you to:

### An on-premises application stack comprises a Windows 2008 R2 presentation server, a Windows 2022 application server, a Windows File Server, and a MS-SQL 2019 database. This application is migrating to an Amazon EC2 instance for the presentation and application tier, Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, and an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database

![An on-premises application stack comprises a Windows 2008 R2 presentation server, a Windows 2022 application server, a Windows File Server, and a MS-SQL 2019 database. This application is migrating to an Amazon EC2 instance for the presentation and application tier, Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, and an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/09/CO_706_1.jpg)

## Solution overview

Throughout this post, a hypothetical application will be used as an example to demonstrate the use case for each migration tool. In this scenario, the application needs to be migrated as soon as possible due to business pressures. However, each of the components comes with its complexity or requirements:

### 

## AWS Application Discovery Service (ADS)

When approaching a migration, it’s common to find limited information available regarding your on-premises components. Discovery tooling provides an opportunity to uncover or validate data about the servers which will be migrated. This then enables data-driven architectures and decisions to be made. AWS Application Discovery Service helps you plan your migration to AWS by collecting usage and configuration data about your on-premises servers. This includes server data, performance data, and dependency data when the agent option is deployed to the server.

In a migration scenario, AWS ADS is commonly used to validate that there are no missing dependencies. Regarding the hypothetical application, let’s imagine that there is a reporting server that the application frequently connects to, unbeknown to the application team. AWS ADS will show the connections that are being established, helping you uncover servers which have been missed from the migration scope. In the proceeding image, the ADS discovery has been visulised in [AWS Migration Hub](/migration-hub/), showing a wide range of servers connecting to the server where the agent is deployed. This provides a backlog for investigation by the application and migration team.

You can use the AWS Application Discovery Service to discover your on-premises servers at no charge. You only pay for the AWS resources that are provisioned to store your on-premises data.

![AWS ADS discovery data visualized in AWS Migration Hub, showing that a single server has many connections to different IP addresses.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/16/ads_replacement.png)

![AWS ADS discovery data visualized in AWS Migration Hub, showing that a single server has many connections to different IP addresses.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/16/ads_replacement.png)

### 

## End-of-Support Migration Program for Windows Server (EMP)

Using a Windows in place upgrade to modernize your end of support servers may not be a straightforward solution if your legacy application has compatibility issues with newer Windows versions. Even if the application is compatible with the newer Windows versions, it would not be possible to migrate it if you don’t have access to up-to-date installation media and installation steps. Further, having an application that can run only on an unsupported version of Windows Server is problematic as you will no longer get free security patch updates. It is difficult to move an application like this to the cloud without significant code changes, which increases the level of effort and timelines to migrate. AWS offers the End-of-Support Migration Program (EMP) for Windows Server to assist:

EMP for Windows Server includes tooling to migrate your legacy applications from Windows Server 2003, 2008, and 2008 R2 to newer, supported versions on AWS, without any code changes. The EMP tool identifies the dependencies your application has on the outdated OS and creates a package that includes the resources necessary for the application to run on the newer version of Windows Server. The package includes all the application files, runtimes, components, deployment tools, and an engine that redirects the API calls from your application to a registry as well as files within the package. This resolves the dependencies and decouples the application from the underlying OS. This enables you to run the packaged application on future version of Windows Server, meaning you don’t have to worry about upgrading these applications when the next end of support event for Windows Server arrives.

![A legacy application has been converted into an EMP compatibility package which includes redirection for the Windows API calls.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/09/CO_706_3.png)

![A legacy application has been converted into an EMP compatibility package which includes redirection for the Windows API calls.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/09/CO_706_3.png)

Going back to the example, using the AWS EMP toolset the legacy application running on the Windows Server 2008 R2 presentation server will be decoupled from the operating system, captured into an EMP package and deployed onto the latest version of Windows Server on AWS.

If you have legacy applications running on end of support Windows servers in scope for AWS migration, I encourage you to read our [EMP documentation](/emp-windows-server/). To gain hands on experience using the tool or if you need support to get started with your EMP journey, please [complete this form](https://pages.awscloud.com/windows-eos-contact-us.html).

### 

## AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)

AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) enables you to rehost a wide range of servers from your source environment to Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) in a highly automated fashion. Install the AWS MGN replication agent on your source server and define the replication settings. This then commences a continuous block-based data replication to a staging area in your AWS account. Once the data fully replicates, you can launch your target Amazon EC2 instance(s), which automatically converts to run on AWS. Using AWS MGN helps minimize time-intensive, error-prone manual processes when rehosting servers.

![An architecture diagram shows applications migrated from an on-premises data center to AWS. Continuous data transfer occurs from the source server(s) to the replication server(s) within a staging area subnet on TCP 1500. Migrated instances reside in the target subnet.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/09/CO_706_4.png)

![An architecture diagram shows applications migrated from an on-premises data center to AWS. Continuous data transfer occurs from the source server(s) to the replication server(s) within a staging area subnet on TCP 1500. Migrated instances reside in the target subnet.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/09/CO_706_4.png)

AWS MGN has a wide range of [supported operating systems](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/Supported-Operating-Systems.html) and can simplify your migration by enabling you to use the same automated process and pattern for many applications. Taking this a step further, AWS has developed a [Cloud Migration Factory](/solutions/implementations/aws-cloudendure-migration-factory-solution/) solution that provides additional automation to facilitate migrating hundreds or thousands of servers to AWS at pace.

In the hypothetical application, we will leverage AWS MGN to perform the migration of the Windows 2022 application server. Despite no longer having the source code or installation media, we can still migrate this server via AWS MGN. This enables the server to be migrated with minimal effort, allowing the application team to dedicate effort to the other components which require more change.

For each source server you want to migrate, you can use AWS Application Migration Service for a free period of 2,160 hours, which is 90 days when used continuously.

### 

## AWS DataSync

Migrating data to the cloud often requires you to dedicate time, budget, and employee resources. In our example application, we need to migrate data from a Windows File Server to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, a fully managed and highly performant file system. However, the data is frequently changing due to it being a live system, which adds to the complexity of the migration. To simplify and alleviate the challenges above, AWS DataSync will be leveraged. It is an online data transfer service that automates, and accelerates moving data between on-premises and AWS storage services. Given it performs incremental transfers of data, it makes it ideally suited to migrate active file systems.

When using AWS DataSync, you first configure an agent to read data from the on-premises system (in our case, the Windows File Server). Next, configure a task to transfer files from on-premises to your target AWS location (in our case, Amazon FSx for Windows File Server). Finally, you can start the data transfer task to replicate the data. Using task scheduling in AWS DataSync, you can periodically execute a transfer task from your source storage system to the destination. For example, you may schedule your data migration to occur every hour. There’s then a recent copy of the data in the target to enable application testing before cutover.

I encourage you to [view the storage systems supported by DataSync](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/what-is-datasync.html), and review our [pricing information for your region](/datasync/pricing/).

### 

## AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)

There is a strong business desire to migrate from Microsoft SQL Server 2019 to an open-source alternative in the hypothetical application. It can be challenging to understand how compatible your source database is with a different target database engine without using tooling. Further, once the compatibility has been understood, the schema and other objects’ conversion must occur. That makes heterogeneous migrations a two-step process. First, use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool ([free download](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/SchemaConversionTool/latest/userguide/CHAP_Installing.html) available on the AWS website) to convert the source schema and code to match the target database. Then use the AWS Database Migration Service (discussed underneath) to migrate data from the source database to the target database.

Alongside offering an automated schema conversion, AWS SCT provides the option to generate an assessment report to understand the complexity and level of effort required to migrate to a given database engine. The image underneath is a screenshot of the executive summary from a sample SCT assessment report. In this example, 90% of the database storage object and 77% of the database code objects can be converted automatically or with minimal changes. Additionally, the areas with complex actions required are highlighted. Using the assessment enables a data-driven approach for your migration. Where you’re performing many heterogeneous database migrations, I recommend running the assessment process against the entire scope to identify quick wins.

![A Database Migration Assessment Report generated from AWS SCT, showing 90% of the database storage object and 77% of the database code objects can be converted automatically or with minimal changes.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/09/CO_706_5.png)

![A Database Migration Assessment Report generated from AWS SCT, showing 90% of the database storage object and 77% of the database code objects can be converted automatically or with minimal changes.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/09/CO_706_5.png)

### 

## AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)

Like the Windows File System, databases can sometimes be challenging to migrate. They store live data that will frequently be changing during the migration project. AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) is the service that can help you migrate databases to AWS quickly and securely. The source database remains fully operational during the migration, minimizing downtime to applications that rely on the database. You only pay for your replication instances and any additional log storage. Each database migration instance includes storage sufficient for swap space, replication logs, and data cache for most replications, and inbound data transfer is free.

AWS Database Migration Service supports homogeneous migrations such as Oracle to Oracle and heterogeneous migrations between different database platforms. In this example, coupling DMS with SCT will enable a heterogeneous migration from Microsoft SQL Server to PostgreSQL. AWS DMS handles all required data type conversions automatically during the migration.

If you have databases to migrate, I encourage you to view the [DMS sources for data migration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Source.html).

## Conclusion

I outlined several AWS migration tools available to simplify your migrations throughout this post. Although I focused on a single application stack, the tools are frequently applied to handle some of the largest migrations, such as data center closures. Using AWS tooling can help simplify your migration, make it more predictable, and accelerate achieving the business goals with a lower level of risk. I highly recommend you explore the tools and services available to see if they can assist in achieving your migration goals.

It’s also worth noting that this is only a subset of our migration tooling and services! Consider exploring additional offerings such as:

**Author:**

![](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2022/05/16/Damien-Renner_author-1.jpg)

Damien is a Migration Specialist for the Migration, Modernization and Management Global Speciality Practice at AWS. He works with enterprises to understand their target business outcomes and transforms them into technology solutions.

![Damien Renner](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/972a67c48192728a34979d9a35164c1295401b71/2023/06/02/rendamie-blog.jpg)

[Migrating to the cloud is a big decision](https://stratusgrid.com/blog/benefits-of-cloud-migration), but the initial migration costs can seem intimidating. But what if you could not only gracefully streamline your migration process but also **save money** while doing it?

AWS understands the cost challenges in cloud migrations and offers a suite of programs designed to make your cloud transition as smooth and cost-effective as possible.

Let's explore these valuable programs and how they can make your cloud journey more affordable.

## Your AWS Migration Savings Toolkit

AWS has designed several solutions to support your organization throughout your [migration journey](https://stratusgrid.com/aws-cloud-migration) by providing **financial incentives, technical expertise, and migration tools.**

By leveraging these programs, organizations can achieve a cost-effective and streamlined migration to the AWS cloud.

The [AWS Migration Acceleration Program (MAP)](https://stratusgrid.com/blog/aws-migration-acceleration-program-map) is a comprehensive, proven cloud migration initiative based on AWS’s extensive experience in migrating thousands of enterprise customers.

[AWS MAP](https://aws.amazon.com/migration-acceleration-program/) provides enterprises undertaking substantial cloud migrations with tools to reduce costs, as well as automate and speed up implementation. If your infrastructure includes Windows servers, the [AWS Windows Migration Accelerator](https://aws.amazon.com/application-migration-service/windows/) program is tailor-made for you. Many organizations struggle to maintain legacy applications running on **unsupported Windows Server versions**. The [End-of-Support Migration Program (EMP) for Windows Server](https://aws.amazon.com/emp-windows-server/) offers a solution by providing tools that enable you to migrate these applications to newer, supported versions on AWS without the need for complex code changes.

Leveraging these tools ensures your critical applications remain secure, functional, and compliant.

Are you looking to move to the AWS cloud? [Contact us at StratusGrid](https://stratusgrid.com/book-a-consultation) to start assessing your current situation and build a migration plan that works for you.

## Practical Tips for a Cost-Effective Migration to the AWS Cloud

While AWS migration programs pave the way for a smooth transition, your journey toward cost efficiency doesn't end there. Think of it as optimizing your travel budget—even with a great deal on flights and hotels, you still need to be mindful of daily expenses.

Similarly, **once you're on AWS**, a proactive approach to [cost management](https://stratusgrid.com/aws-cloud-cost-optimization) can unlock even greater savings.

* **Uses Reserved Instances and Savings Plans:** Utilize these pricing models to secure discounts for predictable workloads. If your workloads are predictable, AWS offers a rewards program for your loyalty. Reserved Instances (RIs) and Savings Plans allow you to commit to a certain level of usage in exchange for significant discounts.

* **Leverage Cost Optimization Tools:** Leverage AWS Cost Explorer and Trusted Advisor to monitor your cloud spending and identify opportunities for optimization. Just as you'd create a budget for a vacation, it's crucial to establish a solid cloud financial management plan. By staying on top of your cloud finances, you'll avoid unpleasant surprises and keep your cloud journey enjoyable and financially sustainable.

Remember, cost optimization isn't a one-time activity. It's an ongoing process that requires continuous monitoring, analysis, and adjustments.

3. **Transferring Large Datasets** - Use Google Cloud's Storage Transfer Service for automated data movement (supports scheduling and security), or Transfer Appliance (a high-capacity server shipped to the customer's location) for extremely large datasets where network constraints make online transfers impractical.

5. **Migrating to Automated, Containerized Deployments** - Leverage Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to automate deployment/scaling/management; containers encapsulate code/config/dependencies; use CI/CD pipelines for automatic build, test, and deployment.

- **Plan for Gradual Rollouts**: Migrate small groups in phases, use traffic splitting/versioning to redirect portions of user traffic gradually.
- **Prepare Dev and Ops Teams**: Maintain communication channels, provide training and resources on GCP technologies.
- **Define How to Retire the Source Environment**: Verify data integrity, test all applications, confirm backup/DR mechanisms in GCP, and obtain formal stakeholder approval before decommissioning.
- **Streamline Deployment**: Establish CI/CD pipelines, adopt infrastructure-as-code (IaC), and containerize workloads for uniform environments.

This is a technical blog post by Nawaz Dhandala (founder of OneUptime) published February 17, 2026, providing a complete walkthrough for migrating petabytes of on-premises data to Google Cloud Storage (GCS) using Google Transfer Appliance. The article argues that for datasets requiring more than a week to transfer over a network, physically shipping data via Transfer Appliance is the most practical and cost-effective option.

KEY FACTS:
- Network transfer is impractical for petabyte-scale data: a 1 PB transfer over a dedicated 10 Gbps connection takes ~10 days at full bandwidth (realistically longer), and 500 TB over a 1 Gbps connection at 80% utilization takes ~58 days.
- Transfer Appliance comes in two sizes: TA40 (40 TB usable) and TA300 (300 TB usable); multiple appliances can be used in parallel for petabyte-scale migrations.

STEP-BY-STEP PROCESS (7 steps):
1. Plan the migration: calculate data volume, count files (small files under 1KB transfer slower), check for files exceeding the 5 TB max size limit, and create destination GCS buckets (e.g., using gcloud storage buckets create with appropriate storage classes like STANDARD and NEARLINE).
2. Order the appliance through Google Cloud Console, select size, provide shipping details, and prepare the data center (network ports of 10/40/100 GbE, power, physical space, staff access).
3. Connect and configure the appliance: it gets an IP via DHCP or static IP, is accessed via CLI, supports NFS/SMB/SCP/SFTP file share modes, and presents as an NFS mount point.
4. Load data using rsync or cp, running multiple parallel transfers for maximum throughput (e.g., using GNU parallel with -j 8); tune NFS options (rsize=1048576, wsize=1048576) and consider tar archiving for many small files.
5. Verify data with checksums (md5sum comparisons), unmount the appliance, and run "ta finalize" which encrypts data at rest using AES-256 with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK); enter the returned passcode in Google's return instructions form.
6. Monitor ingestion in Cloud Console, with email notifications from Google and optional Pub/Sub notifications (e.g., OBJECT_FINALIZE event type).
7. Validate migrated data by comparing file counts and spot-checking checksums between source and destination.

COST CONSIDERATIONS:
- Transfer Appliance pricing includes an appliance fee (per use), onsite usage fee (fixed days included, then per weekday), shipping costs, and operations costs (Class A/B requests); no Transfer Service fee is incurred for physical ingest.
- Comparison example: network transfer of 500 TB costs ~$3,400 in Interconnect fees (10 Gbps at ~$1,700/month for ~2 months) plus engineering time, vs. Transfer Appliance using 2x TA300 units completed in ~10 days.
- For 1 PB migration: order 4x TA300 appliances, load 250 TB each in parallel, complete in 2-3 weeks versus months over the network.

COMMON PITFALLS:
- Not testing with a small transfer first
- Slow source storage (test read speeds before the appliance arrives)
- Millions of small files under 1 KB (archive into tar bundles first)
- Not planning the GCS bucket structure in advance (reorganizing petabytes after ingestion is expensive)

The article concludes: "if your data takes weeks to transfer over the network, ship it instead." The post is part of the OneUptime blog, which promotes OneUptime as an open-source observability platform combining infrastructure monitoring, incident management, status pages, and APM.
</summary>

<summary>
This article from Console Connect (published April 5, 2024, by Alex Hawkes) examines the ongoing issue of cloud data egress fees — the charges incurred when data is transferred out of cloud storage to external locations, between regions, or across availability zones. While getting data into the cloud is free, getting it out triggers egress charges that are often billed in arrears, making them "hidden costs" that catch IT managers off guard.

Key developments covered:
- In Q1 2024, both AWS and Google Cloud announced they would waive egress fees for companies migrating data out of their clouds, but with significant caveats: the provisions are for one-way, permanent migrations only. Google requires account termination after transfer and gives customers 60 days to complete migration, with credits applied to the final bill. AWS also requires a 60-day exit with full removal of all data and workloads (though not necessarily account termination), and notes that repeated migration requests will face "additional scrutiny."
- AWS has provided 100 GB of free data egress per month since 2021.
- The "Hotel California effect" describes the vendor lock-in created by these fees, prompting regulatory attention from European regulators and UK regulator Ofcom, plus the EU's European Data Act (effective September 2025) which aims to make cloud switching easier and fairer.

Cost data:
- AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud typically charge between 5 and 20 cents per GB for data transferred from cloud to on-premises/private data centers.
- Costs vary by volume and geography — intra-region transfers are cheaper, cross-region/continental transfers are most expensive.
- Larger organizations moving terabytes regularly face significant charges.

Solution highlighted: Private network connectivity (internet-bypass solutions) can avoid egress charges. Expert William B. Norton's research shows that if an enterprise exchanges enough cloud data to fill a 25Mbps connection monthly (~7.72 TB), the cost of a private network is fully covered by savings from reduced egress fees, with ongoing savings reaching 40%. Private connections also offer lower latency, less jitter, improved stability, and greater security. The article promotes Console Connect's Software Defined Cloud Interconnect (SDCI) as a more flexible alternative to provider-specific private connections (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Dedicated Interconnect), with pay-as-you-go pricing and 30-40% potential savings on egress charges.
</summary>

Key pricing facts: Egress fees can represent up to 20-30% of a total cloud bill if left unoptimized. Prices typically range from $0.05 to $0.12 per gigabyte depending on volume, and pennies scale into thousands of dollars in monthly overhead at terabyte/petabyte scale. 3. Use VPC endpoints or private links to keep inter-service traffic (e.g., to S3 or managed databases) on the provider's private network rather than the public internet, which triggers standard egress charges.
4. Use availability zone (AZ) affinity—route application and database traffic within the same zone, using other zones only for failover, since cross-AZ traffic is billed.
5. Implement local caching (Redis, memcached) to reduce network hops for frequently accessed data.
6. Set up billing alarms and budget alerts at 50% of expected monthly spend, using tools like AWS Cost Explorer or Google Cloud billing to identify egress-causing resources.

The video concludes that optimizing data transfer requires intentional architecture: auditing current egress, identifying cross-region movement, implementing a CDN and Brotli compression as quick wins, and architecting for AZ affinity with VPC endpoints.

--- SOURCE 10: Oracle Cloud Migration Licensing 2026 ---
URL: https://redresscompliance.com/oracle-database-license-migration-cloud-egress-buyer-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a definitive buyer-side guide to Oracle Database license implications when migrating workloads between clouds (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, OCI, and on-premises) in 2026. Written by Fredrik Filipsson (Co-Founder & Group CEO, ex-Oracle/IBM/SAP), it centers on the transition period of migrations rather than static endpoints, since the licensing risk lives in the transition, not the destination.

**Key topics covered:**

1. **Core factor rule**: In on-premises environments, Oracle's Processor Core Factor Table applies (0.5 factor on Intel/AMD x86). In Authorized Cloud Environments (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud), the Core Factor Table is NOT applicable—every two hyper-threaded vCPUs count as one full Processor license, roughly doubling licensing cost versus on-prem. The core factor discount does not travel to the cloud. Google Cloud is now named in the policy (operative version June 12, 2024).

2. **Policy vs. contract**: The "Licensing Oracle Software in the Cloud Computing Environment" document is a unilateral, non-contractual policy Oracle can revise at any time. Your Oracle Master Agreement (OMA) and ordering documents take precedence. Buyer-side move: pin counting methods, conversion ratios, and mobility rights in signed contracts before migrating.

3. **BYOL portability**: BYOL is reallocation of existing licenses, not new capacity. OCI delivers roughly twice the compute per license as hyperscalers (2 OCPUs per license vs. 1 physical core/2 vCPUs on AWS/Azure/GCP). Embedded Software Licenses (ESL) cannot BYOL at all; Standard Edition counts per-socket, Enterprise Edition per-core. The cheapest platform to license is often not the cheapest to run.

4. **Dual-running trap**: Oracle provides a 100-day overlap window during which both source and target may run on the same licenses. The counter starts on target deployment day, not cutover day. Beyond day 100, double-use is a compliance violation with back-dated audit exposure. OCI and hyperscalers do not enforce license compliance.

5. **Audit risk**: Oracle's GLAS (formerly LMS) treats cloud migrations as documented audit triggers. Findings are retroactive and back-dated. However, the finding is an opening position—independent measurement typically cuts the first number by a third or more, and negotiation can reduce settlements by 40-70%.

6. **Egress costs (2026 rates)**: Entry rates: AWS $0.09/GB, Azure $0.087/GB, Google Cloud Premium $0.12/GB, OCI $0.0085/GB (10TB free), Cloudflare R2 $0.00. AWS and Azure converge at $0.07/GB (50TB+) and $0.05/GB (150TB+). Hidden surcharges: NAT Gateway $0.045/GB and cross-AZ transfer $0.01/GB each way. EU Data Act offers free egress under narrow conditions. On May 1, 2026, Google doubled North America CDN Interconnect/Direct Peering/Carrier Peering rates from $0.04 to $0.08 per GiB.

7. **Migration paths**: Rehost (lift-and-shift) keeps the same metric; replatform can change metrics entirely; refactor (e.g., to PostgreSQL) removes licenses but creates a long dual-running period. The license bill doesn't stop until the last Oracle instance is decommissioned.

8. **Oracle Database@ services**: Oracle Database@AWS, @Azure, and @Google let customers run Exadata/Autonomous Database on OCI infrastructure inside hyperscalers. These involve contracted commitments to Oracle (lock-in) and shift counting toward the OCI-favorable model.

9. **OCI Support Rewards**: Lets you offset on-premises support renewals against OCI consumption—genuine value but also a retention/lock-in mechanism.

10. **Buyer-side checklist**: Pin contract terms in writing before SOW signing; re-size workloads on vCPU counting; compare platforms on effective compute per license; identify ESL and SE workloads separately; log target deployment dates and set hard decommission deadlines within 100 days; model full egress path including surcharges; keep contemporaneous dated records; assume an audit letter will arrive.

The core takeaway: "the risk lives in the transition." Endpoints are easy to license once static; the months of dual-running, egress path, and following audit are where money is won or lost.
</summary>

The article provides a comprehensive guide to Google Cloud Platform's Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs) — automatic, usage-based price reductions for long-running Compute Engine resources.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **What SUDs Are:** Automatic price reductions applied to specific GCP Compute Engine resources when servers run for a significant portion of a billing month. No contract or manual activation required. Maximum blended savings of ~30% if a VM runs the full month.

2. **How SUD Calculation Works (Tiered System, ~730-hour month):**
   - 0–25% of month (0–182 hrs): Standard on-demand rate, no discount
   - 25–50% (~183–365 hrs): 20% discount on hours in that block
   - 50–75% (~366–547 hrs): 40% discount
   - 75–100% (~548–730 hrs): 60% discount
   - Blended maximum: up to 30% total savings

3. **Eligibility:**
   - Eligible: N1, N2, N2D, certain custom machine types, sole-tenant nodes
   - NOT eligible: E2, C2/C3, A2, Cloud SQL, Spot/Preemptible VMs
   - GKE nodes ARE eligible if using eligible machine families (e.g., N2)

4. **Common Traps:**
   - Reseller/invoiced accounts may not pass SUDs through (one Reddit user reported losing $3K+ in unapplied SUDs)
   - Short-lived daily jobs (e.g., 90 min/day ≈ 45 hrs/month) never hit the 182-hour threshold
   - Discount calculated per project and region (cannot be shared across projects)

5. **Tracking SUDs:** Google Cloud Console → Billing → Cost Breakdown → Monthly credits section shows SUD line items. Zero means ineligible machine types or insufficient runtime.

6. **Maximization Strategy:** Use eligible N2 machines for 24/7 baseline workloads (SUDs auto-apply), and use Spot/Preemptible VMs (up to 91% discount) for batch/temporary workloads.

7. **SUD vs. CUD Comparison:**
   - SUD: No contract, automatic, flexible, max ~30% savings, best for unpredictable usage
   - CUD: 1-3 year contract, manual purchase, max up to 70% savings, best for stable 24/7 operations
   - Resource-Based CUDs: Commit to specific hardware quantity in specific region (highest discount, zero flexibility)
   - Spend-Based CUDs: Commit to dollar amount per hour across eligible services (flexible, slightly lower discount)
   - CUDs can be combined with Reservations to secure both price and hardware availability
   - Software license commitments available separately for SUSE/RHEL

8. **Break-Even Example:** A $0.10/hr server (730 hrs = $73/month baseline):
   - With SUD (30% blended): ~$51.10/month
   - With 3-year CUD (55% discount): $32.85/month — but CUD becomes a sunk cost if workload volatility causes underutilization

9. **Key FAQs:** Custom machine types remain eligible; resizing mid-month resets the discount calculation; 30% is only a blended maximum at 100% uptime (a half-month server yields only ~10% effective savings); Spot/Preemptible VMs don't qualify.

The article positions Costimizer as an automated FinOps agent that connects to GCP to identify SUD-qualifying resources and determine optimal transition points to CUDs.

--- SOURCE 14: Google is cutting his Cloud Egress Transfer Costs - Medium ---
URL: https://alatech.medium.com/my-rant-on-cloud-egress-transfer-costs-77e94f0f594a

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an opinion piece by Antonio Lagrotteria (Engineering Manager, Full-Stack Architect, AWS Community Builder) published on Medium, discussing Google Cloud Platform's (GCP) January 2024 announcement that it will eliminate egress/outbound data transfer fees for customers leaving their platform. The author argues that while this appears philanthropic, it's likely a strategic business move, and he explores both sides of the egress cost debate.

**GCP's Motivation (Author's Theories):**
1. Steal market share from AWS and Azure (GCP is a distant third cloud vendor)
2. Anticipate future regulations on egress costs
3. Trigger reactions from other cloud providers and customers

**What Are Egress Costs:** Fees charged by cloud providers when data is transferred out of their network, including intra/extra-region, availability zone, public internet traffic, downloading files, accessing storage/compute, and hybrid (on-prem/cloud) API consumption. These costs can add up significantly for businesses with substantial data transfer needs.

**Reasons to KEEP Egress Costs:**
1. Sustainable cloud provider infrastructure maintenance (revenue funds ongoing development)
2. Natural customer lock-in strategy (prevents easy departure)
3. Educates customers on well-architected, cloud-native designs (discourages inefficient network use)

**Reasons to REMOVE/Reduce Egress Costs:**
1. Free flow of data — fosters innovation and collaboration
2. Earn customer trust — costs are complex to calculate (e.g., AWS Cost Explorer for EC2 and VPC Flow logs is not intuitive), and removing them creates fairness and transparency
3. Data-driven decisions in hybrid setups — costs discourage moving large datasets, limiting analytics and insights, particularly in large enterprises with migration constraints

**Conclusion:** The author hopes this GCP announcement triggers a response from other major cloud providers to seriously reconsider their egress transfer cost strategies, potentially using it as an opportunity to become the undisputed leader in cloud computing.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Part-14: Google Compute Engine (GCE) – Live Migration & Availability Policy Explained 🚀 - DEV Community ---
URL: https://dev.to/latchudevops/part-14-google-compute-engine-gce-live-migration-availability-policy-explained-a6m

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is Part-14 of a GCP learning series by Latchu@DevOps, explaining Google Compute Engine (GCE) Live Migration and Availability Policies.

**Key topics covered:**

1. **Division of maintenance responsibilities**: Users manage VM instance-level updates (OS patches, configuration management) using VM Manager (Patch Management, OS Configuration Policies), while GCP teams handle host-level hardware and software updates for Compute Engine hosts.

2. **Live Migration**: Allows VM instances to keep running even when the underlying host system undergoes maintenance or upgrades. It covers hardware/infrastructure upgrades, power grid or network maintenance, and regular system patching. Live Migration = zero downtime during GCP maintenance.

3. **How Live Migration works**: When a host machine is scheduled for maintenance, running VMs are automatically migrated to another host in the same zone, with VM settings and metadata unchanged and no manual intervention required. It is supported for VMs with local SSDs but NOT supported for GPUs, Spot VMs, and Preemptible VMs.

4. **Availability Policy settings** (configured at VM creation):
   - **On Host Maintenance**: "Migrate VM Instance" (recommended, best for availability) vs. "Terminate VM Instance" (VM stops during host maintenance)
   - **Automatic Restart**: "ON" (recommended, VM restarts automatically after crashes) vs. "OFF" (VM stays stopped until manually started)

5. **Best practices**: Always enable Live Migration unless workloads don't support it, keep Automatic Restart ON for production workloads, and use VM Manager for guest OS updates while relying on GCP for host maintenance.

**Core message**: Users manage the VMs, GCP manages the hosts, and Live Migration bridges the gap to ensure seamless VM operation during Google's backend upgrades or infrastructure events, maximizing uptime and workload resilience with minimal manual intervention.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Live Migration = Zero Downtime During GCP Maintenance", "Supported: VMs with local SSDs. Not Supported: GPUs, Spot VMs, and Preemptible VMs", "Migrate VM Instance (Recommended) → VM is live migrated to another host (Best option for availability)", "You manage the VMs, GCP manages the hosts, and Live Migration bridges the gap!", "Always enable Live Migration (Migrate VM Instance) unless you have workloads that don't support it. Keep Automatic Restart ON for production workloads."

--- SOURCE 2: Multi-region HA in Google Cloud ---
URL: https://medium.com/google-cloud/multi-region-ha-in-google-cloud-823b9f706578

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Sergey Shcherbakov (published April 18, 2024, in the Google Cloud - Community publication on Medium) explores how to achieve multi-region high availability (HA) for business-critical applications on Google Cloud Platform, with a focus on private internal networks. The author is a Strategic Cloud Engineer at Google with over 10 years of experience consulting on software and cloud architectures.

The article begins by explaining that Google Cloud, as a hyperscaler, enables applications to achieve uptime targets of "four nines" (99.99%) or even "five nines" (99.999%) through five key mechanisms: redundancy, load balancing, failover, monitoring & alerting, and self-healing. The article focuses on the first three of these.

**Redundancy**: The article explains Google Cloud's infrastructure hierarchy — clusters, zones, and regions. A single GCE VM cannot survive hardware failure, so redundancy requires running multiple instances. For single-VM outages, multiple instances in a single zone suffice (Fig. 2). For zone outages (which are not impossible), replicas must run across multiple zones (Fig. 3). For full region outages (also not impossible — citing a Google Cloud London data center outage during record heat in 2022), the application must be deployed across multiple regions (Fig. 4).

**Load Balancing**: Google Cloud offers global external load balancers (Global External Application Load Balancer, Classic Application Load Balancer in Premium Tier, Global External proxy Network Load Balancer, Classic Proxy Network Load Balancer) for internet-facing traffic. However, internal load balancers restrict access to internal network clients and currently rely on regional infrastructure, meaning their availability can be affected by a single region outage. Internal load balancer options include: Regional Internal Application Load Balancer, Cross-region Internal Application Load Balancer, Regional internal proxy Network Load Balancer, Cross-region internal proxy Network Load Balancer, and Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer. To address cross-region failover for internal clients, the article recommends using Cloud DNS Geolocation routing policies, which map traffic from source geographies to specific DNS targets based on query origin region.

**Failover**: Cloud DNS health checks are crucial for achieving maximum uptime. For Internal Passthrough Network Load Balancers (L4), Cloud DNS checks health of backend instances with a default 20% healthy threshold — if at least 20% of backend instances are healthy, the load balancer endpoint is considered healthy. For Internal Application Load Balancers, Cloud DNS checks overall load balancer health, and the load balancer itself checks backend health. The article recommends setting DNS record TTL to minimal or even zero values (a tradeoff between availability and DNS load/latency). Internal cross-region application load balancers can automatically failover to replicas in healthy regions during "partial" region outages (when only application backends are unavailable but networking/load balancing still work).

**Configuration with Managed Instance Groups**: The article provides complete Terraform examples (available in the GitHub project GoogleCloudPlatform/professional-services/examples/cloud-dns-load-balancing) demonstrating:
1. Defining GCE Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) in two regions using the terraform-google-modules/vm modules
2. Defining two Cross-regional Internal Network Passthrough Load Balancers (L4 ILBs), one per region
3. Configuring global Cloud DNS record sets with geolocation routing policies and health-checked targets

The MIG-based approach is also relevant to GKE, since Kubernetes node pools are implemented as GCE MIGs. Kubernetes workloads can be made multi-regional by deploying to multiple GKE clusters in distinct regions, using Kubernetes Gateway API, Multi Cluster Ingress, or Terraform.

The article demonstrates testing using Fortio (a load testing tool) run from a GCE VM in the same VPC. The test shows automatic failover and self-healing when a container is stopped — the MIG automatically restarts the service VM, demonstrating the self-healing component of HA.

**Cloud Run Backends**: A second scenario uses Cloud Run (also applicable to Cloud Functions 2nd generation via Serverless Network Endpoint Groups) with global Internal Cross-Region Application Load Balancers. Terraform examples define regional Cloud Run instances with INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_LOAD_BALANCER, Serverless NEGs, and global forwarding rules, target HTTPS proxies, URL maps, backend services with outlier detection, and Cloud DNS routing policies per region.

**Important limitations**: Cloud DNS health checks for L7 application load balancers can only check the state and availability of Envoy proxy instances, NOT the application backends themselves. If a Cloud Run app returns 500 errors, Cloud DNS won't detect it and won't switch load balancer IPs. The Outlier Detection feature of Internal Cross-regional Application Load Balancers can detect application-level malfunctions by monitoring success rates toward each backend (at the cost of wasting a percentage of client requests). Missing or malfunctioning backends are also not detected by Cloud DNS health checks. Only in a full region outage (when load balancer infrastructure is unavailable) would Cloud DNS health checks detect and act.

**Options Choice — key constraints and tradeoffs**:
1. **External vs Internal Load Balancers**: Global External Application Load Balancer provides the best availability guarantees via global anycast VIPs and smart global network routing. Internal load balancers use regional IPs and require Cloud DNS load balancing to address full region outage scenarios.
2. **MIG vs Cloud Run Backends**: Network Passthrough (L4) Load Balancers cannot be configured with Cloud Run backends (no Serverless NEG support). For internal multi-regional apps needing to handle most outage scenarios, L4 ILB with GCE MIGs is the only option. Cloud Run backends require Custom Audiences (2nd generation only) for authenticated clients to work across regions.
3. **L4 vs L7 Load Balancers**: With L4, the application must handle TLS termination, authentication, and request routing itself. L7 load balancers help with those but their internal versions address fewer failure scenarios due to Cloud DNS health check limitations.

**Conclusion**: Google Cloud offers tools for building highly available multi-regional application services even for internal security-restricted corporate use cases. The choice of resource combination depends on individual application requirements and currently supported service features. The author also references his previous article on Application Secrets Encryption in Google Cloud Kubernetes products.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Hyperscalers are designed for massive capacity. They possess immense data center networks spread globally, allowing them to handle the enormous computing demands of large enterprises and applications with vast user bases.", "A common measure of success of such metric is the application service uptime metric often aiming for targets like '99.99%' ('four nines') or even '99.999%' ('five nines') which translate into very few minutes of allowed downtime per year.", "For Internal Passthrough Network Load Balancers (L4), Cloud DNS checks the health information on the load balancer's individual backend instances to determine if the load balancer is healthy or unhealthy. Cloud DNS applies a default 20% threshold, and if at least 20% of backend instances are healthy, the load balancer endpoint is considered healthy.", "The Cloud DNS health checks only check the availability of the internal Google Cloud infrastructure (Envoy proxies) supporting the application (L7) load balancers.", "GCE Managed Instance Groups based scenarios, discussed in this article, are also relevant to the managed Kubernetes service on Google Cloud, GKE, as well. Kubernetes node pools in GKE are implemented as GCE MIGs."
</key_excerpts>

**Key SLOs by Network Service Tier and Region:**

**Premium Tier (Cloud Regions excluding Mexico and Stockholm):**

- Single Instance (Memory Optimized family): ≥ 99.95%
- Single Instance (all other families): ≥ 99.9%

- Instances in Multiple Zones: ≥ 99.95%
- Single Instance (all other families): ≥ 99.9%
- Load balancing: ≥ 99.95%

**Standard Tier:**
- Instances in Multiple Zones: ≥ 99.9%
- Load balancing: ≥ 99.9%

**Financial Credits:** Customers must request credits within 60 days of becoming eligible, providing log files showing Downtime Periods. Credits are applied to future bills and capped at the monthly bill amount for the affected Covered Service in the Region.

**Credit Tiers:**
- For Premium Tier (excluding Mexico/Stockholm): 99.00%-99.99% = 10% credit; 95.00%-99.00% = 25%; <95% = 100%
- For Single Instance (Memory Optimized): 95.00%-99.95% = 10%; 90.00%-95.00% = 25%; <90% = 100%
- For Single Instance (all other families): 95.00%-99.90% = 10%; 90.00%-95.00% = 25%; <90% = 100%

**Definitions:** Downtime means loss of external connectivity or persistent disk access. Downtime Periods require one or more consecutive minutes of Downtime (partial/intermittent under one minute does not count). Covered Services include Instances in Multiple Zones, Single Instances, and Load balancing.

**SLA Exclusions:** The SLA does not apply to pre-GA features, features excluded in documentation, errors caused by factors outside Google's reasonable control, customer or third-party software/hardware, abuses violating the Agreement, or system quotas.

--- SOURCE 4: Migrate across Google Cloud regions: Design resilient single-region environments on Google Cloud  |  Cloud Architecture Center  |  Google Cloud Documentation ---
URL: https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/migrate-across-regions/design-resilient-single-region-environments

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page (last reviewed 2024-12-08) provides guidance on designing resilient, single-region environments on Google Cloud. It is part of a multi-part series on migrating across Google Cloud regions.

**Deployment Archetypes:** The page describes four deployment archetypes ordered by increasing reliability and operational overhead: (1) Zonal (single zone, resists resource failures), (2) Regional/Single-region (multiple zones in one region, resists resource failures and zonal outages), (3) Multi-regional (multiple zones across regions, also resists regional outages), and (4) Global (multiple zones across regions worldwide). Single-region environments require coordination across multiple zones in a single region.

**Choosing Archetypes:** The document advises defining failure models first by considering: which components need failure models, SLO and disaster recovery requirements, how many failure models to define, resources needed to guard against failures, how to detect failures (e.g., Google Cloud Observability alerts), how to test failure models (fault injection, chaos engineering), expected impact of failures, and expected failure duration. When evaluating archetypes, consider how many archetypes are needed, resource requirements, potential future migrations, business criticality, and feature availability. Non-functional requirements like regulatory, locality, and sovereignty constraints may restrict options (e.g., mandatory region usage).

**Choosing a Region:** Functional criteria include geographical proximity to users (using tools like the Google Cloud latency dashboard, GCPing, and the Google Cloud Region Picker), product availability in regions (via Cloud locations), and per-region quota limits. Non-functional criteria include carbon footprint preferences and regulatory compliance (e.g., data sovereignty requirements).

**Design Principles:** Key principles include provisioning regional resources instead of zonal ones where possible, and verifying environments work against failure model assumptions (e.g., simulating zonal outages with regional MIGs).

**Computing Resources:**
- **Compute Engine:** Recommendations include using regional managed instance groups (MIGs) with the EVEN distribution shape, referencing regional resources in instance templates, configuring load balancing and autoscaling, setting up resource reservations for capacity assurance, using zonal DNS names, choosing regional Persistent Disks over zonal ones (for zonal failover), and implementing automated data protection mechanisms.
- **GKE:** Use regional clusters (especially with Autopilot), consider multi-cluster environments for flexibility and availability, and enable Backup for GKE (a regional service) for workload and data protection.
- **Cloud Run:** Services are regional resources replicated across multiple zones, automatically balancing traffic and mitigating zonal outage effects.
- **VMware Engine:** Use multi-node private clouds for production (single-node only for proofs of concept), and consider stretched private clouds that distribute nodes across zones to protect against zonal outages.

**Data Storage Resources:**
- **Cloud Storage:** Buckets with region location type provide redundancy across at least two zones; dual-region across two regions; multi-region across two or more regions.
- **Filestore:** Choose the Enterprise tier for high availability and data redundancy across multiple zones (other tiers are zonal).
- **Bigtable:** Instances are zonal; enable replication across multiple zones or regions for automatic failover during outages.
- **Firestore:** Regional locations replicate across zones within a region; multi-region locations replicate across more than one region.
- **Memorystore:** For Redis, choose Standard tier or Standard tier with read replicas (auto-replicates across zones); for Memcached, let it auto-distribute nodes across zones (but no data replication across zones); for Valkey, choose from zonal and multi-zonal configurations.
- **Spanner:** Configure instances as regional or multi-region; regional configurations maintain one read-write replica per zone; instances can be moved between configurations without downtime.

**Data Analytics Resources:**
- **BigQuery:** Datasets have regional or multi-region locations with data copies in two different zones; handles zonal failures automatically but regional outages need manual planning.
- **Managed Service for Apache Spark:** Clusters are zonal; use auto zone placement and enable high availability mode (must be enabled at creation) for resilience to coordinator node failures or partial zonal outages.
- **Dataflow:** Jobs are zonal resources; configure regional endpoints and let Dataflow automatically select best zone placement rather than forcing a specific zone.
- **Pub/Sub:** Messages stored in a single region and replicated in at least two zones; supports global and regional endpoints, and configurable message storage policies to restrict where messages are processed and stored.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The guidance in this document assumes that you're designing and implementing single-region environments. If you use a single-region environment now, in the future you can migrate to a multi-region environment."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Multi-regional deployment on Compute Engine  |  Cloud Architecture Center  |  Google Cloud Documentation ---
URL: https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/multiregional-vms

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page (last reviewed 2025-08-11) provides a reference architecture for multi-regional deployment on Compute Engine. The document describes a multi-tier application running in active-active mode across two Google Cloud regions, with each region containing independent stacks spanning three zones. The architecture uses infrastructure as a service (IaaS), targeting cloud architects looking to rehost (lift and shift) on-premises applications with minimal changes.

Key architecture components include: a global external load balancer (advertising a single anycast IP via Google Front Ends), regional managed instance groups (MIGs) for web and application tiers, regional internal load balancers, a third-party database (e.g., PostgreSQL) deployed on Compute Engine VMs with cross-region replication and failover, a single VPC network with subnets in two regions, and dual-region Cloud Storage buckets for database backups.

Products used: Compute Engine, Cloud Load Balancing, Cloud Storage, and Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).

Use cases covered: efficient migration of on-premises applications, high availability for geographically dispersed users (with near-zero RTO if data is replicated synchronously), and low latency for users within a geographical area.

A design alternative uses regional load balancers and Cloud DNS instead of a global load balancer, supporting TLS termination in specified regions, serving content from specified regions, and a wider range of connection protocols via Passthrough Network Load Balancer. This alternative supports data residency requirements through geofenced routing policies.

Design considerations are organized across six pillars:
- System design: region selection factors (service availability, machine types, latency, cost, regulatory, sustainability), compute alternatives (GKE containers, Cloud Run serverless), storage options (Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk, Cloud Storage regional/dual-region/multi-region buckets, Filestore), and database choices (Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Bigtable, Spanner, Firestore, or third-party databases like Oracle).
- Security: Cloud Armor for DDoS/XSS protection, no external IPs on VMs (using Private Service Connect or Private Google Access), dedicated service accounts, IAP and Cloud OS Login for SSH security, Cloud KMS for disk encryption, Cloud NGFW policies, and data residency considerations.
- Reliability: robustness against zone/region outages via MIG auto-repair and regional MIGs, autoscaling for stateless MIGs, VM autohealing with application-based health checks, spread placement policies, reservations for capacity, stateful storage options, Backup and DR service, snapshots, Regional Persistent Disk, and database failover mechanisms (including split-brain avoidance).
- Cost optimization: machine type recommendations, custom machine types, Spot VMs for fault-tolerant workloads, autoscaling to reduce cost, and bring-your-own-license (BYOL) strategies for third-party software.
- Operational efficiency: instance template updates via automatic or selective methods, custom OS images, and deterministic instance templates with explicit software versions.
- Performance optimization: machine type selection, vCPU multithreading configuration, Network Service Tiers (Premium vs. Standard), compact placement policies for low inter-VM latency, Tier_1 networking for higher bandwidth, and Cloud CDN caching.

Contributors include Kumar Dhanagopal (Cross-Product Solution Developer) and Samantha He (Technical Writer), with numerous other contributors. Content is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The architecture is aligned with the Google Cloud multi-regional deployment archetype, which ensures that your Google Cloud topology is robust against zone and region outages and that it provides low latency for application users."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: PCI DSS - Compliance ---
URL: https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/pci-dss

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Google Cloud compliance page for PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard). Key points include:

- The PCI Security Standards Council was established by major credit card associations (Visa, MasterCard, American Express, Discover, JCB) to define practices for protecting cardholder data.
- PCI DSS is a set of network security and business best practices guidelines adopted by the council to establish a "minimum security standard" for protecting customers' payment card information.
- The scope of PCI DSS includes all systems, networks, and applications that process, store, or transmit cardholder data, plus systems used to secure and log access to in-scope systems.
- Google Cloud undergoes at least an annual third-party audit to certify individual products against PCI DSS, and the following services have been reviewed by an independent Qualified Security Assessor and determined to be PCI DSS 4.0.1 compliant: Google Cloud, Google Workspace, and Google Workspace Admin SDK.
- Customers remain responsible for ensuring their own applications are PCI DSS compliant (shared responsibility model).
- Google Cloud does NOT have an acquirer available for organizations using Google Cloud (an acquirer is a bank or entity that processes payment card transactions on behalf of another organization).
- PCI DSS reports may be requested via the Compliance Reports Manager, and a shared responsibility matrix is available to explain the division of compliance responsibilities between Google and customers.
- PCI DSS applies to any organization of any size that accepts, transmits, or stores cardholder data.
- Related compliance offerings include ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27017, PCI 3DS, and PCI PIN.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: How to Configure Assured Workloads for HIPAA Compliance in Google Cloud ---

<summary>
This is a OneUptime blog post (dated February 17, 2026, technically validated May 28, 2026) authored by Nawaz Dhandala that provides a comprehensive technical guide for configuring Google Cloud's Assured Workloads service for HIPAA compliance. The post covers the full setup process for healthcare organizations handling Protected Health Information (PHI) on GCP.

Key topics covered:
1. **HIPAA/GCP Basics**: Google Cloud offers a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) that must be signed before handling PHI, but not all GCP services are covered. Assured Workloads automates technical controls.
2. **Prerequisites**: GCP Organization, signed BAA, Assured Workloads Admin role, and linked billing account. Includes commands to verify organization access and enable the assuredworkloads API.

<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page provides an overview of Assured Workloads, a service that enables organizations in the private and public sectors to configure a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls for sensitive workloads in the cloud. The service allows users to apply predefined control packages to folders to simplify management and configuration of regulated workloads while maintaining the scale, cost, and service availability benefits of commercial cloud infrastructure.

**Use cases:** Organizations with strict regulations for data storage, key management, and access (financial services, healthcare, governmental bodies); organizations that must store data within certain regions/countries; and organizations that must control Google Cloud personnel access to their data.

**Key capabilities:**
- **Control packages** (foundation for compliance enforcement) available in three types: regional data boundaries, regulatory data boundaries, and Sovereign Controls by Partners.
- **Regional data boundaries** restrict resource storage to specified geographic regions (e.g., EU Data Boundary restricts to EU-only regions).
- **Regulatory data boundaries** address specific compliance requirements including CJIS, FedRAMP Moderate/High, Healthcare and Life Sciences Controls (HIPAA/HITRUST), IL2/IL4/IL5, ITAR, and IRS Publication 1075.
- **Sovereign Controls by Partners** lets users use a local, trusted partner to manage encryption keys, access justification, and audits.
- **Personnel access control** via Assured Support (available with Enhanced or Premium Support), requiring Google support personnel to adhere to geographical and background check requirements (e.g., FedRAMP High requires US-located personnel with enhanced background checks).
- **Key management** controls vary by package — ITAR requires customer-managed encryption keys (CMEKs) with separate key management projects; support also includes Google-owned/managed keys (FIPS-140-2), Cloud EKM, and key import.
- **Workload updates** allow evaluation and maintenance of control package configurations, applying upgrades when newer versions are available.
- **Violation monitoring** tracks organization policy constraint violations and resource violations, with email notification options.

**Related access control services:** Access Approval (customer approval before Google personnel access), Access Transparency (logs of Google personnel activity), and Key Access Justifications (approve/deny key access requests).

**Control package renaming notice (effective June 2025):** Control package names in the console and APIs changed as of June 2025, reflected in the ComplianceRegime enums used in the Assured Workloads API. Examples include: "EU Data Boundary" became "EU Regions," "US Data Boundary" became "US Regions," "Data Boundary for ITAR" became "International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR)," and various "Regions" names replaced previous naming conventions. Sole-tenancy provides exclusive access to a sole-tenant node—a physical Compute Engine server dedicated to hosting only your project's VMs, providing physical isolation from VMs in other projects and enabling grouping of VMs on the same host hardware.

Key topics covered:

**Overview & Use Cases:** Sole-tenant nodes maintain a one-to-one mapping to the physical server backing the node. VMs on sole-tenant nodes use the same Compute Engine features as other VMs (transparent scheduling, block storage) but with hardware isolation. They help meet dedicated hardware requirements for bring-your-own-license (BYOL) scenarios, security/compliance needs (finance, healthcare, gaming), and workloads requiring per-core/per-processor licensing. Cloud Logging can be used to track historical server usage.

**Node Templates & Node Types:** A node template is a regional resource defining node properties; node types specify total vCPU cores and memory for nodes. The document includes a comprehensive table of 46+ available node types spanning multiple machine families (A2, A3, C2, C3, C3D, C4, C4A, C4D, C4N, G2, H3, H4D, M1, M2, M3, M4, N1, N2, N2D, N4, N4A) with details on processors (Cascade Lake, Sapphire Rapids, AMD EPYC Genoa/Turin/Milan, Emerald Rapids, Google Axion, Skylake, Ice Lake, Broadwell E7), vCPU counts (ranging from 60 to 416), memory (144 GB to 11,776 GB), sockets, cores, and maximum VMs allowed. Some node types support Local SSD (indicated by the `-lssd` suffix).

**Node Groups & VM Provisioning:** Provisioning requires creating a node template, then a node group, then provisioning VMs. Node groups are homogeneous sets of sole-tenant nodes in a specific zone, can be autoscaled, and support machine types with 2+ vCPUs from the same machine series.

**Host Maintenance Policies:** Three options exist:
1. **Default** – VMs live migrate to new sole-tenant nodes before host maintenance events (occurs approximately every 4-6 weeks); suitable for per-user/per-device licenses.
2. **Restart in place** – VMs stop and restart on the same physical server; suitable for fault-tolerant workloads, approximately one hour of downtime.
3. **Migrate within node group** – VMs live migrate within a fixed-sized group of physical servers; reserves 1 holdback node per 20 reserved nodes (table shows 1 holdback for 2-20 nodes up to 5 holdbacks for 81-100 nodes).

**Maintenance Windows:** 4-hour blocks specifying when maintenance can begin; cannot be modified after creation; not supported with the Migrate within node group policy.

**Node Affinity & Anti-Affinity:** Affinity labels (key-value pairs) control VM placement. Default labels include node-group-name, node-name, and projects. Custom labels can be specified at node template creation only.

**Pricing:** Committed use discounts (CUDs) and sustained use discounts (SUDs) apply (only flexible CUDs for sole-tenancy premium); no extra cost for VMs on already-billed nodes; GPUs and Local SSD disks are billed separately; sole-tenancy premium based only on vCPUs and memory.

This is a technical blog post by Roshni Thakur, a Cloud Engineer at The Cloudside View (a GCP/AWS cloud-native and data problem-solving team), covering dynamic and manual scaling strategies in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using Node Auto-Provisioning (NAP) and Custom Compute Classes (CCC).

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **Why Enable Node Auto-Provisioning (NAP):** In GKE Standard clusters, the control plane requires at least one node to host system pods. NAP dynamically creates node pools based on CCC preferences. Without NAP, CCCs only influence scheduling to existing node pools labeled and tainted appropriately.

2. **Enabling NAP:** Run a command with resource limits to avoid over-provisioning, using flags such as `min-cpu=1`, `max-cpu=100`, `min-memory=1`, and `max-memory=256`.

3. **Custom Compute Classes (CCC):** A ComputeClass defines preferences for machine types GKE should prioritize when provisioning nodes, including machine families, Spot vs. On-demand VMs, and autoscaling policies. The `consolidation Delay Minutes` setting allows GKE to delete idle nodes (no pods for the specified time, e.g., 1 minute) to free up unused resources and reduce cost.

4. **Applying CCC to a Namespace:** Recommended so all pods in a namespace automatically use the Compute Class unless specified otherwise. Deploying pods in custom namespaces requires adding a selector.

5. **Validation:** Commands like `kubectl get pod`, `kubectl get node`, and `kubectl get pod -o wide` confirm whether pods triggered node auto-provisioning and whether the correct machine type (e.g., e2 Spot VM) was used.

6. **Manual Node Pools with CCC (without NAP):** Useful when more control is needed (specific machine types or manual node counts). CCC still guides workload scheduling by matching pods to manually created node pools with corresponding labels and taints. Steps include creating a namespace with labels, creating node pools, and deploying workloads. Taints prevent pods from landing on nodes unless tolerations exist, while labels allow CCC to match node preferences.

7. **GKE Autopilot with CCC:** Autopilot handles node provisioning and scaling automatically (no NAP needed), but CCC gives control over how pods are scheduled (e.g., choosing machine families like e2 or n2). Users create a Compute Class, label their namespace, deploy pods, and inspect where pods land using `kubectl get pod -o wide`.
</summary>
