For capabilities similar to AWS Migration Hub, explore AWS Transform.** Migration Hub Orchestrator is offered at no additional cost—users only pay for the AWS resources they provision for migrations. [12]

**AWS Blog — "Automate large-scale migration to Amazon EC2 using AWS Migration Hub Orchestrator"**: AWS Migration Hub Orchestrator serves as the central orchestration service, managing and automating the migration workflow. [15]

**Pump.co — "AWS Migration Hub Pricing"**: Using the Migration Hub itself for collecting discovery data, planning migration, or tracking progress incurs no costs. Costs arise from: data transfer costs; storage costs (EBS by volume type/data stored; S3 tiered pricing); additional AWS services fees (AWS DMS billed by instance hours and data replication volume; AWS Application Migration Service varies by VM usage, network traffic, storage); Refactor Spaces: $0.028 per environment per hour after free trial; $0.000002 per API request with 500,000 free API requests per month. Free Tier: 2,160 free hours of Refactor Spaces environments monthly for three months, plus 500,000 free API calls per month. Case study — Affinidi used AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces to consolidate 20 disparate API endpoints into a single API layer: 50% reduction in developer effort for service APIs, improved stand-up time from days to minutes, 25% decrease in monolithic refactoring costs, scaled from 100 thousand to 2 million digital vaults by 2025-26. [14]

**YouTube — "Introducing AWS Migration Hub Orchestrator"**: Orchestrator helps reduce migration costs and time by removing many of the manual tasks involved in migrating large-scale enterprise workloads. [11]

### 1.4 AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and Related Tools

**AWS Cloud Operations Blog — "AWS offerings available to support your cloud migration"** describes six key tools using a hypothetical stack (Windows 2008 R2 presentation server, Windows 2022 application server, Windows File Server, MS-SQL 2019 database migrating to EC2, FSx for Windows File Server, RDS PostgreSQL):
1. **AWS Application Discovery Service (ADS)** — Collects usage and configuration data about on-premises servers (server, performance, and dependency data when the agent is deployed); used to validate no missing dependencies and uncover missed servers. Free to use; pay only for AWS resources provisioned to store on-premises data.
2. **End-of-Support Migration Program (EMP) for Windows Server** — Migrates legacy applications from Windows Server 2003, 2008, 2008 R2 to newer supported versions on AWS without code changes. Packages application files, runtimes, components, deployment tools, and an API-call redirection engine.
3. **AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)** — Automated rehosting to EC2 via continuous block-based data replication through a staging area. Free for 2,160 hours (90 days continuous) per source server. Can be combined with the Cloud Migration Factory solution for hundreds/thousands of servers.
4. **AWS DataSync** — Online data transfer service automating/accelerating data movement between on-premises and AWS storage; performs incremental transfers; ideal for migrating active file systems (e.g., Windows File Server to FSx for Windows File Server); supports task scheduling.
5. **AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)** — Free tool converting source database schema and code to match a target database engine; generates assessment reports. In the example, 90% of database storage objects and 77% of database code objects could be converted automatically or with minimal changes.
6. **AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)** — Migrates databases quickly and securely while keeping the source database fully operational, minimizing downtime. Supports homogeneous (Oracle to Oracle) and heterogeneous migrations (e.g., SQL Server to PostgreSQL via SCT coupling). Users pay only for replication instances and additional log storage. [9b — source 9 in the fourth tool call block]

### 1.5 AWS End of Support Migration Program (EMP)

**AWS News Blog — "New AWS Program to Help Future-proof Your End-of-Support Windows Server Applications"**: On January 14, 2020, support for Windows Server 2008 and 2008 R2 ended. AWS EMP for Windows Server combines technology with expert guidance to migrate legacy applications to newer, supported Windows Server versions on AWS without any code changes, original installation media, or source code. Requires engagement with an AWS Partner or Professional Services. The technology uses a capture tool that snapshots a machine, monitors the application installation process, identifies files, registry keys, and shortcuts created, and maps the application's dependencies on process and system-level APIs. The resulting package includes all application files, runtimes, components, deployment tools, and an engine that redirects API calls from the application to files within the package, decoupling the application from the underlying OS. Demo showed migrating Microsoft SQL Server 2000 from Windows Server 2003 to run on Windows Server 2016. [23 — per source list]

**AWS blog — "How to upgrade your legacy Windows applications to new versions of Windows Server without refactoring"**: Windows Server 2003 has been End of Support since July 2015; Windows Server 2008 since January 2020. AWS released EMP for Windows Server at re:Invent 2019, with self-service capability available October 15, 2020. Tutorial uses AWS Package Builder (MSI installer on a "packaging machine"), creating compatibility packages. Deployment via `Compatibility.Package.Deployment.exe /AcceptEula /DeployDir`. **Limitations**: EMP can only migrate Windows applications; does not support 16-bit applications, kernel mode drivers, applications with shell extensions, and low-level applications such as anti-virus, firewall, and VPN applications. EMP should only be used when upgrading to a supported OS version is not possible. [24 — per source list]

**Cloudhouse — "AWS EMP End Of Life"**: **AWS EMP officially reaches End of Life on April 30, 2025**, after which it no longer receives security updates, bug fixes, technical support, or online technical content updates. AWS cannot extend support beyond EOL. Cloudhouse Alchemy is presented as successor (same team behind EMP technology). [20 — per source list]

**AWS Reference Notes (dendron.so)** — documentation index page for AWS EMP for Windows Server. [25 — per source list]

### 1.6 Server Migration Service (SMS), CloudEndure, Partner Solutions

- AWS MGN is the evolution of CloudEndure Migration; customers using CloudEndure Migration or AWS SMS are encouraged to switch to AWS MGN. For environments where agents cannot be installed, AWS SMS remains an option. [6]
- Cloudendure/EMP: "AWS EMP End Of Life" notes Cloudhouse Alchemy as the original technology behind AWS EMP, created by the same team. [20]
- IBM notes ecosystem partners (IBM, Microsoft, managed service providers, system integrators) offer consulting and specialized expertise. AWS Application Migration Service simplifies lift-and-shift. [4]

### 1.7 Automation Frameworks and Assessment Tools

- **AWS Migration Evaluator (formerly TSO Logic)** — generates migration scenarios and on-prem TCO calculation. [31]
- **Cloud Migration Factory** — can be combined with AWS MGN for migrating hundreds or thousands of servers. [9b]
- **CloudZero** lists tools for calculating AWS TCO: CloudZero (real-time cost monitoring, AWS MAP support, Slack alerts), AWS Pricing Calculator (native tool), CloudChomp's CC Analyzer (automated discovery, on-prem TCO calculation), and Migration Evaluator (formerly TSO Logic, generates migration scenarios). [31]
- AWS re:Post community guidance on large-scale enterprise migration best practices covers assessment and planning, stakeholder alignment, phased approach, testing and validation, monitoring and replication, resource management, tools and services, performance and cost optimization, dependency management, communication and coordination; "cloud migration is an iterative process, so be prepared to adapt your approach as needed throughout the journey." [13]

## 2. COST MODELING

### 2.1 AWS TCO Analysis and Cloud Economics

**CloudZero — "Guide To Calculating TCO On AWS And Tools To Help"** (published September 27, 2025; updated July 31, 2026): Defines AWS TCO as the sum of all costs associated with migrating, hosting, running, and maintaining applications, workloads, and data on AWS, typically calculated over 3-5 years. 5-step process: (1) Calculate existing infrastructure cost (equipment, datacenter, software, payroll, maintenance, security, upgrades); (2) Consider opportunity costs and hidden costs (downtime, idle capacity, facility renovations); (3) Calculate AWS migration costs across three phases: assessment/discovery, mobilization, and migration (the most costly phase); (4) Calculate monthly AWS charges based on services used, resource consumption models (On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans), and purchase method; (5) Compare AWS TCO vs. on-premises TCO. Pitfalls that increase AWS TCO: over-provisioning resources, lack of automated scaling, poor cost monitoring, underutilizing spot instances, ignoring reserved instances/savings plans, not optimizing reserved capacity, inefficient storage management, ignoring software license costs, and overlooking security/compliance requirements. [31]

**Hykell — "AWS performance SLA"**: Organizations can reduce costs by 30-50% by tiering services based on business impact rather than pursuing uniform high availability. Multi-region active-active architectures can increase costs 3-5x. Multi-AZ deployments double compute costs and introduce data transfer fees. [32]

### 2.2 AWS Data Transfer and Egress Pricing

**DigitalOcean — "Understanding AWS's Egress Costs"**: AWS charges $0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB of outbound data to the public internet, dropping to $0.085 per GB for the next 40 TB, $0.07 per GB for the next 100 TB, and $0.05 per GB beyond 150 TB. Applies to both EC2 and S3. Inbound (ingress) is free for most services. AWS charges $0.02 per GB for data transferred between different AWS regions. S3 data transfer out to the internet ranges from $0.05 to $0.09 per GB depending on volume. CloudFront CDN charges regional data transfer out fees of at least $0.02 per GB and up to $0.114 per GB for certain regions. AWS egress pricing can be more than five times as expensive as DigitalOcean's flat $0.01 per GiB. A Forrester TEI report cites a 186% ROI over three years for DigitalOcean customers. Cost examples: small business with 5 TB outbound ($460.80) plus 2 TB inter-regional ($40.96) totaling ~$501.76; larger deployment with 100 TB outbound ($7,987.20) plus 50 TB inter-regional ($1,024) totaling ~$9,011.20. (Pricing data accurate as of August 2023.) [33]

**nOps — "AWS Egress Costs & How to Avoid Them"** (published June 7, 2026): Public internet: ~$0.09/GB for first 10 TB/month with tiered discounts; first 1 GB/month free. Between AZs: ~$0.01/GB per direction (even within same region). Between regions: ~$0.02–$0.09/GB, never free. NAT Gateways: charged per hour AND per GB. **2025 Pricing Changes**: (1) Free Tier increased from 1 GB to 100 GB/month (excludes China and GovCloud); (2) Egress fee waivers for legitimate, planned, AWS-approved cloud migrations off AWS. Hidden costs: cross-service API calls, VPC Peering and Transit Gateway (per-GB + data processing fees), Interface Endpoints/PrivateLink (per-hour and per-GB), load balancer to backend traffic, logging/monitoring/telemetry pipelines. Comparison (2025): AWS 100 GB/month free tier, $0.09/GB starting rate, charges cross-AZ traffic, waives fees for migration off AWS; GCP 5 GB/month free tier, $0.12/GB starting rate, free same-zone traffic; Azure 5 GB/month free tier, $0.087–$0.09/GB starting rate, free intra-region traffic. Lightsail includes 1–7 TB free egress monthly depending on plan, then $0.09/GB. [34]

**Forrester — "Amazon AWS Joins Google Cloud In Removing Egress Costs"**: AWS announced removal of egress fees when migrating data to another cloud provider or on-premises, following Google Cloud's January announcement. Unlike Google, AWS doesn't require customers to fully exit or close their accounts, but AWS does require a **60-day exit, full removal of all data and workloads**, and warns repeated migration requests will face "additional scrutiny." Both AWS and Google messaging imply one-way movements. AWS has provided 100 GB of free data egress per month since 2021 (except GovCloud and China). Later the same day, Microsoft Azure also announced removal of its data transfer fees when canceling/deleting an Azure subscription. [35]

**Cloudflare — "What is AWS data transfer pricing?"**: Amazon S3 free transfers: first 100 GB per month transferred out to the Internet (aggregated across all AWS services and Regions except China and GovCloud); data transferred between S3 buckets in the same Region; data transferred from S3 to AWS services within the same Region; data transferred out to Amazon CloudFront. S3 pricing example (US West-Northern California): first 10 TB/month at $0.09/GB; next 40 TB/month at $0.09/GB; next 100 TB/month at $0.07/GB; greater than 150 TB/month at $0.05/GB. US customers typically pay $0.02/GB for transferring data from S3 to a different AWS availability zone. More than half of C-level executives and DevOps professionals cite significant or unexpected cloud spending as their biggest challenge. [36]

**AWS Cost and Usage Report — "Understanding data transfer charges"**: Five categories: (1) Within-region transfers (UsageType `Region-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes`; charged for both inbound and outbound, two line items per transfer); (2) Between-region transfers (only the outgoing source region line item is charged; e.g., `USE2-APS3-AWS-Out-Bytes`); (3) Data transfer out to internet (`Region-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes`); (4) Direct Connect traffic (public virtual interfaces: `DataXfer-In`/`DataXfer-Out`; private/transit: `DataXfer-In:dc.3`/`DataXfer-Out:dc.3`); (5) S3 Transfer Acceleration and CloudFront traffic (CloudFront uses `Region-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes` or `-OBytes` with product code `AmazonCloudFront`). [37]

### 2.3 Microsoft SQL Server and Windows Licensing on AWS

**AWS Prescriptive Guidance — "Understand SQL Server licensing"**: Three AWS licensing categories: (1) License included (pay-as-you-go); (2) BYOL with Microsoft License Mobility for products like SQL Server with Software Assurance (SA) — can bring to shared or dedicated tenancy; (3) BYOL without license mobility (e.g., Windows Server), which requires dedicated options. **Cost data — monthly on-demand costs for c5.xlarge running 24/7**: Windows Server + SQL Server Enterprise = $1,353/month; Windows Server + SQL Server Standard = $609/month; Windows Server only = $259/month; Compute only/Linux = $127/month. Optimization strategies:
- Perpetual Windows Server licenses purchased before 10/1/2019 (or true-ups under Enterprise Agreements signed before that date) can be deployed on Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts.
- Physical-level licensing on dedicated hosts (e.g., 48 licenses for 48 cores/96 vCPUs on an R5 dedicated host with Datacenter/Enterprise editions) can save up to 50% on SQL Server licensing vs. vCPU-based shared tenancy.
- SQL Server consolidation: two 2-vCPU instances into one 4-vCPU instance can reduce licensing by 50% (SQL Server requires minimum four core licenses per instance).
- Downgrading SQL Server Enterprise to Standard can significantly reduce costs. TDE is available in Standard since SQL Server 2019; failover clustering with FSx for Windows File Server is an alternative to Always On availability groups.

- References AWS Optimization and Licensing Assessment (AWS OLA) and right-sizing. [27]

### 2.4 Oracle Licensing on AWS

**Cintra — "Oracle BYOL vs AWS Licensing"** (published 02 Dec 2024): **License Included (LI)**: AWS includes the Oracle Database license with RDS, bundled into the hourly price; only available for Oracle Standard Edition One and Two (restricted to SE2 per AWS Service Terms section 10.3.1); cannot host third-party services. **BYOL**: required for all Oracle editions other than SE1/SE2, and for all editions on Amazon EC2. Under Oracle's Cloud Licensing Policy, **two AWS vCPUs equal one Oracle license**. RDS BYOL example: 160 physical cores/320 vCPUs with cloud factor 0.5 = 160 Oracle licenses. EC2: r7i Shared Tenancy (160 cores/320 vCPUs, factor 0.5 = 160 licenses); r7iz.metal-16xl (160 cores/320 vCPUs, factor 0.5 = 80 licenses); r7iz dedicated hosts (192 cores/384 vCPUs, factor 0.5 = 96 licenses). Three common mistakes: overlooking Oracle support policies, neglecting license compliance management, assuming immunity from Oracle audits (using Oracle on AWS RDS can be a significant audit trigger). Hourly licensing is exclusively available on Amazon RDS. [38]

**MigrationCost.com — "Oracle Database to AWS Migration Cost (2026)"**: **Core licensing rule**: In January 2017, Oracle introduced a 2:1 vCPU conversion ratio for AWS EC2 (and Azure VM) compute — two AWS vCPUs require one Oracle Processor licence. This effectively doubles Oracle licence costs on EC2 BYOL vs. on-premise. The 2:1 rule does NOT apply to RDS for Oracle (due to a separate AWS-Oracle agreement) or OCI. Four destination paths: (1) RDS for Oracle SE2 with License Included: +10 to +25% run-rate vs on-prem; (2) RDS for Oracle EE with BYOL (no 2:1 penalty): -10 to +10% run-rate; (3) Oracle on EC2 BYOL Dedicated Hosts (2:1 penalty): +15 to +40% on licence; (4) Aurora PostgreSQL via SCT (no Oracle licence): -60 to -80% on database total cost. For any workload above 4 vCPUs, RDS for Oracle BYOL is cheaper than EC2 BYOL. Exceptions requiring EC2: RAC, specific Data Guard configs, Database Vault, Advanced Security Option. Aurora PostgreSQL via SCT: SCT automates 70-90% of schema conversion; remaining 10-30% of PL/SQL requires manual conversion. Migration takes 1-4 weeks for SCT analysis, 4-16 weeks for PL/SQL conversion, plus 4-12 weeks for app-side changes. Total migration cost per database: $60K-$300K. Oracle EE with SULS costs $47,500 per processor licence plus 22% annual support ($58K/year fully loaded). A 16-vCPU Oracle EE workload costs ~$465K/year in licensing vs $35K-$60K/year on Aurora. Break-even on $150K migration is typically 4-8 months. Worked 10-database scenario (12 months): net totals Low $868K, Typical $1.888M, High $4.21M. Terminating Oracle licences post-migration saves ~22% of purchase price annually in SULS; terminating 8 EE processor licences saves ~$102K/year permanently. Single database under 1 TB costs $20K-$80K to migrate; larger (5-50 TB) cost $80K-$400K each. RDS migrations of a single database under 5 TB take 4-12 weeks; Aurora migrations take 12-36 weeks. Large estates of 20+ databases run 12-36 months. [39]

**House of Brick — "Oracle Database Licensing for AWS Migrations"**: Oracle's Cloud Policy counts vCPUs rather than physical cores; the core factor table does not apply. Rules: two vCPUs count as one Oracle processor license with multi-threading enabled; one vCPU equals one license with multi-threading disabled; for Standard Editions, four or fewer vCPUs count as one socket license (rounding up in increments of four); max 16 vCPUs for Standard Edition, max 8 vCPUs for SE1 and SE2. Alternatively, traditional core-based licensing can be used with AWS Dedicated Hosts or Bare Metal servers. **Multi-AZ and Cross-Region Replicas**: every active Multi-AZ or Cross-Region replica requires its own Oracle license (double the vCPUs for BYOL counting). Cross-Region automated backups do not require licensing until activated. **Multitenant**: more than three pluggable databases in a container database requires licensing the Multitenant option. **DR and Backups**: DR environments with Oracle software must be fully licensed; Oracle contract allows offsite backup testing four times per year with a maximum calendar days per test; GoldenGate is separately licensed (source and target) with 1-year term licenses available at 20% of perpetual license cost; Data Guard must be fully licensed on both sides. **Container Licensing**: any EC2 instance with a container running Oracle software must be licensed. Comparative table: on-premises 160 physical cores, core factor 0.5 = 80 licenses for VMware on x86; Amazon RDS BYOL 160 vCPUs = 160 licenses; Amazon EC2 shared tenancy = 160 licenses vs. bare metal = 80 licenses vs. dedicated hosts = 96 licenses. [40]

**Redress — "OCI vs AWS for Oracle: Two Conversion Rules"** (published September 8, 2025; updated July 29, 2026): Oracle's Authorized Cloud Environment policy covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, but NOT OCI. On authorized clouds: two vCPUs count as one Processor license (with hyperthreading enabled); the 0.5 x86 core factor does NOT apply, effectively doubling license counts; SE2 limited to instances up to 8 vCPUs. On OCI: one Processor license maps to two OCPUs. Worked example (16 physical cores): Data center = 8 Processor licenses; AWS/Azure/Google = 16 Processor licenses (no core factor); OCI = 8 Processor licenses. Gap: 8 licenses ≈ $380,000 at list price, plus 22% annual support. Hyperthreading: turning it off does NOT reduce license counts on authorized clouds. **Real Application Clusters is NOT available on authorized clouds** (only on OCI, Exadata Cloud at Customer, or Oracle-operated multicloud services). Amazon RDS for Oracle license-included only covers SE2; EE requires BYOL on RDS. About 6 in 10 platform comparisons built in 2024-2025 found the license count was the largest line in the five-year model. [41]

## 3. DOWNTIME AND BUSINESS CONTINUITY RISKS

### 3.1 AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS)

**AWS DRS Pricing page**: Flat hourly fee of **$0.028 per source server per hour** (flat rate regardless of disk count, storage size, number of drill/recovery launches, or AWS Region). No upfront costs, minimum fees, or resources to manage. Pricing includes continuous data replication, test launches, recovery launches, and point-in-time recovery. Additional charges: replicating source servers consumes EBS storage and EC2 compute billed separately. **Pricing Example #1 (100 on-premises servers, 200 disks/30TB, 3.3% daily change rate, 730 hours)**: AWS DRS charge = 100 servers × $0.028/hour × 730 hours = $2,044.00; EBS volumes $1,425.00 (50% gp3 at $0.08/GB-month = $1,200; 50% sc1 at $0.015/GB-month = $225); EBS snapshots (default 7-day retention) $1,846.50 ($0.05/GB-month); EC2 Replication Servers $1,053.54 (14 t3.small at $0.0208/hour + 3 m5.2xlarge at $0.384/hour); **TOTAL MONTHLY COST: $6,389.03** (US-East N. Virginia, On-Demand). **Pricing Example #2 (8-hour DR drill launching 100 recovery instances)**: EBS volumes $28.49; EC2 instances $94.46; **TOTAL: $122.94**. Technical notes: one equally sized EBS "staging disk" per source disk; Replication Servers are low-cost t3.small EC2 instances by default, each handling up to 15 staging disks; costs for fully provisioned recovery servers incurred only during drills and recovery. [43]

**AWS Storage Blog — "Optimize costs and speed up replication with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery"**: AWS DRS offers RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes. Cost structure: $0.028/hour service cost per source server; staging disk costs; snapshot data (PIT schedules: every 10 min for last hour, hourly for 24 hours, daily for 7 days — configurable from 1-365 days); replication servers (one t3.small EC2 at $0.0236/hour per 15 source volumes); conversion servers (less than $0.05 per launched recovery instance); target failover EC2 instances (e.g., $0.1699/hour for t3a.xlarge). Optimization example: optimizing a 75 TB provisioned fleet (30 TB in use) down to 36 TB reduces initial sync time from 6.944 days to 3.333 days and monthly cost from $9,356 to $4,703.45 (US East/N. Virginia, July 18, 2022). AWS DRS is a sound choice for Pilot Light DR strategies. [44]

**AWS DRS Concepts documentation**: **RTO**: typically 5–20 minutes, highly dependent on OS boot time — Linux servers typically boot within 5 minutes; Windows typically within 20 minutes. **RPO**: continuous block-level replication enabling crash-consistent RPO in the sub-second range. In-memory application data is not replicated until written to source volumes. **PIT Snapshots**: crash-consistent recovery points from EBS Snapshots. Default retention: 1 PIT per 10 minutes for the prior hour, 1 per hour for prior 24 hours, 1 per day for prior 7 days. Only the "Day" retention limit is configurable (1–365 days). "Use most recent data" attempts to create an on-demand PIT Snapshot representing a sub-second RPO, waiting up to 10 minutes. [45]

**Substack — "AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)"**: Fully managed service powered by CloudEndure. Features: continuous data replication with low RPO and options for synchronous/asynchronous replication; automated failover and recovery with automatic DNS updates; pay-per-use pricing eliminating idle standby infrastructure; EC2-based recovery, cross-region recovery, on-demand recovery drills; real-time monitoring via Amazon CloudWatch; encryption (in-transit and at-rest) and compliance support (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). 2025 updates include: enhanced automated recovery workflows with application-specific recovery sequencing; integration with AWS Backup; expanded region availability (Africa/Cape Town, Asia Pacific/Jakarta and Kuala Lumpur, South America/São Paulo); FIPS 140-2 certified encryption, deeper IAM role-based access control, Amazon GuardDuty monitoring; support for tens of thousands of VMs; DR support for containers on ECS/EKS/Fargate and serverless on Lambda; advanced analytics with automated risk assessment via CloudWatch and QuickSight; improved live DR drill testing; new planning tools including visual DR Planner and cost estimator; integration with Veeam and Commvault; enhanced regulatory compliance support (GDPR, HIPAA, SOC). Limitations: compatibility constraints with some legacy systems, recovery window variability, network bandwidth/latency bottlenecks for large data transfers, learning curve. [46]

### 3.2 DR Strategies: Multi-AZ, Multi-Region, Active-Passive vs Active-Active

**N2W — "AWS Disaster Recovery: 4 Strategies"** (updated 2026): Four DR strategies: (1) **Backup and Restore** — most cost-effective (AWS Backup); highest RTO/RPO (hours); (2) **Pilot Light** — critical core elements always running, non-essential off until needed; recovery in minutes; (3) **Warm Standby** — scaled-down but always-on environment that can quickly scale up; near-instant recovery; (4) **Multi-Site (Hot Standby)** — identical live environment running concurrently; near-zero RTO/RPO but highest cost. Bonus: Multi-AZ and Multi-Region. **Major AWS US-East-1 regional outage in late 2025 lasted ~15 hours due to a DNS resolution failure in the Region's control plane**, taking down workloads across all Availability Zones simultaneously. Organizations that stayed online were running active-active or active-passive across multiple Regions. Key lesson: treat the Region as a failure domain. [47]

**AWS Architecture Blog — "Disaster Recovery (DR) Architecture on AWS, Part I: Strategies for Recovery in the Cloud"**: Defines disaster as "any event that prevents a workload or system from fulfilling its business objectives in its primary location." RTO and RPO are the two primary objectives; lower numbers cost more. Multi-AZ protects against localized disruptions; Multi-Region protects against events impacting multiple data centers. Four strategies (highest to lowest RTO/RPO): Backup and restore; Pilot light (critical data live, e.g., Aurora global database replicating to read-only cluster; compute idle/shut off); Warm standby (live data plus minimum deployment at reduced capacity, e.g., one EC2 instance per tier); Multi-site active/active (two or more Regions actively accept requests with data replicated, e.g., DynamoDB global tables). Even with replication, backups are still necessary to protect against data deletion/corruption. [48]

**AWS Whitepaper — "Disaster recovery options in the cloud"**: Four strategies. **Backup and Restore**: use IaC (CloudFormation or AWS CDK); services include EBS snapshots, DynamoDB backups, RDS/Aurora snapshots, EFS, Redshift, Neptune, DocumentDB, FSx; AWS Backup centralizes and supports cross-Region/account copying; S3 object versioning and CRR. **Pilot Light**: core infrastructure (databases, object storage) always on; application servers loaded but deprovisioned until failover; continuous cross-region async replication services include S3 Replication, RDS read replicas, Aurora global databases, DynamoDB global tables, DocumentDB global clusters, ElastiCache Global Datastore. **"With Amazon Aurora global database, if your primary Region suffers a performance degradation or outage, you can promote one of the secondary regions to take read/write responsibilities in less than one minute even in the event of a complete regional outage."** AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery implements the Pilot Light strategy using block-level replication. Traffic management via Route 53 (ARC recommended for data plane failover), AWS Global Accelerator, or CloudFront. **Warm Standby**: scaled-down but fully functional copy in another Region; can handle traffic immediately at reduced capacity without additional action (unlike pilot light which requires "turning on" servers); uses EC2 Auto Scaling to scale out; note: Auto Scaling is a control plane operation and lowers resiliency. **Multi-site Active/Active**: workload runs simultaneously in multiple Regions; write strategies: "write global" (single Region handles all writes, promoted on failure), "write local" (closest Region, e.g., DynamoDB global tables with last-writer-wins reconciliation), "write partitioned" (partitioned by key, e.g., bi-directional S3 replication). **"For maximum resiliency, you should use only data plane operations as part of your failover operation. This is because the data planes typically have higher availability design goals than the control planes."** AWS Resilience Hub validates RTO/RPO targets. [49]

**AWS Compute Blog — "Building resilient multi-Region Serverless applications on AWS"**: **Active-Passive**: one Region "Active" handles all production traffic; other Regions "Passive" replicating data and configurations, with readiness levels: Hot Standby (fully deployed), Warm Standby (partially deployed), Pilot Light (minimal core infrastructure). AWS serverless pay-for-value pricing means organizations pay primarily for data replication rather than idle compute. Lambda provisioned concurrency keeps functions warm for failover but incurs costs regardless. **Active-Active**: multiple Regions actively serve traffic concurrently; highest availability but expensive; requires rigorous engineering for data synchronization, conflict resolution, retry mechanisms/circuit breakers; each Region must handle full application load if another fails. The demo uses CloudWatch alarms and a manual approval process — "automated failover is not recommended" for critical applications. Route 53 health check configuration: 10-second request interval with failure threshold of 2. Chaos engineering tools: chaos-lambda-extension and AWS Fault Injection Service (AWS FIS). Cross-Region observability requires monitoring Region A's resources from Region B; CloudWatch enables cross-account and cross-Region monitoring. [50]

**AWS Architecture Blog — "Disaster Recovery Solutions with AWS managed services, Part 3: Multi-Site Active/Passive"**: "Multi-Site Active/Passive" (warm standby) is best for business-critical workloads with higher availability requirements. Seven components demonstrated with a payment transaction processing application: (1) Amazon Route 53 health-checked routing policies (active/passive failover); (2) Amazon EKS control plane (regional, single-tenant); (3) EKS data plane using EC2 Auto Scaling groups with one node in secondary Region that scales up on failover; Velero with Portworx manages persistent volume snapshots stored in S3 (replicated cross-Region via S3 CRR); (4) Amazon OpenSearch Service cross-cluster replication (active-passive follower/leader model; available on Elasticsearch 7.10 or OpenSearch 1.1+); (5) Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL cross-Region read replicas (can be promoted to standalone source servers); (6) Amazon ElastiCache Global Datastore (fully managed cross-Region replication with automatic async replication); (7) Amazon Redshift A/A approach with data flowing via SNS and S3, Lambda functions distributing to both Regions, SQS queues with Extended Client Library. [51]

**AWS Architecture Blog — "Disaster Recovery (DR) Architecture on AWS, Part IV: Multi-Site Active/Active"**: Offers the lowest RTO/RPO but higher cost and complexity. Traffic routing: Route 53 geolocation routing (deterministic, keeps user data in specific Regions, controls write routing) or latency routing. Read/write patterns: **Read-local/write-local** (DynamoDB global tables replicate within a second; "last writer wins" reconciliation); **Read-local/write-global** (one global write Region; uses DynamoDB global tables with write redirection, or Aurora global database with write forwarding over AWS network <1 second replication latency, or ElastiCache Global Datastore); **Read-local/write-partitioned** (each record assigned a "home Region" by first write or partition key; writes route back to home Region). Failover: Route 53 DNS record updates (with appropriately low TTL) or AWS Global Accelerator (non-DNS, static IPs, traffic dials/weights). [52]

## 4. PERFORMANCE AND SCALABILITY POST-MIGRATION

### 4.1 Performance Characteristics by Migration Approach

- **Lift-and-shift (Rehost)**: moves applications to AWS without changes, "without having to make any changes to the applications, their architecture, or the migrated servers" [6, 9]; delivers ~30% cost savings even without cloud optimizations (GE Oil & Gas) [1, 5]; performance is generally preserved since applications run natively on EC2, but elastic scaling requires follow-on optimization (right-sizing, RI commitments, phased modernization roadmap) [5].
- **Replatforming**: minor optimizations without changing core architecture (e.g., SQL Server to Amazon RDS, containerizing with App2Container, AWS Graviton processors) [2, 3, 4].
- **Re-architecture**: enables cloud-native features — elastic scaling, serverless, microservices [1, 2]. AWS Prescriptive Guidance: "Refactor is not recommended for large migrations because it involves modernizing the application during the migration" — instead rehost/relocate/replatform first and modernize after [3].

### 4.2 Scalability Capabilities (Auto Scaling, Serverless)

**Spacelift — "Scaling AWS Infrastructure: Auto Scaling & Other Services"**: Vertical scaling (upgrading EC2 instance type or RDS class) is limited by max capacity, may require downtime, best for monolithic/single-node apps. Horizontal scaling (Auto Scaling EC2 instances, adding Aurora replicas) is theoretically unlimited, no downtime, ideal for distributed/stateless apps. **AWS Auto Scaling** automatically increases/decreases compute resources based on demand (e.g., if web server memory usage exceeds 90%, a new instance is added; removed once usage drops below threshold). Supports scheduled scaling. ALB divides load between EC2 instances or Lambda functions. RDS Multi-AZ places a standby database in another AZ. RDS Read Replicas enhance read performance, auto-synced in real time (available in Aurora and RDS for MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server). Amazon Aurora offers high availability and performance at global scale. Event-driven architecture with SQS and Lambda; Lambda scales by default creating more function instances based on incoming event volume. [57]

**AWS Auto Scaling docs — "Predictive scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling"**: Predictive scaling analyzes historical load data to detect daily/weekly patterns and forecasts future capacity needs so EC2 Auto Scaling can proactively increase capacity. Well suited for: cyclical traffic; recurring on-and-off workload patterns (batch processing, testing, periodic data analysis); applications that take a long time to initialize causing latency impact during scale-out events. Benefits: faster scaling by launching capacity in advance of forecasted load, and potential cost savings by avoiding over-provisioning. [58]

**AWS Architecture Blog — "Let's Architect! Serverless architecture on AWS"**: Half of new applications built by Amazon use AWS Lambda (Andy Jassy, 2020 re:Invent keynote). Topics include event-driven architecture with Amazon EventBridge, serverless patterns (Lambda Power Tuning for memory configuration), transforming rather than transporting data, orchestrating workflows with Step Functions. [59]

**AWS HPC Blog — "A serverless architecture for high performance financial modelling"**: **RenaissanceRe** (one of the world's leading reinsurance companies; 2021: $8B gross premiums, ~$18B capital under management) migrated its high-performance financial modelling system from an on-premises cluster (Python web server + Celery cluster of 9 servers with 512GB RAM and 48 CPU cores each, RabbitMQ, Redis, SAN) to a "serverless first" AWS architecture. Portfolio rollup executes Monte-Carlo risk models across 7,000+ deals, processing ~45TB of data and producing 600GB of raw analytic output per run (~5 runs per day); real-time deal analytics requires thousands of runs per day. New architecture: AWS Step Functions as execution planner building a DAG of deal dependencies stored in Amazon ElastiCache for Redis; Amazon Kinesis "Job" stream; AWS Lambda for high-priority real-time deal analytics; **AWS Fargate for bulk portfolio rollup computations — up to 3,000 containers running in parallel during a full run**; Amazon S3 as computational data lake; Amazon SQS for standard priority jobs; Amazon EventBridge for error handling (failed jobs resubmitted up to three times). S3 key-partitioning supports 100GiB/s data transfer rates on ~20GiB of input data split across 15-20k files. [60]

**AWS Whitepaper — "Microservices on serverless technologies"**: AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate integrated with API Gateway enable fully serverless applications that greatly decrease operational complexity. As of April 7, 2023, AWS Lambda functions can progressively stream response payloads back to clients, significantly improving time to first byte. Amazon Aurora Serverless is an on-demand, auto-scaling database. [61]

**AWS re:Post — "Building a Serverless Architecture on AWS"**: Serverless provides automatic scaling, high availability, and pay-as-you-go pricing. Key services: Lambda, API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB, Step Functions, SNS & SQS. [62]

**Relevant Software — "Microservices on AWS"**: Microservices architecture market projected to grow from $5.31 billion in 2023 to ~$21.61 billion by 2030 (CAGR 18.66%). AWS holds 32% of the global cloud infrastructure market. [63]

### 4.3 Latency Considerations for Financial Trading Workloads

**AWS Industries Blog — "Rethinking the low latency trade value proposition using AWS Local Zones"**: At re:Invent 2021, NASDAQ announced partnership with AWS to transform Capital Markets and migrate its North American markets to the cloud. AWS launched Local Zones in New York, Chicago, Kansas City, and Minneapolis (September 2021), enabling low-latency trading workloads with exchange access requirements as low as **1 millisecond**. Proof Trading's institutional equities execution platform on AWS achieves latency of **~50μs between AWS servers within the same availability zone and ~400μs across availability zones**. Recommended architecture: latency-sensitive execution components in Local Zones (close to exchanges); high-performance supporting systems (strategy development, capital management) in resilient Availability Zones. [64]

**AWS Web3 Blog — "Optimize tick-to-trade latency for digital assets exchanges and trading platforms on AWS (Part 2)"**: Five-tier hierarchy of latency impacts, ordered by impact: Placement & Region (100ms), Network Path Engineering (2ms), Instance & Bare Metal selection (200µs), OS Tuning & Kernel Bypass (50µs), Application Tuning (5µs). **Placement decisions have approximately 20,000x more latency impact than application tuning.** "No amount of cache-line alignment or lock-free queue tuning recovers the milliseconds you lose by deploying in the wrong Region or routing traffic through an unnecessary network hop." Market maker trading hot-path: (1) Market Data Ingestion (kernel bypass DPDK with PTP timestamping); (2) Packet Processing & Normalization (single-threaded parsing with huge pages and busy polling); (3) Signal Generation (all-in-memory state, NUMA-aware); (4) Risk Assessment (in-memory deterministic checks, async logging to NVMe); (5) Order Construction & Transmission (kernel bypass send with wire timestamping, direct NIC access, placement close to matching engine). Benchmark tool: github.com/aws-samples/trading-latency-benchmark. Optimization layers: Placement (same Region and AZ as exchange gateway; AWS Direct Connect for hybrid); Network Path (avoid ELB, Transit Gateway, NAT, or inspection appliances; use VPC Peering; shared Cluster Placement Groups; "EC2 hunting"); Instance Selection (largest instance size for full-slot exclusive access; bare metal .metal guarantees single tenancy — benchmark results show metal instances provide 6-14% p50 improvement and 15-29% p99.9 improvement over full-slot instances, e.g., m8azn: 17.7µs vs 18.9µs p50; m5zn: 20.3µs vs 23.6µs p50; C7i 24xl: 20.3µs vs 21.7µs p50); Time Synchronization (Amazon Time Sync Service, free, hardware timestamps require physical NIC traversal); Networking (network-optimized instances m6in, c6in, m8azn reduce tail latency up to 85% at p99.9, increase single-flow bandwidth 5x; use latest ENA driver; ENA Express is rarely right for HFT — increases CPU overhead and inflates p50; conventional ENA with DPDK, XDP zero-copy, or SR-IOV preferred); Storage (instance store offers sub-millisecond latency but ephemeral; EBS io2 Block Express competitive for persistent); OS Tuning (Linux kernels 6.1+ deliver lower latency; Ubuntu with kernel 6.12+ preferred, followed by Rocky Linux and RHEL; tail latency improved almost universally after tuning, max latency dropped 27% even where p50 barely changed on m8azn.metal; Intel c7i and AMD m5zn benefit most at 28-36% p50 improvement; Graviton c8g offers exceptional consistency — 21.4µs p50, 23.4µs p99.9 — with minimal tuning). [65]

## 5. SECURITY AND COMPLIANCE

### 5.1 AWS Compliance Certifications and Programs Overview

**AWS Compliance page**: AWS supports **143 security standards and compliance certifications**, including PCI-DSS, HIPAA/HITECH, FedRAMP, GDPR, FIPS 140-3, and NIST 800-171. Third-party validation for thousands of global compliance requirements, continually monitored across finance, retail, healthcare, government. On-demand compliance reports available through AWS Artifact. Shared responsibility model: AWS manages components from the host OS and virtualization layer down to physical facility security; the customer is responsible for the guest OS (including updates and security patches), associated application software, and configuration of the AWS security group firewall. Compliance tools: AWS Audit Manager (continuously audits AWS usage to simplify risk assessment and compliance), Amazon GuardDuty (intelligent threat detection and continuous monitoring), AWS Artifact (no-cost, self-service portal for on-demand access to AWS compliance reports), AWS Security Assurance Services. AWS gives customers ownership and control over their customer content through tools that determine where content is stored, secure it in transit or at rest, and manage access. [67]

**AWS Compliance Programs page**: Three categories: (1) **Certifications and Attestations** (assessed by third-party independent auditors; broken down by global, Americas, Asia Pacific, EMEA); (2) **Laws, Regulations and Privacy** (customers remain responsible; AWS offers supporting functionality, enablers, and legal agreements such as the AWS Data Processing Agreement and Business Associate Addendum; no formal certification available to CSPs in these domains); (3) **Alignments and Frameworks** (compliance playbooks, mapping documents, whitepapers). Highlights the **AWS European Sovereign Cloud** — a new independent cloud entirely within the EU designed for digital sovereignty needs. [68]

### 5.2 PCI DSS

**AWS Security Blog — "Fall 2025 PCI DSS compliance package available now"**: AWS announced the Fall 2025 PCI DSS compliance package, adding two new AWS services and one new AWS Region to scope. Evaluation conducted by Coalfire, a third-party Qualified Security Assessor (QSA). Accessible through AWS Artifact. **AWS is the first cloud service provider to offer compliance reports in NIST's Open Security Controls Assessment Language (OSCAL) format** — an open-source, machine-readable (JSON) format. The PCI DSS report package (including the PCI DSS AOC and AWS Responsibility Summary) in OSCAL format is available separately in AWS Artifact. [69]

**Medium (Dhaval Soni) — "PCI DSS Compliance Readiness with AWS Security Hub"**: PCI-DSS is administered by the PCI Security Standards Council (founded by American Express, Discover, JCB International, MasterCard Worldwide, and Visa Inc.). Applies to entities storing, processing, or transmitting cardholder data (CHD) or sensitive authentication data (SAD). **AWS is certified as a PCI DSS Level 1 Service Provider (the highest level of assessment available), but customers must manage their own PCI-DSS compliance certification.** Customers can rely on AWS Attestation of Compliance (AOC) for the portion of the CDE deployed in AWS; the "AWS PCI DSS Responsibility Summary" is available through AWS Artifact. AWS Security Hub checks against PCI-DSS, CIS Benchmark, and best practices; collects data from Guard Duty, Inspector, Config, Macie, and third-party partners. Supports three standards: CIS AWS Foundations, PCI DSS 3.2.1, AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. Standard is validated by AWS Security Assurance Services LLC (AWS SAS), a team of Qualified Security Assessors (QSAs). Security Hub and AWS Config are regional resources — enable in all regions used. [70]

### 5.3 SOC Reports

**AWS Compliance — "SOC Compliance"**: Three types of AWS SOC Reports (audited by Ernst & Young LLP): 
- **SOC 1 Report**: description of AWS control environment and external audit of defined controls and objectives; available via AWS Artifact; covers 12-month period ending 3/31, 6/30, 9/30, or 12/31; audited under SSAE No. 18/AT-C section 320 and ISAE 3402; audience: customer management and auditors; relevant to internal controls over financial reporting (ICFR).
- **SOC 2 Report (Security, Availability, Confidentiality, & Privacy)**: external audit meeting AICPA Trust Services Criteria; available via AWS Artifact; covers 12-month period ending 3/31 or 9/30; audited under SSAE No. 18/AT-C sections 105 and 205, and TSP section 100A (2017 Trust Services Criteria); NDA required to review.
- **SOC 3 Report (Security, Availability, Confidentiality, & Privacy)**: publicly available; same audit standards as SOC 2 but does not disclose AWS internal information.
- AWS publishes SOC 1 reports quarterly and SOC 2/3 twice per year, each covering the previous 12 months, released ~9-10 weeks after the reporting period end. Reporting cycles: Spring (April 1-March 31, SOC 1/2/3 issued late May), Summer (July 1-June 30, SOC 1 only issued late August), Fall (October 1-September 30, SOC 1/2/3 issued late November), Winter (January 1-December 31, SOC 1 only issued late February). The SOC Continued Operations Letter (Bridge Letter/COL) is updated monthly in AWS Artifact. **In January 2026, AWS announced general availability of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud** — a dedicated independent cloud for Europe entirely within the EU, with its own SOC 2 report covering independent EU corporate structures, EU-resident personnel, and strict residency requirements. [71]

**Linford & Company — "AWS Security Tools: How to Simplify SOC 2 Compliance"**: Recommended baseline controls: strong passwords and MFA; IAM user groups, roles, policies; delete root account access keys; enable CloudTrail; use AWS Control Tower for complex multi-account environments. Five AWS security tool groups for SOC 2: (1) Logging and Monitoring (CloudTrail, CloudWatch, GuardDuty); (2) AWS Trusted Advisor (real-time guidance; Basic/Developer covers basic security checks; Business/Enterprise offers broad checks); (3) Amazon Inspector (automated security assessment; CVEs, CIS Benchmarks, network reachability; integrates with Security Hub); (4) AWS Security Hub (comprehensive view of security alerts across all accounts; automated response and remediation with CloudWatch); (5) AWS Audit Manager (audit and manage AWS usage; frameworks for SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, HITRUST, FedRAMP, GDPR; select framework, define scope, activate assessment, review, delegate monitoring, generate audit-ready reports). [72]

**AWS re:Post — "How to be SOC2 compliant"**: AWS Audit Manager comes with a prebuilt SOC 2 framework (SSAE No. 18 SOC Report 2); all standards in Security Hub must be enabled and necessary AWS Config rules enabled. Security Hub standards include AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (v1.2.0, v1.4.0, v3.0.0), NIST 800-53, PCI DSS (v3.2.1, v4.0.1), AWS Resource Tagging Standard. SOC 2 compliance is mostly about organizational controls; auditors look at how infrastructure is provisioned and changed — using IaC (e.g., Terraform) with compliance controls embedded early makes demonstrating compliance easier. AICPA Trust Services Criteria (CC1-CC9) are in AWS Artifact's SOC 2 report; everything else (access reviews, change management, incident response, vendor management) is the customer's responsibility. Recommended services: AWS Audit Manager, AWS Config, AWS CloudTrail, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS IAM, AWS Security Hub, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS KMS, VPC/security groups/Network ACLs, AWS Backup. SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria categories: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy. [73]

### 5.4 Security Hub, AWS Config, Control Tower, Audit Manager, KMS

**AWS Security Hub — "Standards reference for CSPM"**: Eight supported standards: (1) AWS Foundational Security Best Practices; (2) AI Security Best Practices (network isolation, encryption, VPC placement, AWS KMS key usage); (3) AWS Resource Tagging; (4) CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark; (5) NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5; (6) NIST SP 800-171 Revision 2; (7) PCI DSS; (8) Service-managed standard, AWS Control Tower. "Security Hub CSPM standards and controls don't guarantee compliance with any regulatory frameworks or audits. Instead, they provide a way to evaluate and monitor the state of your AWS accounts and resources." If consolidated control findings are enabled, a single finding is generated per control even across multiple standards. [74]

**AWS User Guide for Federally Regulated Financial Institutions in Canada** (October 2025 edition): AWS operates two Regions in Canada — Canada (Central) in Montreal and Canada West (Calgary) — each with three Availability Zones. AWS compliance certifications relevant to FRFIs: CCCS Medium Cloud Security Profile (150 services assessed as of November 2023) and Protected B High Value Assets (PBHVA) assessment (149 services); ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, ISO 9001; PCI DSS Level 1; SOC 1, SOC 2, SOC 3. **AWS Artifact provides access to 2,600+ security controls and compliance documents.** OSFI Guidelines coverage: B-10 (Third-Party Risk Management, effective May 1, 2024), B-13 (Technology and Cyber Risk Management, effective January 1, 2024), E-21 (Operational Risk Management and Resilience, published August 22, 2024; full adherence by September 1, 2026; testing for all critical operations by September 1, 2027). AWS recommends the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF), AWS Well-Architected Framework (six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability), Financial Services Industry Lens, and NIST Cybersecurity Framework alignment whitepaper. Shared responsibility: for IaaS like EC2, customers handle the guest OS, patches, and security group configuration; for abstracted services like S3 and DynamoDB, customers manage data, encryption, asset classification, and IAM permissions. [75]

**AWS Compliance / re:Post on SOC 2**: AWS Artifact is a no-cost, self-service portal for on-demand access to AWS compliance reports. [67, 73]

**Packt video — "AWS Data Security: Regulated Industries and AWS Compliance Programs"**: Strongly regulated industries include financial services, healthcare, and public sector. AWS compliance does not automatically make a customer's deployment compliant; customers may need to enhance the platform with intrusion detection/prevention systems, specific configurations, web application firewalls, or specific data encryption. AWS provides artifacts (certificates, audit reports, documentation) accessible via the AWS Management Console under the Security section, under NDA. [76]

# Discover and assess your database workloads migration to Google Cloud using Migration Center

##### Arkapravo Banerjee

Data Management Specialist

##### Nimrod Shavit

Senior Product Manager

##### Try Gemini Enterprise Business Edition today

The front door to AI in the workplace

Organizations continue to adopt the public cloud to deliver better business and IT outcomes. However, migration — and modernization — is a complex, multifaceted challenge. It involves understanding the current state of infrastructure and applications to determine what the future state should look like and how to get there. And all this occurs across multiple stakeholders using myriad tools, processes, and implementation partners. But wait, don’t let that scare you off – we have good news, too! 

[Google Cloud Migration Center](https://cloud.google.com/migration-center/docs/migration-center-overview), a unified platform to help accelerate migration from current on-premises or cloud environments to Google Cloud, is designed to streamline your cloud journey with intelligent, data-driven insights and actionable recommendations. This will help you make critical decisions on the optimal migration and modernization pathways for your organization.

Migration Center lets you discover and assess both servers and databases, which are critical components of your IT infrastructure. In this blog we will focus on databases discovery and assessment journey within Migration Center. 

The databases discovery and assessment journey consists of three main phases:

Let’s look at each of these in greater depth.

#### Try Google Cloud for free

Start building with $300 in free credits for new customers. All customers get free usage of 20+ products, up to monthly limits.

### **Discovery and collection of source database details**

**Database configuration and metrics collection** Collecting Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL and PostgreSQL source database configurations is executed using [open-source collection scripts](https://cloud.google.com/migration-center/docs/discover-and-import-databases).

You can run the script in your source system either in the database server directly or from a remote server that has access to the database. Here is an example for running the script from a bastion/jump server:

Upon completion the script automatically creates an archive of the extracted configuration and metrics (one ZIP file per database instance) that you can upload into Migration Center.

**Note:** If you are running the script from a bastion/Jump server and not directly the database server, then pass the Parameter “--vmUserName” to collect the host’s specification details. 

**Uploading discovery artifacts to Migration Center**

Once you’ve generated the output files, you can upload them to Migration Center to perform the product assessment by following these steps: 

Open **Google Cloud console > MIgration Center** home page. Go to **Discovery > Data Import > Add Files > Upload Files**

In the next step, choose the file format as “**Database Import File**” and then upload all your DMA output zip files and click on **Upload Files.**

You can now review the uploaded database deployments in Migration Center Assets section.

### **Technical fit assessment**

You can find all the discovered servers and databases in the Assets section of Migration Center. The list of database deployments surfaces high-level details of discovered databases along with a high-level fit score for Cloud SQL and AlloyDB.  

To review a detailed configuration, click on the source databases you want to assess, and the available data: source logical database configurations, hosting server configurations, performance data, feasible cloud products, the fit score, and target instance sizing. 

You can also review the technical fit report by clicking on the fit score (e.g., fit with effort), which lists unsupported features/parameters/flags that were identified in the source databases and that will need to be mitigated when migrating to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB.

![https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/image2_cqvxFcJ.max-1500x1500.png](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/image2_cqvxFcJ.max-1500x1500.png)
![https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/image2_cqvxFcJ.max-1500x1500.png](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/image2_cqvxFcJ.max-1500x1500.png)

### **Cost estimates**

Assessing the cost of running servers and databases in the cloud in Migration Center is a three-step process:

Group together the servers and/or databases (in one or multiple groups) to be assessed.

Create one or more migration preferences that will serve as migration scenarios to assess.

Create a TCO report by assigning groups to up to four preferences. 

**1. Create group**

To create the pricing report, you need to create a group using the assets you want to evaluate for cost estimates. Go to **Discovery -> Groups -> Create Group.**

Select the relevant servers and/or databases that you would like to assess as a group. We recommend creating groups that categorize your source environment (e.g., applications, environments, etc.). 

**2. Create migration preferences**

[Migration preferences](https://cloud.google.com/migration-center/docs/migration-preferences) are basically a set of parameters that you can define to represent a migration scenario. You can create multiple migration preferences and use them to generate “what if” scenarios in TCO reports to compare costs for the servers and databases in the cloud. For example, you can create migration preferences for **different editions of Cloud SQL** with options for **high availability** and **backups** enabled. 

To create a migration preference, go to **Migration Center > Discovery > Migration Preferences > Create MIgration Preference**. 

**3. Create a TCO report for your server and database workloads**

In the TCO report you can review source environment details, cost estimates for servers and databases, and export the report in Google Slides or CSV formats. Below is an example of the databases cost estimates:

![https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/image1_GsFKUkS.max-1000x1000.png](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/image1_GsFKUkS.max-1000x1000.png)
![https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/image1_GsFKUkS.max-1000x1000.png](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/image1_GsFKUkS.max-1000x1000.png)

With Migration Center, our goal is to put the information you need when doing a migration and modernization project at your fingertips, so you can reduce the time, energy, and cost of these projects. As you navigate your journey to the cloud, we’re here to help with Migration Center. [Start using Migration Center](https://console.cloud.google.com/migration?gtm_source=blog&gtm_source_id=%5Bstreamline-migration-and-modernization-to-google-cloud-with-migration-center%5D) today, or to learn more, check out the web pages for [Migration Center](https://cloud.google.com/migration-center/docs/) and [Rapid Discovery and Assessment Program](https://cloud.google.com/solutions/cloud-migration-program?e=48754805&hl=en) (RAMP).

![https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/19_-_Infrastructure_Modernization_o5CKMmf.max-700x700.jpg](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/19_-_Infrastructure_Modernization_o5CKMmf.max-700x700.jpg)

By David Yahalom • 7-minute read

## Overview

M igrating to the public cloud is a complex task that requires analysis, planning, and the execution of a comprehensive organisational and technical strategy aligned with enterprise objectives. This blog explores into the Cloud Migration Centre, a solution designed to address issues such as understanding the existing environment, identifying assets across on-premises or other cloud infrastructure, evaluating compatibility with Google Cloud services, determining the optimal Google Cloud environment, and estimating cloud migration operating costs.

Approximately 68% of enterprise businesses are prepared to migrate to cloud, while IDC says about 75% of enterprise workloads are not in the public cloud. By the year 2024, a significant majority of businesses aim to allocate 80% of their IT hosting budget to cloud-based solutions. This includes investments in private cloud services, Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS). According to IDC’s forecast, the IaaS market is expected to expand to a remarkable $448 billion by the close of 2025.

Google Cloud Migration Center serves as a central hub for managing and orchestrating cloud migration initiatives. It provides a comprehensive set of tools and capabilities that help organisations.

In this part of the blog, we will look into cost estimation, discover assets and assess infrastructure, and In the following part of the blog, we will further explore the planning process and migration strategies.

## Estimate Cloud Costs

Gaining an understanding of the approximate migration costs is a critical step prior to commencing any migration project. Migration Center generates a rapid cost estimate of future cloud costs based on the size and configuration of the resources in the current on-premises environment.

This is a quick and high level estimate, and actual costs may vary depending on specific usage patterns. However, it is a good starting point for budgeting cloud migration projects.

Migration Center offers several cost calculators for different scenarios:

**On-Premise Migration:**Provides a rapid cost estimate for migrating on-premises infrastructure to Google Cloud. It requires minimal inputs (e.g., vCPU cores, storage footprint, memory) and allows customisation of default assumptions.

**SAP Workloads:**Enables the generation of cost estimates for hosting SAP workloads on Google Cloud. Allows users to choose pricing tracks, migration timespans, and specify applications and sizes for deployment. Built-in sizes contribute to estimating SAP system requirements with minimal inputs.

**Data Warehousing:**Facilitates a quick cost estimate for running data analytics and warehousing setups on BigQuery serverless data warehouse on Google Cloud.

**Business Benefits:**

*   **Efficient Cost Estimation:**Quickly and efficiently estimates the costs of Google Cloud products and services for infrastructure migration.
*   **Optimised Configurations:**Recommends optimised configurations for workloads, contributing to estimating the total cost of ownership on Google Cloud.
*   **Comprehensive Cost Calculation:**Offers a single tool to calculate costs for running various Google Cloud services, considering factors like CPU cores, memory, storage, and specific workloads (e.g., Oracle, SAP, Microsoft SQL server, OS foundations).
*   **Long-Term Projection:**Considers a 5-year timeframe to gauge migration costs, providing a long-term projection and transparency in cost planning.

## Discover Assets

Discovery is about finding all the components of infrastructure, including physical machines, VMs, and databases hosted on-premises or on other cloud providers. Migration Center streamlines asset inventory creation by automating the scanning of on-premises environments. This automation frees up valuable time and resources that would otherwise be dedicated to manual data collection.

However, for organisations that prefer manual control, Migration Center also offers the option to manually upload infrastructure data.

**Collection Methods**

*   Download and run the discovery client CLI (mcdc) and scan your infrastructure.
*   Install the discovery client on a Windows machine and allow it to periodically scan infrastructure and gather configuration and performance data.
*   Collect data from your infrastructure hosted on other cloud providers with automated scripts, and upload it to the Migration Center.
*   Manually fill in template tables with infrastructure data, including specifications, performance, and disk data, and upload them to the Migration Center.
*   Upload infrastructure data generated with RVTools directly into the Migration Center.

## Assess Infrastructure

Assessing infrastructure is a critical step in any migration process, regardless of whether you are migrating to the cloud, a new data centre, or a new IT infrastructure provider. With Migration Center and other integrated Google Cloud products, such as StratoZone, you can dive deep in the analysis and get a holistic view into your environment.

*   Understand potential targets in Google Cloud and get suggestions on the Google Cloud services to migrate your assets to, and know the costs in advance.
*   Understand the Implications including potential benefits, risks, and resource requirements
*   Use Migration Center to create and compare various “what-if” scenarios, evaluating the impact of different migration approaches.
*   Based on comprehensive assessment, make an informed decision about the structure and configuration of cloud environment.

# Migration Center overview Stay organized with collections Save and categorize content based on your preferences.

 

Google Cloud Migration Center is a unified platform that helps you accelerate your end-to-end cloud journey from your current on-premises or other cloud environments to Google Cloud. With features like cloud spend estimation, asset discovery of your current environment, and a variety of tooling for different migration scenarios, Migration Center provides you with what you need for your migration.

Curious to learn a bit more? Check out this quick video on Migration Center.

## Explore Migration Center

The tools within Migration Center let you estimate your cloud costs, scan and assess your infrastructure, and plan your migration without making changes to your applications or workloads. Read more about each of these key feature sets.

### Estimate your cloud costs

Migration Center lets you generate a rapid cost estimate of future Google Cloud costs based on the size and configuration of your current on-premises or other cloud environment resources ([Preview](https://cloud.google.com/products#product-launch-stages)).

Learn how to [generate a rapid cost estimate](/migration-center/docs/generate-estimate).

### Discover your assets

Migration Center helps you create an inventory of your assets, including servers, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, and PostgreSQL databases, by automatically scanning your on-premises environment. By automating as much of this as possible with Migration Center, it saves your organization time and energy that would otherwise be spent collecting this data manually.

However, if you don't want automatic data collection for your assets, you can also choose to manually upload your infrastructure data into Migration Center.

Learn how to [discover your assets](/migration-center/docs/start-asset-discovery).

### Assess your infrastructure

With Migration Center, you can dive deep in the analysis and get a holistic view into your environment.

* Generate total cost of ownership reports based on the migration preferences that you specify according to your business objectives and constraints.
* Identify application and network dependencies to know which components you must migrate together.
* Get data-driven suggestions based on a technical fit assessment on the Google Cloud products to migrate your assets to, and know the costs in advance.

Learn how to [assess your infrastructure](/migration-center/docs/view-assets).

### Plan your migration

By using the detailed assessment, you can plan your migration, while lowering the overall migration risks. Migration Center provides you with many tools to help you in this journey, including best practices to plan a migration and prescriptive recommendations on what you should migrate and how.

Learn how to [plan your migration](/migration-center/docs/migration-planning-overview).

### Migrate

# Google Cloud Landing Zone: What It Is and Why It Matters to Your Migration

##### Authors

* **Anis Zekri**EMEA Google Cloud Infrastructure Tribe Leader at Devoteam
* **Rute Marques**Content Manager

---

##### Share

[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.devoteam.com/expert-view/google-cloud-landing-zone-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters-to-your-migration/)   [X](https://x.com/share?url=https://www.devoteam.com/expert-view/google-cloud-landing-zone-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters-to-your-migration/&text=Google%20Cloud%20Landing%20Zone:%20What%20It%20Is%20and%20Why%20It%20Matters%20to%20Your%20Migration)   [Linkedin](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https://www.devoteam.com/expert-view/google-cloud-landing-zone-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters-to-your-migration/&title=Google%20Cloud%20Landing%20Zone:%20What%20It%20Is%20and%20Why%20It%20Matters%20to%20Your%20Migration)

Estimated reading time: 7 minutes

## Table of contents

* [What’s a Google Cloud Landing Zone](#h-what-s-a-google-cloud-landing-zone)
* [Why It Matters Before You Migrate](#h-why-it-matters-before-you-migrate)
* [DIY vs. Guided Setup](#h-diy-vs-guided-setup)
* [6 Common Mistakes](#h-6-common-mistakes)
* [What a Good Google Cloud Landing Zone Looks Like](#h-what-a-good-google-cloud-landing-zone-looks-like)
* [Final Thoughts](#h-final-thoughts)

Most Google Cloud migrations that stall or go over budget share a common problem, and it rarely has anything to do with workloads being moved. The issue is what came before: a cloud environment that wasn’t properly set up to receive them.

That foundation is what a landing zone provides. Get it right, and your migration has somewhere solid to land. Get it wrong, and you’ll spend months unwinding decisions that felt fine at the time.

This article covers what **Google Cloud Landing Zone** is, why it matters before you migrate a single workload, and what separates a well-configured environment from one that creates problems down the line.

## What’s a Google Cloud Landing Zone

A landing zone is a pre-configured, governed cloud environment that your workloads migrate into. Think of it as the infrastructure layer you build before you build anything else – the groundwork for everything else.

In Google Cloud terms, a landing zone typically covers:

* **Organisational Governance:** Ensuring consistent structure across global business units.
* **Networking & Connectivity:** Building a secure “private highway” for your data.
* **Strategic IAM:** Defining who (and what AI agents) can access sensitive company IP.
* **Security & Compliance:** Hard-coding regulatory requirements so they can’t be bypassed.
* **AI-Readiness:** Ensuring the foundation can support Generative AI and Large Language Models without leaking proprietary data.
* **Full-Stack Observability:** Establishing centralised logging, monitoring, and tracing so that every layer of your environment, from infrastructure to AI model performance, is visible, measurable, and actionable.
* **Infrastructure Automation (IaC):** Leveraging “Infrastructure as Code” to deploy, scale, and update the environment automatically, ensuring consistency and eliminating manual human error.
* **Financial Guardrails:** Implementing real-time visibility to prevent “cloud sprawl” and unexpected AI costs.

None of this is glamorous, but every decision made here ripples through every workload, every team, and every project that follows.

## Why It Matters Before You Migrate

The temptation in most migration projects is to start moving things. There’s pressure to show progress, and spinning up a VM or migrating a database feels like momentum.

But workloads carry assumptions about the environment they’re running in. They assume certain network paths exist, specific IAM roles are in place, and billing is structured in a way that makes cost attribution possible.

**If those assumptions aren’t backed into your landing zone before migration begins, you end up retrofitting, which is significantly harder than doing it right the first time**.

You end up configuring IAM while services are live, restructuring networking while teams depend on connectivity, and cleaning up billing data after costs have already been misattributed for months.

A landing zone forces those decisions early, when changing them is cheap.

## DIY vs. Guided Setup

Google provides solid starting points. The [Cloud Foundation Toolkit](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/cloud-foundation-toolkit) offers Terraform modules for common landing zone patterns, and the [Google Cloud Setup Checklist](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/enterprise/cloud-setup) walks through the key configuration steps. For teams with strong Google Cloud Platform expertise and straightforward requirements, these are genuinely useful.

But most enterprise environments aren’t straightforward. Compliance requirements vary by industry and region, multi-team environments need governance models that generic blueprints don’t fully address, and hybrid connectivity – integrating Google Cloud Platform with existing on-premises infrastructure – introduces complexity that requires decisions that aren’t documented in any checklist.

**The gap between following Google’s documentation and having an environment that’s actually right for your organisation is where most of the risk lives.**

It’s also where experienced partners like [Devoteam](https://www.devoteam.com/google-cloud/) add the most value. Not by doing something mysterious, but by having seen enough landing zones to know which decisions bite teams later.

Diamond Google Cloud Partner

## Planning a Google Cloud migration?

Explore Devoteam’s Google Cloud services.

[explore now](https://www.devoteam.com/google-cloud/it-infrastructure-modernisation/)

## 6 Common Mistakes

Those come up repeatedly across landing zone projects:

1. **Overly permissive IAM.** Grating broad roles early to unblock trams feels pragmatic in the moment. It creates a security and compliance problem that’s painful to walk back once people are used to the access they have. Start with least privilege and document exceptions.
2. **Flat network design.** Putting everything in a single VPC with no segmentation is simple to set up and creates headaches at scale. Shared VPC with proper subnet segmentation by environment (dev, staging, prod) and team is worth the upfront complexity.
3. **Understanding “Shadow AI”.** If your landing zone doesn’t make it easy for developers to access AI tools securely, they will find ways around it, using unvetted models and public tools. A well-configured landing zone provides a “paved path” to innovation.
4. **No resource labelling strategy.** Labels are how you attribute costs, filter resources, and enforce policies. Without a consistent labelling taxonomy agreed upfront, you end up with inconsistent metadata that makes cost visibility and governance significantly harder.
5. **Missing cost guardrails.** Budget alerts and billing export to BigQuery should be configured from day one, not once someone notices an unexpected invoice. By then, the data you need to investigate is already gone or hard to reconstruct.
6. **Treating the landing zone as a one-time task.** Landing zones evolve. As your Google Cloud Platform footprint grows, the governance model needs to keep pace. Build in a review process from the start rather than treating initial setup as a closed chapter.

## What a Good Google Cloud Landing Zone Looks Like

Every organisation’s requirements are different, but some patterns hold consistently.

**Resource hierarchy is designed around how the organisation works**. Projects are grouped by team or application domain, with folder-level policies that enforce guardrails without requiring per-project configuration.

**Networking** **is built for the long term**, and not just the immediate migration. Shared VPCs with environment-specific subnets, firewall rules documented and version-controlled, and hybrid connectivity whether via VPN or Dedicated Interconnect – tested before any workloads depend on it.

**IAM is explicit and least-privileged by default**. Custom roles replace built-in ones where scope is too broad, service accounts are tied to specific workloads rather than shared, and access is reviewed on a defined schedule.

**Logging and monitoring are active before the first workload arrives**. Cloud Audit Logs, Security Command Center, and billing export to BigQuery are configured from day one, not retrofitted once something goes wrong.

## Final Thoughts

A landing zone is the first real decision in any Google Cloud migration, but it’s only one piece of the picture. If you’re thinking about what it takes to build a cloud environment that’s ready for AI workloads and not just for today’s infrastructure, our [ebook](https://go.devoteam.com/hubfs/Migrating%20to%20an%20AI%20-ready%20cloud_Ebook_Devoteam%20Cobranded.pdf) is a good place to start.
