| DDoS bill protection |

## Global Front End

[Global Front End](/docs/networking/cross-cloud-network/global-front-end/gfee-overview) combines Cloud Armor, [global external Application Load Balancers](/load-balancing/docs/application-load-balancer),  [Service Extensions](/service-extensions/docs/overview), and  [Cloud CDN](/cdn/docs/overview) into one solution to help deliver, scale, and secure your internet-facing applications. With the  [Global Front End Enterprise](/docs/networking/cross-cloud-network/global-front-end/gfee-overview#global-front-end-enterprise) billing tier, pricing for these products is consolidated under a [single pricing plan](/vpc/network-pricing?e=48754805#global-front-end-enterprise).

Enabling Global Front End Enterprise in a project enables specific Cloud Armor Enterprise features for your global external Application Load Balancer, but doesn't change the Cloud Armor tier at the project level. Resources other than global external Application Load Balancers (such as internal load balancers or regional load balancers) within the same project continue under their current Cloud Armor pricing tiers (Cloud Armor Standard or Cloud Armor Enterprise). When you disable Global Front End Enterprise, active Cloud Armor protections are determined by the project-level tier. The Google Cloud console does not restore a previous tier automatically. You must immediately and manually designate a Cloud Armor billing tier (either Cloud Armor Standard or Cloud Armor Enterprise PayGo) to avoid security policy degradation or unexpected billing changes.

The following table summarizes how enabling Global Front End Enterprise affects resources depending on the project's Cloud Armor tier.

| Resource type | Project tier: Cloud Armor Standard | Project tier: Cloud Armor Enterprise (Paygo or Annual) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Global external Application Load Balancers** | Enables specific Cloud Armor Enterprise features with consolidated billing:  * Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules * Adaptive Protection * Google Threat Intelligence * DDoS attack visibility * Address Groups | Enables all Cloud Armor Enterprise features with consolidated billing |
| **All other resources** (for example, regional external Application Load Balancers or internal load balancers) | Unaffected (Cloud Armor Standard features and pricing) | Unaffected (Cloud Armor Enterprise features and pricing) |

## Subscribe to Cloud Armor Enterprise

Subscribing to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual requires a one-year (12-month) commitment. Only users with the billing account role and permissions can subscribe the billing account to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual. Alternatively, you can enroll in Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo with no commitment.

To use the additional services and capabilities in Cloud Armor Enterprise, you must first enroll in Cloud Armor Enterprise. You can subscribe to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual and enroll individual projects, or you can enroll a project directly in Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo.

We recommend that you enroll your projects in Cloud Armor Enterprise as soon as possible because activation can take up to one hour. Upgrading from Cloud Armor Standard to Enterprise typically won't disrupt your application's availability. However, when you make changes to your security policies you must carefully consider the billing implications.

### External Application Load Balancer and external proxy Network Load Balancer

After a project is enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise, the forwarding rules within the project are added to the enrollment. In addition, all backend services and backend buckets are counted as protected resources and are metered for the Cloud Armor Enterprise protected resources cost. The backend services and backend buckets in Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual are aggregated across all enrolled projects in a billing account, whereas the backend services and backend buckets in Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo are aggregated within the project.

*Always-on* protection for forwarding rules, backend services, and backend buckets includes mitigation from L3 and L4 volumetric and network protocol-based DDoS attacks. Protection from application layer threats including L7 DDoS requires a user-created security policy with mitigating rules in place.

### Hierarchical security policies

When you attach a hierarchical security policy, each of the projects that inherit the hierarchical security policy must be enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise. This includes all of the projects in an organization or folder with a hierarchical security policy that aren't explicitly excluded, and all projects with a hierarchical security policy attached directly to the project.

* Projects that are linked to a Cloud Billing account with a subscription to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual are automatically enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual if they aren't already enrolled.
* Without a Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual subscription, projects are automatically enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo when they inherit a hierarchical security policy. If you subscribe the billing account to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual after your project was automatically enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo, the project isn't automatically enrolled to Annual. For more information about Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo, see [Cloud Armor Standard versus Cloud Armor Enterprise](/armor/docs/armor-enterprise-overview#standard_versus).
* If you update a hierarchical security policy to exclude a project *after* the project has been automatically enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise, the project isn't automatically unenrolled. To manually unenroll your project, see [Remove a project from Cloud Armor Enterprise](/armor/docs/armor-enterprise-using#remove-project).
* You can't remove a project from Cloud Armor Enterprise while it has any inherited hierarchical security policies.

Auto-enrollment can take up to the next business day to complete. During this time, your hierarchical security policies are effective and no Cloud Armor Enterprise costs are incurred. When your project is enrolled, audit logs are updated to reflect the project's Cloud Armor Enterprise status. You also see the new project tier in the Google Cloud console.

Projects are auto-enrolled only when at least one backend service for global external load balancers uses HTTP, HTTPS, HTTP2, H2C, or GRPC.

For more information about hierarchical security policies, see the [hierarchical security policies overview](/armor/docs/hierarchical-policies-overview).

## DDoS response support

DDoS Response support provides 24/7 help and potential custom mitigations from DDoS attacks from the same team that protects all Google services. You can engage response support during an attack to help mitigate the attack, or you can reach out proactively to plan for an upcoming high volume or potentially viral event (one which might attract an unusually high amount of visitors).

Proactive support is available for all Cloud Armor Enterprise customers, even if they haven't completed a DDoS posture review. Proactive support lets us apply preconfigured rules that target common DDoS attack types before the attack reaches Cloud Armor. To engage DDoS response support, see [Get support for a DDoS case](/armor/docs/getting-support#ddos-case).

### DDoS posture review

The goal of the DDoS posture review is to improve the efficiency and efficacy of the DDoS response process. During the review process we learn about your unique use case and architecture, and verify that your Cloud Armor security policies are configured according to our [best practices](/armor/docs/best-practices). This helps you increase your preemptive resilience to DDoS attacks.

The DDoS posture review is provided to customers who subscribe to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual and have a [Premium account](/support/docs/premium) for Cloud Customer Care.

### Eligibility for DDoS response support

The following criteria qualify you to open a case and receive help from the Cloud Armor DDoS response support team:

* Your billing account has an active Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual subscription.
* Your billing account has a [Premium account](/support/docs/premium) for Cloud Customer Care.
* The Google Cloud project with the workload that is under attack is enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual.
  + If you use [cross-project service referencing](/load-balancing/docs/https#cross-project), both the frontend and backend service projects must be enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual.
* For customers who subscribed to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual *after* September 3, 2024: The project with the workload that is under attack must have undergone an annual DDoS posture review.

Even when customers don't qualify for support, our Cloud Customer Care team provides assistance during an attack by helping with rule debugging, behavior clarification, and specific concerns with existing policies.

To engage DDoS response support, see [Get support for a DDoS case](/armor/docs/getting-support#ddos-case).

## DDoS bill protection

Cloud Armor DDoS bill protection requires your project to be enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual. It provides credits for future Google Cloud usage for some increases in the bills from Cloud Load Balancing, Cloud Armor, and network internet, inter-region, and inter-zone outbound data transfer as a result of a verified DDoS attack. If a claim is recognized and a credit is provided, the credit cannot be used to offset existing usage; the credit can only apply to future usage. The following table demonstrates what resources are covered by DDoS bill protection:

| Endpoint Type | Covered Usage Increase |
| --- | --- |
| * External Application Load Balancer * External proxy Network Load Balancer | Cloud Armor | Cloud Armor Enterprise data processing fee |
| Network | Outbound data transfer |
| Inter-region |
| Inter-zone |
| Carrier Peering |
| Load balancer | Inbound data processing fee |
| [Outbound data processing fee](/vpc/network-pricing#lb) |
| Cloud CDN | Cloud CDN egress fee |
| Cache data transfer out |
| Cache fill |
| HTTP/HTTPS cache lookup requests |
| Media CDN | Media CDN egress fee |
| Cache data transfer out |
| * Regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer * Protocol forwarding * Public IP addresses (VMs) | Cloud Armor | Cloud Armor Enterprise data processing fee |
| Network | Outbound data transfer |
| Inter-region |
| Inter-zone |
| Carrier Peering |
| Load balancer | Inbound data processing fee |
| [Outbound data processing fee](/vpc/network-pricing#lb) |

To engage DDoS bill protection, see [Engaging DDoS bill protection](/armor/docs/armor-enterprise-using#ddos-bill-protection).

## Migrating projects between billing accounts

Beginning September 3, 2024, if you migrate your project from one billing account to another while subscribed to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual, but your new billing account isn't subscribed to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual, your project reverts to Cloud Armor Standard after the migration completes—unless your project has effective hierarchical security policies, in which case your project is downgraded to Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo. Therefore, if you want to keep your project in Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual without downtime, we recommend that you subscribe your new billing account to Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual *before* you begin the migration process. You can also migrate your subscription from one billing account to the other by reaching out to [Cloud Billing support](/support/billing).

Projects enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo are not affected by billing account migration.

## Downgrading from Cloud Armor Enterprise

When you [remove a project from Cloud Armor Enterprise](/armor/docs/armor-enterprise-using#remove-project), any security policies that use rules with Cloud Armor Enterprise-exclusive features (advanced rules) become frozen. Frozen security policies have the following properties:

* Cloud Armor continues to evaluate traffic against rules in the policy, including any advanced rules.
* You cannot attach the security policy to new targets.
* You can only perform the following operations on the security policy:
  + You can [delete security policy rules](/armor/docs/configure-security-policies#delete-rules).
  + If you don't change the rule priority, you can update advanced rules so that they no longer use Cloud Armor Enterprise-exclusive features. If you modify all advanced rules in this way, your policy is no longer frozen. For more information about updating security policy rules, see [Update a single rule in a security policy](/armor/docs/configure-security-policies#update-rules).

You can also re-enroll in Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual or Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo to restore access to your frozen security policies.

### Disabling Global Front End Enterprise

When you disable Global Front End Enterprise in a project:

* Active Cloud Armor protections revert to the tier active at the project level.
* The Google Cloud console does not automatically restore a previous tier or designate a fallback tier.
* To avoid security policy degradation or unexpected billing, you must manually and immediately select a Cloud Armor billing tier (either Cloud Armor Standard or Cloud Armor Enterprise PayGo).

### Advanced network DDoS protection

Advanced network DDoS protection is only available to projects enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise. When you remove a project with an active advanced network DDoS policy from Cloud Armor Enterprise, you are still billed for the feature based on [Cloud Armor Enterprise pricing](https://cloud.google.com/armor/pricing#google-cloud-armor-pricing).

We recommend that you delete any advanced network DDoS protection rules before you unenroll your project from Cloud Armor Enterprise, but you can also delete advanced network DDoS protection rules after downgrading.

## Terms and limitations

Cloud Armor Enterprise has the following terms and limitations:

* **Generally**: If a Project enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise experiences a third-party denial of service attack on a protected endpoint ("Qualified Attack") and the conditions described in the next section are met, Google provides a credit equivalent to the Covered Fees, provided that the Covered Fees incurred exceed the Minimum Threshold. Load tests and security assessments performed by or on behalf of Customer are not Qualified Attacks.
* **Conditions**: Customer must submit a request to Cloud Billing Support within 30 days after the end of the Qualified Attack. The request must include evidence of the Qualified Attack, such as logs or other telemetry indicating the timing of the attack and the Projects and resources that were attacked, and an estimate of the Covered Fees incurred. Google will reasonably determine whether credits are due and the appropriate amount. Other conditions for particular Cloud Armor features are included in the Documentation.
* **Credits**: Any credits provided to Customer in connection with this Section have no cash value and can only be applied to offset future Fees for the Services. These credits expire 12 months after being issued or upon termination or expiration of the Agreement.
* **Definitions**:
  + **Covered Fees**: Any Fees incurred by Customer as a direct result of the Qualified Attack for the following:
    - Ingress and outbound data processing for the Google Cloud Load Balancer Service.
    - Cloud Armor Enterprise data processing for the Cloud Armor Service.
    - Network egress, including inter-region, inter-zone, internet, and Carrier Peering egress.
  + **Minimum Threshold**: The minimum amount of Covered Fees that are eligible to be credited under this Section as determined by Google from time to time and disclosed to Customer on request.

It covers applications deployed on Google Cloud, on-premises, or other infrastructure providers.

**Cloud Armor Standard vs. Enterprise:** Cloud Armor is offered in two tiers. Standard includes pay-as-you-go pricing, always-on L3/L4 DDoS protection, automated security policy application across various load balancers (Global/Classic/Regional external Application Load Balancers, external proxy Network Load Balancer, Cloud CDN, Media CDN), and WAF rule capabilities including preconfigured OWASP Top 10 rules. Enterprise adds all Standard features plus bundled WAF usage, third-party named IP address lists, Google Threat Intelligence, Adaptive Protection for L7 endpoints, advanced network DDoS protection for pass-through endpoints, DDoS attack visibility, hierarchical security policies, and (Annual only) DDoS bill protection and DDoS response team services.

**Pricing table highlights:**
- Standard: Pay-as-you-go, per policy/rule/request
- Enterprise Paygo: $200/month per project, $200/month per protected resource after first 2
- Enterprise Annual: $3000/month per billing account, $30/month per protected resource after first 100, with 12-month commitment

Enabling Global Front End Enterprise in a project enables specific Cloud Armor Enterprise features for global external Application Load Balancers without changing the project-level Cloud Armor tier.

Eligibility requires active Enterprise Annual subscription, Premium account, and project enrollment in Enterprise Annual. Customers subscribing after September 3, 2024 must have undergone an annual DDoS posture review.

# What does Google Cloud Armor do?

Google Cloud Armor is a security service that integrates with Cloud Load Balancing to protect back-end services and apps from DDoS traffic.

![Chris Jackson](/content/dam/ps/blog/migration/app/uploads/2023/02/Chris-Jackson-headshot.jpeg)

By Chris Jackson

Jun 08, 2023 • 3 Minute Read

![Please set an alt value for this image...](/content/dam/ps/blog/migration/app/uploads/2022/06/676240-22-Brand-ACG-BlogHeaders-Batch2-Header3-copy.jpg)

Web applications provide a place to shop, game, stream content, manage finances, and so much more. It’s critical that organizations [protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of their most vital and profitable applications](https://www.pluralsight.com/blog/cloud/5-pillars-cloud-security).

Google’s answer: Google Cloud Armor.

## What is Google Cloud Armor?

Given these web app security risks, Google [empowers its cloud customers to protect their apps](https://acloudguru.com/blog/engineering/cloud-apps-secure-by-design) with the Google Cloud Armor service. This security service integrates with Cloud Load Balancing to protect your back-end services and apps from distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) traffic that could compromise the availability of these assets. GCP Armor leverages Google's global threat intelligence feeds and machine learning to recognize DDoS traffic targeting your Google Cloud Platform (GCP) resources and block that malicious traffic flow.

## What does Google Cloud Armor do?

Google Cloud Armor incorporates a web application firewall (WAF) to protect web apps against many of the security risks listed on the [OWASP top 10 list](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/). GCP customers can leverage GCP Armor's WAF function to block web app attacks using pre-configured WAF rules. Customers also have the ability to customize WAF rules and define conditions for filtering traffic based on IP origin, HTTP request headers, and other attributes.

### What are the most common web application security risks?

The nonprofit organization Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) created a list of some of the most notorious web application security risks on the internet. This list includes cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks and SQL injection (SQLi) attacks that can read confidential data stored in a [SQL database](https://www.pluralsight.com/blog/it-ops/google-cloud-sql).

In XSS attacks, adversaries may inject malicious code into a web application or compromise a client's browser. And let’s not forget DDoS attacks that seek to bring down web apps by overwhelming the application with massive traffic flow.

### Starting out with GCP and not sure what certification is right for you?

Check out [this post](https://acloudguru.com/blog/engineering/which-google-cloud-certification-is-best-for-me) that identifies all the latest GCP cloud certifications, what they cover, and how you can use them to further your career.

## Is Google Cloud Armor free?

Google Cloud Armor has two pricing tiers: Standard and Managed Protection Plus.

For Standard users, GCP Armor is a pay-as-you-go service with per-month or per-request costs. WAF requests are $0.75 per million requests, WAF security policies are $5 per policy per month, and WAF rules are $1 per rule per month. While this tier has no time commitment and no data processing fee, it doesn’t offer any protected resources.

For Managed Protection Plus users, GCP Armor is an annual subscription service that starts at $3,000 per month. Protected resources above the 100 included with the subscription cost an additional $30 per resource per month. While all WAF requests, security policies, and rules are included with this subscription, it has an added data processing fee.

### New to GCP and want to learn how to secure resources and apps in Google Cloud?

Login to your ACG account to watch our [Introduction to Google Cloud Security](https://learn.acloud.guru/course/b624331f-8c99-49b2-86e9-30301ea9a732/dashboard) course. This course takes a look at Google Cloud Armor, Cloud Firewall, Cloud Identity, and other essential principles for securing your GCP resources.

![Close button](/content/dam/rebrand2025/icons/close-dark.svg)

#### Advance your tech skills today

Access courses on AI, cloud, data, security, and more—all led by industry experts.

Over the years, he has tested web applications for vulnerabilities, helped deploy SIEM platforms and more. He is passionate about teaching cybersecurity and committed to learning new technologies.

URL: https://medium.com/@CloudifyOps/the-7-rs-of-cloud-migration-explained-which-strategy-is-right-for-you-ad2dd90beb7c

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by CloudifyOps (a Cloud & DevOps technology company) provides a comprehensive guide to the "7 Rs of Cloud Migration" — a decision-making framework for categorizing, prioritizing, and executing application migrations to the cloud. The framework evolved from Gartner's original 5 Rs to AWS's 6 Rs, and now includes a 7th strategy called Relocate.

The seven strategies are:
1. **Rehost (Lift and Shift)** — Fastest route; move infrastructure to cloud with minimal changes. Example: financial services firm migrating 200 VMs to AWS EC2 ahead of data centre lease expiry.
2. **Replatform (Lift and Reshape)** — Targeted cloud optimizations without redesigning core architecture. Example: migrating on-premises PostgreSQL to Amazon Aurora.
3. **Refactor/Re-Architect** — Cloud-native rebuild with microservices, stateless architecture, managed services, and CI/CD. Example: logistics platform achieving 10x deployment velocity and 99.99% uptime on Amazon EKS.
4. **Repurchase (Drop and Shop)** — Replace legacy apps with SaaS alternatives (Salesforce for CRM, Workday for HR, ServiceNow for ITSM). Example: manufacturing company replacing 15-year-old CRM with Salesforce.
5. **Retire** — Decommission systems no longer needed. Example: healthcare organization retiring 30 underused applications.
6. **Retain (Revisit Later)** — Keep applications on-premises when compliance constraints or risk outweigh near-term benefits, particularly for government/classified data.
7. **Relocate (Hypervisor Lift, the 7th R)** — Move entire VMware virtualization estates to cloud-hosted environments (VMware Cloud on AWS, Azure VMware Solution) without changing hypervisor, applications, or tooling. Differs from Rehost (which moves VMs to native cloud infrastructure); Relocate moves "the data centre virtually." Example: insurance company migrating 400 VMs with zero changes and zero retraining.

The article provides a four-step framework for choosing strategies: (1) portfolio discovery and assessment, (2) score each application across business criticality, technical complexity, compliance requirements, and cloud/AI readiness, (3) map applications to the 7 Rs, and (4) plan and execute in waves.

It advocates for an industrialized, AI-driven migration platform approach, claiming benefits including: accelerated timelines by 30–50%, reduced modernization rework by 25–40%, and reduced planning effort by 40–60% for refactoring. The article emphasizes AI readiness (API enablement, event-driven compatibility, data extraction capability, architecture modernity) as a migration-time criterion, and presents a four-stage legacy-to-AI-ready journey: Stabilize (Rehost/Relocate), Optimise (Replatform/Repurchase), Modernize (Refactor), and AI-Enable.

Key takeaways: Rehost/Relocate are best for speed and low disruption; Refactor delivers maximum long-term value; Replatform balances effort and benefit; Repurchase accelerates modernization via SaaS; Retire and Retain reduce scope/cost/risk; most enterprises use all seven strategies; and AI-driven platforms bring intelligence and automation to every migration stage.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This article from Apps4Rent (published July 31, 2026) provides a comprehensive guide to Azure migration strategies based on the "6 Rs" framework of cloud migration, which originated from Gartner and was popularized across the industry. The framework consists of six strategies ordered from least to most transformation: Rehost (lift and shift to Azure VMs with no changes), Replatform (move with targeted upgrades to managed services), Refactor/Rearchitect (restructure applications to be cloud-native), Repurchase (replace with SaaS products), Retire (decommission unused workloads), and Retain (keep on-premises for now).

Key highlights include:

It's best for deadline-driven moves, datacenter exits, or vendor-constrained apps. Azure Hybrid Benefit allows applying existing Windows Server/SQL Server licenses to reduce VM costs.
- Replatforming swaps components for managed services without code rewrites (e.g., SQL Server on VM to Azure SQL Managed Instance, IIS web apps to Azure App Service, file servers to Azure Files, or apps to containers). It delivers the best return per engineering hour.

Common mistakes to avoid include blanket rehosting or refactoring, one-to-one sizing, ignoring licensing strategy (Hybrid Benefit, reserved instances), migrating dependencies apart, and having no day-2 plan. --- SOURCE 4: The 7 R's of Cloud Migration | IBM ---
URL: https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/7-rs-cloud-migration

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IBM Think article, published 13 October 2025 by Stephanie Susnjara and Ian Smalley, explains the 7 R's of cloud migration—a framework of seven strategic approaches (rehost, relocate, replatform, refactor, repurchase, retire, retain) for moving applications and workloads to the cloud. Each application has unique architecture, dependencies, and business needs, so the framework helps organizations evaluate each situation and select a migration path balancing speed, cost-efficiency, and long-term value.

**Origin of the 7 R's:** The framework evolved from the initial 5 R's (rehost, refactor, revise, rebuild, replace) introduced by Gartner in 2010. AWS expanded it to 6 R's in 2016 by adding "Retire," then added "Retain" in 2017 to complete the 7 R's. Today most enterprises use hybrid and multicloud strategies.

**Cloud migration overview:** Cloud migration is the process of moving applications, data, workloads, and IT infrastructure from on-premises data centers to cloud-based infrastructure. Benefits include cost optimization, scalability, disaster recovery, business continuity, and access to AI/ML technologies. The global cloud market was valued at USD 752.44 million in 2024 and projected to grow to USD 2,390.19 billion by 2030.

**Types of cloud migration:** data center migration, hybrid cloud migration (which can achieve 2.5 times more value than single public cloud, per IBM IBV report "Mastering Hybrid Cloud"), cloud-to-cloud migration, multicloud migration, and workload-specific migration.

**Challenges:** undocumented dependencies in legacy systems, performance issues, network latency, security and compliance concerns, and skills gaps (approximately 58% of global decision-makers report cloud skills remain a considerable challenge, per an IBM IBV 2023 report). Cloud costs can spiral without proper governance.

**The 7 R's explained:**
1. **Rehost (lift-and-shift):** Moves applications as-is without changing code or architecture, typically via VMs. Best for quick migrations or when lacking resources to rearchitect.
2. **Relocate:** Moves virtual machines directly between environments without modifying applications, typically VMware-based workloads.
3. **Replatform:** Makes targeted optimizations during migration (e.g., migrating SQL databases to managed services like Amazon RDS, or containerizing apps) without changing core architecture.
4. **Refactor (rearchitect):** Completely rearchitects applications into cloud-native solutions, typically breaking monoliths into microservices or adopting serverless computing, working with DevOps practices.
5. **Repurchase (drop-and-shop):** Replaces existing applications with cloud-based SaaS alternatives.
6. **Retire:** Identifies and decommissions applications no longer needed, eliminating unnecessary costs.
7. **Retain (revisit):** Keeps applications on-premises for now, with plans to revisit migration later—applies to recently upgraded/stable apps, apps with compliance issues, or complex dependencies.

**Strategy guidance:** Effective migration starts with comprehensive discovery and assessment. Organizations typically begin with low-risk, quick-win applications to build momentum, then migrate complex apps later. Plans should include success criteria, rollback procedures, data migration planning, and stakeholder coordination. Governance and cost management frameworks (resource tagging, budget alerts, regular cost reviews) should be established before migration begins.

**Tools and partners:** Cloud providers offer tools like AWS Application Migration Service, IBM Cloud migration services, and Azure Migrate. Ecosystem partners (IBM, Microsoft, managed service providers, system integrators) extend capabilities with specialized expertise.
</summary>

URL: https://www.netapp.com/blog/aws-cvo-blg-strategies-for-aws-migration-the-new-7th-r-explained

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from NetApp (authored by Sudip Sengupta) explains the "7 Rs of Cloud Migration" — a framework of strategies for moving applications and data from on-premises infrastructure to the cloud. The 7 strategies are: rehost, relocate, replatform, refactor, repurchase, retire, and retain.

The framework has evolved over time: Gartner first introduced the 5 Rs model in the early days of cloud computing. AWS expanded it to a 6 Rs model by adding "Retire," then introduced the 7 Rs model by adding "Retain" (recognizing that not all workloads should move to the cloud).

The seven strategies in detail:
1. **Rehost ("Lift and Shift")** — Move on-prem applications and dependencies as-is to cloud IaaS without changing core infrastructure; easy for enterprises lacking cloud-native expertise.
2. **Relocate ("Hypervisor-Level Lift and Shift")** — Migrate server collections (e.g., VMware or Kubernetes) to cloud versions of the same platform (e.g., GKE, EKS) with minimal downtime and no source code rewrites.
3. **Replatform ("Lift and Reshape")** — Move applications to cloud with some platform optimization while keeping source code and core architecture unchanged; enables cloud-native capabilities like automation.
4. **Refactor ("Re-architect")** — Re-architect workloads from the ground up for cloud-native capabilities (serverless, autoscaling, distributed load balancing); most complex and costly but most future-proof; often breaks monoliths into microservices.
5. **Repurchase ("Drop and Shop")** — Swap internally administered systems for third-party managed SaaS services from the cloud provider; reduces operational overhead and ties IT costs to revenue.
6. **Retire** — Terminate or downsize applications no longer useful in production; first step toward modern cloud-native adoption.
7. **Retain ("Revisit")** — Keep workloads on-premises when they cannot be retired or migrated (due to dependencies, compliance, security, or lack of immediate business value).

The article includes a detailed comparison table covering use-cases, pros, and cons of each strategy. Key considerations include: Retire is cheapest but risks incompatibility with interconnected stacks; Relocate is quickest but limits cloud-native capabilities; Refactor is best for high-usability complex applications but requires extensive planning, training, and monitoring.

The article concludes by highlighting NetApp's solutions for supporting AWS cloud migration and provides links to NetApp's guide to migrating enterprise workloads and cloud migration case studies.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a detailed blog article from The Competenza (a software development and cloud migration services company with offices in the USA, UAE, Australia, and India) published June 25, 2026, by Nishant Agrawal. The article provides a comprehensive comparison of two cloud migration strategies: Lift and Shift (rehosting) vs. Re-architecting (refactoring).

**Key Content:**

**Lift and Shift (Rehosting):**
- Definition: Transferring applications to the cloud with minimal or no code changes
- Cost range: $40,000–$150,000+ (small business apps $40K-75K, mid-sized enterprise $75K-120K, large enterprise workloads $120K-150K+)
- Benefits: Rapid migration, lower development costs, reduced business risk, rapid payback, enables data center exits
- Disadvantages: Technical debt carries over, limited cloud optimization, greater long-term costs, scalability limitations, reduced innovation potential
- Best for: data center consolidation, M&A integrations, time-sensitive projects, tight budgets, cloud-first initiatives, stable/low-change applications

**Re-architecting (Refactoring):**
- Definition: Redesigning applications to fully leverage cloud-native technologies, microservices, containers, and serverless computing
- Cost range: $200,000–$600,000+ (small modernization $200K-300K, mid-sized $300K-500K, large complex systems $600K+)
- Benefits: Cloud-native scalability, better performance, reduced long-term costs, improved security, AI/automation readiness, reduced technical debt
- Disadvantages: Higher initial capital, extended timeframes (months to years), increased complexity, change management requirements
- Best for: growth-focused organizations, legacy systems with high technical debt, SaaS product development, digital transformation projects

**Comparison Highlights:**
- Lift and shift: faster migration (weeks vs. months), lower upfront cost, but higher long-term operating costs and limited cloud-native capability
- Re-architect: slower, higher initial investment, but superior long-term ROI, scalability, performance, security, and AI-readiness
- Re-architect is the better option for nearly all long-term factors (infrastructure, maintenance, operational, scalability, security, technical debt, long-term ROI); lift and shift wins on initial migration costs and short-term ROI

**Security Considerations:**
- Lift and shift risks: legacy security gaps, excessive user permissions, poor cloud configurations (misconfigured storage buckets, firewalls, unsecured APIs), limited cloud-native security features
- Re-architecting enables zero-trust access, encryption, automated checks, microservices isolation, and DevSecOps (automated security testing, continuous compliance monitoring, secure CI/CD pipelines)
- HIPAA (PHI protection, encryption, audit logs, access controls) and GDPR (data privacy, consent management, breach notifications, data residency) compliance must be planned from the start

**Cloud Provider Perspectives:**
- AWS: best for fastest lift and shift migration, legacy app migration, enterprise digital transformation, cloud-native development (EKS, Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, Aurora)
- Azure: best for Microsoft-centric infrastructure, hybrid cloud, .NET modernization, regulated industries (Azure Migrate, Site Recovery, AKS, Functions, Cosmos DB)
- Google Cloud: best for AI/ML projects, Kubernetes/microservices, data-intensive workloads (Migrate to VMs, GKE, Cloud Run, Vertex AI, BigQuery)

**Recommendation Framework:**
- Choose lift and shift for speedy cloud adoption, reduced initial expenses, minimal business impact
- Choose re-architect for digital transformation, cloud-native innovation, AI-readiness, scalability, long-term value
- Choose a hybrid approach (recommended for most enterprises) to move stable workloads quickly via lift and shift while re-architecting mission-critical applications

The article includes 7 questions for business leaders and 7 questions for IT teams to consider when choosing a migration strategy, plus a per-workload framework. The company notes it has delivered 300+ solutions for 150+ global businesses across fintech, education, eCommerce, healthcare, and logistics industries.
</summary>

URL: https://www.sequentur.com/lift-and-shift-vs-re-platform-vs-re-architect-choosing-the-right-cloud-migration-strategy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Sequentur blog article (an IT managed services provider) providing a detailed guide on cloud migration strategies for small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs). The core thesis is that migration strategy must be decided per-workload, not per-project, and that the "cheapest strategy that delivers what the business needs" is the right approach.

The article covers five migration strategies that matter for SMBs (drawn from the cloud industry's "6 R's" framework):
1. **Retire** - turn the workload off entirely (lowest cost, highest ROI per dollar)
2. **Retain** - leave the workload on-prem (for latency, compliance, or cost reasons)
3. **Repurchase** - replace with a SaaS equivalent (often the most underrated strategy)
4. **Lift-and-shift (rehost)** - move unchanged to a cloud VM (fastest, lowest risk, but no operational savings)
5. **Re-platform** - move with some cloud-native features adopted (moderate effort, the "sweet spot" for most SMB workloads)
6. **Re-architect (refactor)** - rebuild cloud-native (highest cost, only for core business apps with 5-10 year horizons)

A sixth "R" (Relocate - moving VMware to managed VMware-on-cloud) is noted but dismissed as overkill for SMBs in the 15-250 employee range.

Key data points include:
- Lift-and-shift: $3,000-$15,000 per single Windows Server migration; often costs slightly MORE per year than on-prem due to ongoing cloud bills with no operational changes; 1-4 weeks per workload
- Re-platform: 30-80% more project effort than lift-and-shift; $10,000-$40,000 for SQL workloads; operational savings recoup the higher one-time cost in 12-24 months; 4-16 weeks per workload
- Re-architect: 5-20 times the cost of lift-and-shift; typically $150,000-$750,000 for a line-of-business app at a 40-person business; 6-24 months timeline
- Typical full SMB migration combining multiple strategies lands in the 3-to-9-month range

The article provides a per-workload decision tree: (1) does anyone use it? No → Retire; (2) should it be in cloud at all? No → Retain; (3) does a mature SaaS exist? Yes → Repurchase; (4) critical, 5+ years, architecturally limited? Yes → Re-architect; (5) can it run on managed service? Yes → Re-platform; (6) default → Lift-and-shift.

A worked example uses a 40-person law firm with 11 workloads showing a realistic mix: 4 retire/retain, 4 repurchases (email→M365, file server→SharePoint/OneDrive, document management→NetDocuments/iManage, time/billing→Clio/Centerbase), 2 re-platforms (SQL→Azure SQL DB, Active Directory→hybrid Entra), 1 lift-and-shift (practice management app), and 1 retain (specialty discovery review tool).

The article lists 10 common migration mistakes, including picking one strategy for the whole project, lift-and-shifting everything, re-architecting the wrong workload, skipping repurchase evaluation, forgetting retire/retain, and letting the platform (Azure vs AWS) pick the strategy. The piece concludes with Sequentur's promotional content, client testimonials, and FAQs about their managed IT services.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The right migration is the one that uses the cheapest strategy that delivers what the business needs for that specific workload, not the most ambitious strategy applied across the board."
</key_excerpts>

**What Is Cloud Migration?** Cloud migration is the process of moving some or all digital operations to the cloud. There are three main types: on-premises to cloud, cloud to cloud, or cloud to on-premises. The "5 Rs" strategies were first defined in Gartner's model in 2011.

A critical step is ensuring the application still has access to the same documents and data once in the cloud (e.g., Microsoft Azure Files allows cloud VMs to mount file shares identical to on-premise environments, making lift and shift possible). Cloud vendors like AWS and Azure work to make this approach as easy as possible.

**2. Refactor:** Moving applications to cloud infrastructure while re-architecting them to better suit the cloud environment. This involves modifying existing software or a large chunk of the code base to take advantage of cloud features, flexibility, and elasticity. It is much more complex than other approaches, requiring application code changes and careful testing to avoid regressions and ensure better resource utilization. While the most time-consuming and resource-intensive, it can provide the highest return on investment long-term.

**3. Replatform:** The middle ground between rehost and refactor. It's similar to rehosting but involves some modification of the application to take advantage of new cloud infrastructure.

**NetApp Cloud Volumes ONTAP:** The article highlights NetApp Cloud Volumes ONTAP as the leading enterprise-grade storage management solution, delivering secure storage management services on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. It supports up to 368TB of capacity and supports use cases such as file services, databases, DevOps, and enterprise workloads. It specifically assists with lift and shift migrations. NetApp BlueXP classification is a tool that automatically discovers, maps, classifies, and acts on enterprise data, helping identify private data needing protection and pinpointing duplicate and stale data for clean migrations.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Choose the best migration and modernization strategy for you ---
URL: https://vfunction.com/resources/guide-migration-strategies-basics-lift-and-shift-refactor-or-replace

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an informational guide from vFunction (a cloud and application modernization company) titled "Migration Strategies Basics: Lift and Shift, Refactor, or Replace?" It serves as a comprehensive resource for organizations considering application modernization and cloud migration strategies.

**Key context:** The article notes that industry analyst IDG reports "Application/legacy system modernization" has risen to become a top priority for CIOs in 2022, driven by the pace of technology innovation and accelerated by the pandemic. Gartner defines application modernization services as addressing "the migration of legacy to new applications or platforms," including re-platforming, re-hosting, recoding, rearchitecting, re-engineering, interoperability, replacement, and retirement.

**Why modernize:** The article explains that monolithic applications (defined as apps with all or most functionality within a single process or container) often represent core business functionality and significant revenue. Companies modernize to enhance user experience, keep employees productive, protect sensitive data, and gain cloud benefits like scaling and security.

**Assessing legacy applications:** Gartner recommends evaluating six factors:
- Business fit (competitors modernizing and gaining market share)
- Business value (modular architectures allow faster value delivery)
- Agility (accelerated development and time-to-market)
- Cost (pay-as-you-go model lowers operating costs)
- Complexity (tight coupling in monoliths makes changes difficult)
- Risk (changes to monoliths can have unpredictable downstream effects)

**Migration/modernization strategies covered:**
1. **Encapsulation** – Makes application features accessible as APIs without modernizing the underlying system; a stop-gap approach that accrues technical debt.
2. **Lift and Shift** (includes rehost and replatform) – Moving apps to the cloud; the article cautions this "genuinely does not modernize anything" and can simply move technical debt to the cloud.
3. **Rehost** – Migrating without modifying code, data, or functionality; quick but risks disruption and poor early user experiences.
4. **Replatform** – Minimal code changes to run on a new platform (e.g., newer OS); cheaper and lower-risk but requires automation and careful scope control.
5. **Refactor** – Reorganizing and optimizing existing code to reduce technical debt and improve performance, security, and usability; provides long-term cost savings and ROI but requires advanced skills and carries risk of errors.
6. **Rearchitect** – Breaking applications into microservices for individual cloud migration; offers flexibility and scaling but requires significant investment and automation tools.
7. **Rewrite** – Rebuilding applications while retaining intellectual property and unique selling propositions; substantial time and expense investment.
8. **Replace** – Swapping to a new SaaS or software solution; reduces maintenance burden but may face user adoption challenges and loss of customization.

**Company positioning:** The article concludes by promoting vFunction's AI-driven platform and "factory model purpose-built for cloud-native modernization," which helps software architects incrementally modernize legacy application portfolios. The page also links to vFunction resources including a 2025 report on "Architecture in Software Development: Rethinking the Role of Architecture in the Age of AI" and case studies on modernizing Fortune 500 applications.
</summary>

This is a Flexera blog article about Microsoft's Azure Hybrid Benefit program, a licensing benefit that allows businesses to use their existing on-premises operating system and application licenses in Azure, resulting in reduced hourly costs for cloud services.

**Key Points:**

- **What is Azure Hybrid Benefit?** Microsoft's licensing benefit that requires Microsoft Software Assurance. It applies to Microsoft Windows, Microsoft SQL Server, and certain Red Hat and SUSE licenses for Linux environments. Instead of paying license costs included in the hourly rate of cloud services, businesses can apply their current licenses to Azure services and receive a lower hourly cost.

Includes 180 days of dual-use rights and supports unlimited virtualization on Azure Dedicated Host and Azure VMware Solution.

- **Linux VM benefits:** Eliminates the software fee for existing Linux VMs since Red Hat or SUSE licensing costs are already covered—users only pay VM compute costs. Post-deployment conversion requires no production redeployment, and Azure, Red Hat, and SUSE offer co-located technical support with a unified Azure Portal/CLI interface including scalable batch conversions.

- **Promotional content:** The article promotes Flexera's Spot solution for Azure cost optimization and FinOps practices, plus related Flexera resources including the 2025 State of the Cloud report and the 2026 State of ITAM Report (insights from 500+ ITAM professionals).

<summary>
This article provides pricing guidance for SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, covering the various licensing options available and how to minimize costs.

**Free-Licensed SQL Server Editions:**
- **SQL Server Developer edition**: Free license with all Enterprise features, suitable for development, testing, and proofs of concept — but cannot be used in production. Only VM costs are incurred.
- **SQL Server Express edition**: Free license for lightweight production workloads (≤4 cores, <1-GB memory, ≤50 GB/database). Many production features like Enterprise-level disaster recovery aren't available. Only VM costs are incurred.
- Note: SQL Server 2025 introduces separate Enterprise Developer and Standard Developer editions.
- Smaller VM sizes (e.g., D2as_v5) are recommended to save money for these workloads.

**Paid SQL Server Editions:**
- **Web**: Small web sites
- **Standard**: Small to medium workloads
- **Enterprise**: Large or mission-critical workloads

**Two Licensing Payment Options:**

1. **Pay Per Usage (Pay-as-you-go)**: Per-second cost of the VM includes SQL Server license cost. Cost is the same for all SQL Server versions (2012 SP4 to 2025) and depends on the number of VM vCPUs. Recommended for:
   - Temporary or periodic workloads (e.g., seasonal events, weekly business analysis)
   - Workloads with unknown lifetime or scale
   - Note: The Azure portal's "Select a VM size" estimate only shows compute and OS costs — it does NOT include SQL Server licensing costs for Web, Standard, and Enterprise editions.

2. **Azure Hybrid Benefit**: Bring your own SQL Server license (Standard or Enterprise) with Software Assurance to get a discount on license allocation, while still paying for base compute, storage, and backups. Recommended for:
   - Continuous 24x7 workloads
   - Workloads with known lifetime and scale
   - Benefits include cost savings on license allocation and **free licensing for one passive secondary replica for high availability and one passive secondary for disaster recovery per SQL Server** — cutting HA licensing costs by more than half. As of November 2022, this free passive replica benefit also applies to pay-as-you-go licensing.

**Cost Reduction Tips:**
1. **Correctly size your VM**: SQL Server licensing cost is directly tied to vCPU count, so choose a VM size matching your CPU, memory, storage, and I/O needs.
2. **Shut down your VM when possible**: For non-continuous workloads, shut down and deallocate the VM during inactive periods. Important: Shutting down and deallocating is the only way to avoid charges — simply stopping the VM still incurs usage charges.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn page provides a comprehensive migration overview for moving SQL Server databases to Azure SQL Managed Instance. It is applicable to databases running on-premises or on cloud platforms including Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS for SQL Server, Google Compute Engine, and GCP Cloud SQL for SQL Server.

**Overview & Considerations:** Azure SQL Managed Instance is a recommended fully managed target for SQL Server workloads, offering complete instance isolation with native virtual network support and 99.99% availability. Key evaluation factors include number of servers/databases, database sizes, and acceptable business downtime during migration. Planning should include all databases needing colocation and instance-level objects (logins, credentials, SQL Agent jobs, operators, server-level triggers).

**Choosing a Target:** Guidelines include using CPU baseline for core provisioning, memory baseline for vCore selection, I/O latency baseline to choose between General Purpose (>5 ms latency) and Business Critical (<3 ms latency) tiers, and throughput baseline for file preallocation. Some features like In-Memory OLTP are only available in the Business Critical tier. A SQL Server VM alternative is recommended when direct OS/file system access is needed, strict dependencies exist on unsupported features (FileStream/FileTable, PolyBase, cross-instance transactions), staying on a specific SQL Server version is required, or compute requirements are lower than a managed instance offers.

**Migration Tools:** Recommended tools include Azure Migrate (discovery/assessment), native backup and restore (.bak files), Log Replay Service (cloud service based on log-shipping), and the Managed Instance link feature (online migration using Always On availability technology with near real-time replication, supporting SQL Server 2016-2022). Alternative tools include transactional replication, bulk copy (bcp), Import/Export Wizard/BACPAC, Azure Data Factory, and command line tools (PowerShell/Azure CLI).

**Feature Interoperability:** SSIS packages in SSISDB (SQL Server 2012+) can be migrated via Azure Database Migration Service. SSRS reports can be migrated to Power BI paginated reports using the RDL Migration Tool. SQL Server Analysis Services tabular models (2012+) can migrate to Azure Analysis Services or Power BI Premium. Always On failover cluster instances and availability groups become obsolete on the target as high availability is built in. SQL Agent jobs can be migrated via offline Database Migration Service or manually scripted in T-SQL. SQL logins can be migrated via Database Migration Service, including Windows logins when configured with Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) access. Transparent data encryption certificates must be migrated before native restore. System database restores are not supported. In-Memory OLTP requires Business Critical tier.

**Known Issues:** Restore operation failures can occur if accelerated database recovery (SQL Server 2019+) has persistent version store (PVS) set to a non-PRIMARY file group. Accelerated database recovery can't be enabled on the target if disabled on source. Service Broker can't be used on the target if disabled on the source database.

**Advanced Features:** Managed backups, point-in-time restore, built-in high availability, Microsoft Entra authentication, auditing, threat detection, row-level security, dynamic data masking, Azure SQL Analytics, and automatic tuning are available. Some features require changing database compatibility level to 150.

**Migration Assets:** Resources include a data workload assessment model/tool, a PowerShell utility for moving on-premises SQL Server logins, and a Perfmon data collection automation tool using Logman. The page was last updated June 2, 2026.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Dependency analysis in Azure Migrate Discovery and assessment - Azure Migrate | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/migrate/concepts-dependency-visualization?view=migrate

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn article describes dependency analysis in Azure Migrate, a feature that identifies dependencies between discovered on-premises servers (VMware, Hyper-V, physical servers, and servers on public clouds like AWS and GCP). The feature provides several advantages: reviewing network dependencies and grouping inter-dependent servers into applications, identifying servers that must be migrated together, and helping avoid surprise outages after migration by ensuring nothing is left behind.

Azure Migrate offers two dependency analysis options:
1. **Agentless dependency analysis** - Generally available for VMware VMs, Hyper-V VMs, physical servers, and servers in other public clouds. Supported in both Azure Public Cloud and Azure Government. This is the recommended approach.
2. **Agent-based dependency analysis** - Supported only in the classic view (not the new experience), using the Service Map solution in Azure Monitor. Requires installing agents on each source server. Supported in public cloud but NOT supported in Azure Government. The classic view is scheduled for deprecation by the end of 2026; no new servers can be onboarded for agent-based analysis.

**How agentless analysis works:**
- Captures TCP network connection data from enabled servers without installing agents.
- Connections between source server/process and destination server/process/port are logically grouped into dependencies.
- Data can be visualized in a map view or exported as CSV.
- The Azure Migrate appliance polls TCP connection data every 5 minutes, gathering process names with active connections, application names running those processes, and destination ports.
- Gathered data is processed on the appliance and sent to Azure Migrate every 6 hours.

The page was last updated on 2026-06-19.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Preparing for Azure with Azure Migrate Application and Code Assessment ---
URL: https://www.codemag.com/Article/2405051/Preparing-for-Azure-with-Azure-Migrate-Application-and-Code-Assessment

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, written by Mike Rousos and published in CODE Magazine's May/June 2024 issue (last updated December 26, 2025), introduces Azure Migrate application and code assessment, a new developer-focused feature for analyzing ASP.NET and ASP.NET Core applications to plan re-platforming to Azure PaaS environments. The tool is available as both a Visual Studio 2022 extension and a .NET command-line SDK tool (dotnet-appcat), and it scans source code, configuration, and binaries to identify issues that need to be addressed before migrating to Azure App Service, AKS, or Azure Container Apps. A Java version also exists.

The tool fills a gap in Azure Migrate's existing capabilities by providing source-code-level insight, complementing its existing discovery and assessment features (Data Migration Assistant, App Service Migration Assistant). In Visual Studio, users right-click a solution, select "Re-platform to Azure," create a new report, select top-level projects (dependencies are analyzed automatically), and choose whether to analyze source code only or also binary dependencies. Analysis takes seconds to minutes and produces a report dashboard with totals and graphics.

Issues are categorized into four severities: Mandatory (e.g., Windows authentication needing to be changed to Azure AD), Optional (e.g., moving settings from web.config to Azure App Configuration/Key Vault), Potential (e.g., SQL Server connectivity depending on whether the database is accessible from Azure), and Information (none currently in the .NET version). Each incident includes a unitless story point estimate for relative effort comparison. Incidents can be tracked as Active, Resolved, or N/A, and reports maintain state when saved. Reports can be exported as HTML (most readable), CSV (spreadsheet), or JSON (machine-readable).

The article includes a walkthrough analyzing the eShop "Northern Mountains" sample (github.com/dotnet/eshop), which produced 41 incidents across nine issue types in 16 projects: 8 mandatory, 8 optional, 25 potential. Key findings included RabbitMQ usage (mandatory - 8 incidents), database usage (8 incidents), connection strings (6 incidents), hardcoded URLs (5 incidents, all false positives since they work via Aspire), caching/Redis usage (5 incidents), HTTP usage (4 incidents), local file usage (1 incident, marked N/A), and static content (3 optional incidents). Most issues related to external dependencies needing to be made available in Azure.

The CLI tool is installed via `dotnet tool install -g dotnet-appcat` and run with the `appcat` command (e.g., `appcat analyze solution.sln`). It supports a non-interactive mode for scripting: `appcat analyze eShopLegacyMVC.csproj -s HTML -r OutputPath --code --non-interactive`. Note that the solution must build without errors when using the CLI.

Future roadmap features include GitHub Copilot Chat integration, the ability to specify multiple Azure target environments (e.g., Windows App Service vs. AKS with Linux containers, already available in the Java version), and binary output analysis (scanning compiled binaries directly without a source solution). Documentation is available at https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/migrate/appcat/overview.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Azure Site Recovery Costs: Breakdown and Optimisation | Critical Cloud ---
URL: https://criticalcloud.ai/blog/azure/azure-site-recovery-costs-breakdown

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Critical Cloud provides a detailed breakdown of Azure Site Recovery (ASR) costs and optimization strategies. ASR is a pay-as-you-go disaster recovery service with no upfront hardware or software costs, but it accumulates four separate cost components continuously once protection is enabled.

**The four cost components:**
1. **Licence fees per protected instance** – Billed hourly per protected VM or physical server, with a 31-day free trial per new instance. Rates vary by workload type (Azure-to-Azure, VMware/Hyper-V to Azure, physical server to Azure).
2. **Cache storage** – Requires a General Purpose v2 storage account in the source region. Costs depend on the storage SKU and data volume; high-I/O workloads (databases, transaction processing) can incur significant costs.
3. **Target storage** – Replicated data lands on Managed Disks in the target recovery region, paid continuously regardless of whether failover occurs. This is often the largest cost component — e.g., a 1 TB Premium SSD protecting a production database VM costs full price in the recovery region from the moment protection is enabled. Optimization: use Standard SSD or Standard HDD where RTO allows.
4. **Network charges for replication traffic** – Initial replication incurs a one-time egress charge for full disk copy; ongoing delta replication charges standard inter-region transfer rates. Optimization: schedule replication during off-peak hours (e.g., 20:00–06:00 GMT).

**Compute costs during failover** – Replication itself incurs no compute costs, but failed-over VMs (test or actual) run at standard VM compute rates. Test failovers should be temporary; leaving them running is an avoidable cost.

**Comparison to alternatives:** ASR competes primarily with Veeam Data Platform (perpetual licence or subscription model, more economical for organisations with existing on-premise infrastructure but requires owning backup infrastructure) and Zerto (annual subscription with per-VM pricing, sub-second RPO continuous data protection). ASR's minimum RPO is ~5 minutes for VMware workloads with typical recovery points every 15-30 minutes for Azure-to-Azure, making it cost-competitive for workloads with RPO requirements in the 15-minute to 1-hour range.

**Cost management best practices:** Right-tier target storage, promptly clean up test failover resources (using Azure Policy or budget alerts), audit protected instance list quarterly to catch orphaned protection, tag ASR resources with a consistent tag (e.g., `dr-layer` or `asr`) for Azure Cost Management filtering, and schedule off-peak replication where RPO allows.

The article concludes by promoting Critical Cloud's services — managing Azure environments for tech-led SMBs using Datadog as an observability foundation, including 24×7 incident management, and noting their status as the world's first Powered by Datadog accredited partner. The article is dated June 7, 2026, and appears in the Azure backup/recovery insights section of the Critical Cloud blog.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: Azure Site Recovery vs Traditional DR | Cost & Comparison ---
URL: https://www.infrassist.com/blog/azure-site-recovery-vs-traditional-disaster-recovery

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a blog post from Infrassist (published November 14, 2025) comparing Azure Site Recovery (ASR) with traditional on-premises disaster recovery (DR), providing detailed cost analysis and real-world implementation guidance for Managed Service Providers (MSPs) serving mid-sized businesses.

**Traditional DR Costs:**
- Upfront hardware for mid-size enterprises (500-2,000 employees): $150K-300K
- Monthly costs: colocation ($2,000-5,000), network ($500-1,500), maintenance contracts ($2,000-4,500, roughly 18-22% of hardware cost/year)
- Hardware refresh cycles every 3-5 years create a perpetual spending trap
- Five-year reality check for 50 VMs: $200K hardware + $480K operations + $100K mid-cycle refresh = $780,000 total (~$13,000/month)
- ~20% of SMEs cite affordability as primary barrier to DR adoption

**Azure Site Recovery Costs (50-VM environment):**
- ASR licenses: 50 VMs × $31 = $1,550/month
- Test failover compute: 10 VMs × $120 = $1,200/month
- Storage (LRS): 15TB × $19/TB = $285/month
- Replication bandwidth: 2TB × $87/TB = $174/month
- Azure Backup add-on: 15TB × $10/TB = $150/month
- Total Azure: $3,359/month; complete monthly cost with services: $5,259
- Savings of 56-65% versus traditional DR ($12K-15K monthly)
- Key cost advantages: no depreciation, zero overprovisioning, less labor during disasters, no refresh cycles

**Side-by-Side Comparison (Traditional vs. Azure):**
- Upfront cost: $150K-300K vs. $0
- Monthly cost: $12K-18K vs. $3K-5K
- RTO: 2-8 hours vs. 15 minutes
- RPO: 1-4 hours vs. 15-30 minutes
- Testing: production disruption risk vs. isolated, zero impact
- Azure wins all categories, including scalability, maintenance, and month-to-month contracts

**Real Client Case Study (Virginia manufacturing firm):**
- 75-person precision machining company in Roanoke, VA running VMware vSphere 6.7 on aging HP Nimble array with zero DR
- Traditional quote: $200,000 upfront + $3,000/month (new Nimble array $120K, replication software $25K, secondary site $35K, implementation $20K)
- Azure implementation: 12 production VMs migrated over 4-6 weeks using Azure Migrate; 4TB initial sync over 50Mbps (~72 hours); successful test failover on first try
- Results after 6 months: $200K avoided (invested in CNC equipment instead), new monthly DR cost $4,200, five-year savings of $456,000, RTO dropped from 4+ hours to 15 minutes, RPO improved from 8 hours to 30 minutes, quarterly tested failovers established, and foundation built for full cloud migration in 2026

**When to Choose Each Approach:**
- Traditional DR: recent hardware purchases, owned datacenter space, bandwidth under 10Mbps, specific data residency regulations
- Azure: hardware at end-of-life, no current DR, sub-one-hour RTO needs, cloud-curious companies, capital constraints
- Hybrid: tiered protection (critical ERP locally with 5-minute RTO, Tier 2/3 systems in Azure), multi-location strategies — can reduce total DR cost 60% versus all-on-prem

**Lessons from Real Deployments:**
1. Bandwidth assessments lie — spikes can reach 10x average; always add 40% buffer
2. Test failovers catch configuration drift — half of quarterly tests reveal issues
3. Real competition is "do nothing," not other DR vendors
4. Margin comes from testing/documentation services, not monitoring
5. DR experience naturally leads clients to ask about full cloud migration

**FAQs:**

URL: https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/site-recovery

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides Azure Site Recovery pricing information from Microsoft. Azure Site Recovery is a disaster recovery service that coordinates automated replication and recovery of protected instances at a secondary location.

**Pricing Structure:**
- Azure Site Recovery is billed based on the number of instances protected
- Every instance is FREE for the first 31 days of protection
- After 31 days, charges apply per instance protected (both for recovery to customer-owned sites and to Azure)
- Azure Site Recovery between Azure regions is charged at the same rate as Azure Site Recovery to Azure
- Billing is calculated using the average daily number of protected instances over a monthly period (e.g., protecting 20 instances for half a month and none for the other half results in an average of 10 protected instances)

**Key FAQ Points:**
- The 31-day free period applies to every new instance, regardless of how long a customer has been using the service
- Even during the free period, customers may incur charges for Azure Storage, storage transactions, data transfer, and compute charges for recovered VMs
- Azure Hybrid Benefit allows up to 40% or more savings using Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance
- Test recoveries are limited to brief DR testing within one week every 90 days

**Licensing Requirements (by recovery site type):**
- On-Premises: Fully licensed servers or end-customer licenses via Disaster Recovery Software Assurance benefit
- Service Provider (dedicated/shared hardware): Licensed via SPLA (Services Provider License Agreement)
- Azure: Disaster Recovery Software Assurance benefit applies (changed in January 2015 Product Use Rights); Azure Hybrid Benefit can be leveraged

**Additional Details:**
- Azure Site Recovery replication for SQL Server is covered under the Software Assurance Disaster Recovery benefit
- Azure does not support persistent MAC addresses, so MAC-based license models cannot be used for migration/DR
- Prices are estimates only and vary based on agreements, purchase date, and currency exchange rates
- US government entities can purchase Azure Government services via licensing solution providers or pay-as-you-go subscriptions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Thomas Maurer (EMEA Global Black Belt for Sovereign Cloud at Microsoft), published December 7, 2021, provides an overview of Extended Security Updates (ESU) options for Windows Server and SQL Server reaching end of support, particularly when running workloads in Microsoft Azure and Azure Stack.

Key dates and facts:
- SQL Server 2012 Extended Support ends July 12, 2022.
- Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 Extended Support ends October 10, 2023.
- Free Extended Security Updates are available for customers running these workloads in Azure, including Azure Virtual Machines, Azure Dedicated Host, Azure VMware Solution, Azure Nutanix Solution, and Azure Stack (Hub, Edge, and HCI).
- For on-premises environments (without Azure) with active Software Assurance or subscription licenses, ESU can be purchased annually: 75% of the latest version's license cost for year one, 100% for year two, and 125% for year three. Customers pay only for servers they need to cover.

How to obtain ESU:
- In Azure: Windows Server ESU is delivered automatically via Windows Server Update Service (WSUS). SQL Server ESU is obtained by registering the subscription with the SQL Server IaaS Agent extension.
- On-premises: Windows Server ESU is delivered like a regular Windows Update. SQL Server ESU requires connecting the SQL Server to Azure Arc.

The post recommends upgrading to the latest versions (SQL Server 2022, Windows Server 2022) or modernizing to Azure PaaS as the best long-term option, but notes ESU provides time for organizations that need to delay modernization. Additional resources include Microsoft Ignite 2021 announcements about ESU on Azure Stack HCI, and links to Microsoft Docs support lifecycle pages and deployment guides.
</summary>

"An additional capacity of running Windows Server in Azure or on Azure Stack HCI, Hub, and Edge, is that you get extended security updates (ESU) included for free for Windows Server and SQL Server which are out of mainstream support."

--- SOURCE 2: Microsoft Extended Support ---
URL: https://www.uscloud.com/microsoft-extended-support

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from US Cloud (a Microsoft Enterprise Support provider) explains Microsoft Extended Support and how organizations can extend their Microsoft software support lifecycle to increase ROI. Key topics covered include:

1. **What is Microsoft Extended Support?** - Adds 5 years to mainstream support. During Extended Support, security updates are included at no additional cost, but Microsoft will not accept requests for warranty support, design changes, or new features. Not available for consumer, consumer hardware, or multimedia products.

2. **Mainstream vs Extended Support** - Mainstream Support is the first lifecycle phase and includes incident support (no-charge, paid, or hourly), security update support, and the ability to request non-security updates. Incident support benefits are only available during Mainstream Support. The page includes a detailed table of end-of-support dates for various products (Windows Server 2008-2022, Skype for Business, SQL Server 2005-2019, Exchange 2007-2019), showing begin/end of mainstream and end of extended support dates. Notably, Windows Server 2016 ends extended support 01/11/2027, Windows Server 2019 ends 01/9/2029, and Windows Server 2022 ends 10/14/2031.

3. **Extended Security Updates (ESU)** - Provide an additional 3 years of critical security updates beyond Extended Support, distributed in three consecutive 12-month increments. ESUs do NOT include new features, non-security updates, or design changes. They must be purchased separately from Unified Support. Free ESUs are available for: SQL/Windows Server 2008/R2 (when moving workloads to Azure VMs as-is), Windows 7 (via Windows Virtual Desktop through January 2023), and Dynamics AX 2009/AX 2012/R2 (when purchasing Dynamics 365 Finance/Supply Chain/Commerce). Azure Hybrid Benefit can provide discounts for eligible customers.

4. **Service Packs** - Both Mainstream and Extended Support require the supported service pack to be installed. When a new service pack is released, Microsoft provides 12 or 24 months of support for the previous one (Windows client/servers and Dynamics: 24 months; Office, Servers, Developer tools, consumer software: 12 months). If a service pack is released, support for the previous version ends two years later. Starting with SQL Server 2017, no service packs will be released (modern servicing model). Examples given include Windows Server 2008 R2 and Windows Server 2012/R2 lifecycle details, showing R2 versions inherit the original OS's end cycles rather than restarting a full 5 years.

5. **Microsoft End of Life** - Lists products reaching end of support in 2022, including Visual Studio LightSwitch, Windows 7/Server 2008/R2 ESU Year 2 (Jan 2022), Dynamics AX 2009/2012, .NET Framework 4.5.2-4.6.1 (April 2022), Internet Explorer 11 on Windows 10 SAC (June 2022), SQL Server 2008/R2 ESU Year 3, SQL Server 2012, and many System Center 2012 products (July 2022), plus various products ending October and December 2022. Also mentions the Modern Lifecycle Policy where products under active Software Assurance are supported indefinitely until Microsoft gives 12 months' notice of termination.

6. **Third-Party Microsoft Support** - Third-party providers (like US Cloud) can replace or extend Microsoft Premier/Unified contracts, with ESU contracts still recommended for 3 years beyond the 5-year mainstream and 5-year extended support periods. Significant savings are available by moving away from Microsoft for support of both Cloud and on-premise products.

The page concludes with a promotional section for US Cloud, stating that 91% of enterprises that bring a US Cloud estimate to Microsoft see immediate discounts, with clients saving 30-50% vs Unified support.
</summary>

"Microsoft extended support adds 5 years to mainstream MS support. Extend further with ESU security updates and 3rd party Microsoft support."

--- SOURCE 4: Clarification on ESU cost for SQL Server 2016 on Windows Server 2016 in Azure VMware Solution - Microsoft Q&A ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5882155/clarification-on-esu-cost-for-sql-server-2016-on-w

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread (dated May 2026) discussing whether Extended Security Updates (ESUs) for SQL Server 2016 and Windows Server 2016 running in Azure VMware Solution (AVS) are free or incur charges, particularly after July 2026 and in light of Microsoft's April 1, 2026 pricing consistency announcement.

Key findings from the answers:

1. **SQL Server 2016 ESUs in AVS**: Both the moderator and AI answer confirm ESUs remain free in AVS while the ESU program for that version is active, provided VMs are properly Azure Arc-enabled and configured with the SQL Server extension/management components. The April 1, 2026 pricing consistency announcement applies primarily to NEW ESU offerings introduced after that date; existing offerings like SQL Server 2016 are not called out as changing to the new pricing model. When the ESU program for SQL Server 2016 ends, ESUs are no longer available at all (free or paid).

2. **Windows Server 2016 ESUs in AVS**: Also free as part of the Azure ESU benefit when running in Azure destinations (including AVS), but with different operational handling. There is currently no mechanism in AVS to register Windows Server licenses in the portal, so extra configuration and potentially a support request may be needed for activation/renewal. This does not introduce an ESU charge—it only reflects that AVS is not automatically wired like native Azure VMs. However, depending on agreement/enrollment type, Windows Server ESUs may involve additional licensing charges, which is why documentation references support-assisted onboarding steps.

3. **Key differences between SQL Server and Windows Server ESUs in AVS**: The differences are operational (configuration/tracking), not pricing-based. SQL Server requires Azure Arc enablement and the Azure Extension for SQL Server; Windows Server has no in-portal license registration mechanism. Software Assurance is not required for free ESUs in Azure, but is required for Azure Hybrid Benefit base licensing discounts.

The thread includes a follow-up from the original poster noting they heard conflicting information from other forums that all existing and new subscription holders need to pay ESU fees. The moderator clarified that payment statements apply to on-prem/non-Azure environments or cases where VMs aren't properly onboarded to Azure services—not to correctly configured AVS workloads.

The thread also notes that one earlier answer came from an AI robot, and the moderator recommends validating commercial/licensing details with a Microsoft account team or licensing specialist since entitlement details can vary by contract and enrollment model. A moderator note also states this is a technical forum, not the best venue for commercial questions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Customers who use Windows and SQL Server Extended Security Updates released on or after April 1, 2026, will see the same pricing whether they purchase in Azure or outside Azure." - Microsoft pricing consistency announcement
</key_excerpts>
