This Microsoft Learn page announces the retirement of Azure Spring Apps, a fully managed service for running Java Spring applications jointly built by Microsoft and VMware by Broadcom. Key details:

**Retirement Timeline:**
- March 17, 2025: All Azure Spring Apps plans (Basic, Standard, Enterprise) entered a three-year retirement period and stopped accepting new customers.
- March 31, 2028: Official retirement date when all plans will be completely discontinued.

**Migration Recommendations:**
- Microsoft and Broadcom recommend **Azure Container Apps** and **Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)** as the primary replacement services.
- Azure Container Apps is a fully managed, serverless container service with enhanced Java features for managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting Java apps at scale.
- AKS is a managed container orchestration service using Kubernetes with automated updates, monitoring, and scaling.
- Alternative options include Azure App Service (PaaS) and Tanzu Platform Spring Essentials on Azure Container Apps for Enterprise users of Spring commercial support/Tanzu components.

**Key Customer Impacts:**
- Existing customers (those with a service instance created before March 17, 2025) can continue operating until March 31, 2028, including creating, updating, or deleting instances within the same tenant/subscription.
- Support (SLA assurance, infrastructure updates, maintenance, container image updates) continues until the retirement date.
- No new features will be built for Azure Spring Apps during the retirement period; new features are being prioritized on Azure Container Apps.
- Three Tanzu components (App Live View, App Accelerator, App Configuration Service) will be out of support after August 2025 due to Broadcom's TAP 1.12 lifecycle ending; Microsoft reserves the right to remove these components if a critical vulnerability is identified.

**Migration Tooling:**

- Migration guidance documents were released in January 2025 for migrating to Azure Container Apps, AKS, and switching from Tanzu components.

**Pricing Notes:**
- Azure Spring Apps operates on a consumption-based model (pay for vCPU and memory).
- Azure Container Apps offers both a consumption model (per-second billing) and a dedicated model with single tenancy, specialized hardware, and more predictable pricing.

**Other Facts:**
- The retirement decision does not affect Microsoft's overall Java on Azure investment; investment in Azure Container Apps and Java tooling is increasing.

Customers should migrate using options like the app routing add-on or App Gateway for Containers (AGC)
- Managed system node pools (covered above)
- Windows Server 2025 support is GA

**Public previews:**
- AKS on bare metal: New offering that removes hypervisor layer for edge scenarios, running AKS directly on bare metal (one-node clusters in public preview). Built on Azure Local small form factor stack. Hardware requirements published in documentation. Suitable for retail, edge locations, and edge AI workloads (e.g., hosting open-source models in limited-connectivity environments). Presented by Shan (product PM).

The session concluded with open Q&A covering subscription types (cost management capabilities currently for enterprise and MCA subscriptions; migration in progress for legacy subscription types), and a request for feedback on bringing managed system node pools to AKS Standard.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"There's a rule of thumb out there. If you have to do something in technology and you can draw your tool chain of all the pieces parts and it exceeds five pictures, you have something very complicated to do." — Ken Kilty on AI scaling complexity

"To reiterate this, absolutely no customer data of any sort leaves the customer subscription. This is important. The Anyscale control plane is really a command and control mechanism... but everything lives, breathes, and stays in the customer subscription." — Ken Kilty

"Automatic is offering this new SLA that guarantees pod readiness within 5 minutes at the 99.9th percentile for all automatic clusters as a default. If pods don't come up within that 5 minutes then you'll get your money back... most managed Kubernetes services including AKS until now have offered only guarantees on the control plane uptime." — Casey on AKS Automatic SLA

"It's absolutely recommended for production clusters. In fact, that's really one of the main places we would see customers using it... it's actually designed for production. Things like redundancy and all the best practices to make sure things are up and running are already there." — Brian Redmond on AKS Automatic for production

"The Ingress project was always something that I think was retrofitted into Kubernetes from the early stages... gateway API is a much more robust API and a better way to do things like ingress configurations. You don't want to be on Ingress NGINX after that date because you won't start to see security patches and updates and that's not a situation anyone should be in." — Brian Redmond on Gateway API GA
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/blog/introducing-azure-container-service-aks-managed-kubernetes-and-azure-container-registry-geo-replication

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Azure blog post announcing the preview of AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service), a new managed Kubernetes service, along with the general availability of managed SKUs for Azure Container Registry (ACR) and the preview of ACR geo-replication.

Key announcements and details:

1. **AKS Preview Launch**: Microsoft announced the preview of AKS, its new managed Kubernetes service. It features an Azure-hosted control plane, automated upgrades, self-healing, easy scaling, and a simple user experience. Kubernetes support on Azure Container Service (ACS) grew 300% in the previous six months.

2. **Pricing**: AKS is free — customers only pay for the VMs they use, with no hourly charge for management infrastructure, unlike other cloud providers. The blog states users will "pay nothing for the management of your Kubernetes cluster, ever."

3. **Kubernetes Focus**: Microsoft is shifting its managed container service focus to Kubernetes, which has emerged as the open source standard for container orchestration. Notable context: Brendan Burns (co-creator of Kubernetes) leads Azure's container efforts, and Microsoft acquired Deis (a Kubernetes innovation company) earlier in 2017. Microsoft continues to contribute upstream to Kubernetes and develop tools like Draft.

4. **Continued Support for Other Orchestrators**: Microsoft will continue supporting the existing ACS deployment engine for Docker Enterprise and Mesosphere DC/OS, working with Docker and Mesosphere to offer enhanced integration of their enterprise offers in the Azure Marketplace (with easy in-place upgrades to enterprise editions offering 24×7 support).

5. **Azure Container Registry (ACR) GA**: Managed SKUs for ACR are now generally available, providing a private registry scaling through three new sizes.

6. **ACR Geo-Replication Preview**: A first-of-its-kind feature allowing customers to manage a single registry replicated across any number of regions via a click of a map. Container image pushes/pulls route to the closest registry, enabling management of global deployments as one entity.

The blog includes a demo showing how easy it is to provision a new AKS cluster, upgrade from Kubernetes 1.7.7 to 1.8.1, and scale from 3 to 10 nodes. The announcement is attributed to The Microsoft Azure Team.

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### DIMENSION 1: TOOLING AND SERVICES

#### 1.1 Azure Migrate — Discovery, Assessment, Dependency Analysis

**Azure Migrate product overview (Microsoft):** Azure Migrate is described as a comprehensive cloud migration tool designed to help organizations streamline their path to the cloud through assessment, migration, and modernization. Key capabilities include: seeing the IT estate clearly, deciding faster with guided options, migrating and modernizing servers/databases/web apps, and optimizing performance, cost, and management. Azure Migrate embeds security and compliance, offers cost optimization through Azure Accelerate, and supports modernization of workloads to Azure App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service, and other Azure services. The product page highlights customer stories from Fortune Brands, Solv, and Syensqo, and its FAQ covers the difference between Azure Migrate and Azure Site Recovery. [15]

**Azure Migrate release history (What's New, Microsoft Learn, page last updated June 22, 2026):** Azure Migrate "helps you discover, assess, and migrate on-premises servers, apps, and data to the Azure cloud platform." Notable features by date: [11]

- **May 2026 (Public preview):** Automatic discovery of applications by grouping workloads discovered through the Collector, Appliance, or CSV import, using server naming patterns, inferred environments, and server roles.
- **April 2026 (Public preview):** Reserved tags to enrich data with business context (environment: Prod, Dev, Test, UAT; migration intent: Migrate, Retain, Retire), which influence assessments, SKU calculations, pricing, and migration planning. MongoDB assessments with readiness, right-sizing recommendations, and cost estimates for Azure Document DB or MongoDB on Azure VMs.
- **March 2026 (Public preview):** Reports feature for executive-level migration/modernization insights (including security and business case insights), tailored to strategies like PaaS (AI-ready), Azure Virtual Machines, or Azure VMware Solution (AVS). General Availability of Gen2 VM migration to Trusted Launch Azure VMs (UEFI-based Secure Boot and vTPM). Azure Copilot migration agent for conversational VMware migration planning. Security insights expanded to cover Web apps and Databases (not just Servers and Software).
- **November 2025:** Three new built-in RBAC roles: Azure Migrate Owner (end-to-end), Azure Migrate Decide & Plan Expert, and Azure Migrate Execute Expert, enabling least-privilege access. Windows Server redeployment to Azure using Infrastructure as Code (IaC) templates (public preview). GitHub Copilot assessment for code insights in web app assessments targeting AKS or Azure App Service. Arc-based discovery for assessing Arc-enabled on-premises servers and SQL instances without new infrastructure. Wave Planning for structured large-scale migrations with waves, sequencing, visualization, tracking, and monitoring.
- **October 2025:** Integrated Security insights (public preview) with dashboard, auto-detection of unsupported OS/software, pending updates, CVEs, and recommendations for Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Azure Update Manager. Software inventory enhancements: review software across all servers, sanitized/classified categories, support status, vulnerabilities, potential Azure targets, and scoping/filtering. Dependency visualization across multiple servers with intuitive navigation, node interaction, filtering by netstat data, per-server view, and high-affinity server grouping.
- **September 2025:** PostgreSQL discovery and assessment (public preview) for migration to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, with configuration-based assessment, cost estimation, and readiness categorization. General Availability of ZRS (Zone-Redundant Storage) Disks migration support.
- **July 2025:** SSH authentication for Linux servers in VMware and Hyper-V appliance stacks (GA).
- **June 2025:** End-to-end migration of Gen2 VMs to Trusted Launch VMs (public preview) for all migration scenarios; Sustainability insights in Business Case for emissions estimation and ESG goal support.
- **May 2025:** Premium SSD v2 disk support (GA); Ultra Disk migration support (public preview); ZRS Disk migration (public preview); upgraded agent-based migration stack (GA); application awareness features including inventory view across tiers, tags, enhanced dependency analysis, application assessment, and Action Center.
- **February 2025:** MySQL discovery and assessment (public preview).
- **November 2024:** AVS cost assessments with AV64 host type and Azure NetApp Files; Enterprise Linux (RHEL/SLES) migration via Azure Hybrid Benefit; business case creation for Azure Arc onboarding.
- **October 2024:** RVTools XLSX import reads storage data from vPartition and vMemory sheets.
- **April 2024:** Movere service retired (March 1, 2024); SAP discovery and assessment; Java (Tomcat) web app assessment for App Service and AKS.
- **March 2024:** Spring Boot app discovery/assessment via Kubernetes appliance.
- **February 2024:** Azure Hybrid Benefit savings for Enterprise Linux subscriptions.
- **December 2023:** Cost savings from Azure management services in business cases.
- **November 2023:** ASP.NET web app assessment for AKS and App Service Containers with TCO comparison.
- **September 2023:** Spring Boot app discovery/assessment.
- **August 2023:** Windows Server and SQL Server license support posture insights; ESU savings estimation.
- **July 2023:** System Center Operations Manager 2019 UR3+ integration; Windows OS upgrade during migration.
- **June 2023:** Microsoft Defender for Cloud security cost savings in business cases.
- **May 2023:** SQL Server discovery/assessment GA.
- **April 2023:** Business case for .csv imported servers; Hyper-V/physical/bare-metal environments; SQL Always On support; Windows Server Azure Hybrid Benefit savings.
- **March 2023:** Web app discovery/assessment for Hyper-V and physical servers.
- **February 2023:** SQL Always On failover cluster and availability group discovery; ASP.NET web app modernization on AKS.
- **January 2023:** Azure savings plan for compute; business case .xlsx export; Sweden geography support.
- **December 2022:** Software inventory and agentless dependency analysis GA for Hyper-V/bare-metal/other clouds; business case for VMware; Azure Private Link GA.
- **November 2022:** Sudo user account for agentless dependency analysis; test migration network/subnet selection; OS disk swap; pause/resume replication via PowerShell.
- **2021:** Multiple vCenter discovery via single appliance; Ultra Disks support; at-scale software inventory GA; app containerization for App Service containers and AKS; SQL Server discovery/assessment preview; concurrent replication of 500 VMs; 4 TB OS disk support via agent-based migration.
- **2020:** Availability zone migration; UEFI VM migration to Gen2 VMs; Power BI assessment dashboard; dependency analysis on 1,000 VMs concurrently; 32 TB data disks; Azure Government support; script-based appliance installation; agentless VMware migration at 300 VMs per vCenter.
- **2019 (current version, July 2019):** Unified migration platform with single portal; assessment and migration tools including Azure Migrate Server Assessment and Server Migration tools; Azure Migrate appliance for agentless discovery; two VMware migration methods (agentless and agent-based); database assessment/migration; web app migration; Azure Data Box integration; physical server assessment; import-based assessment; application discovery; agentless dependency visualization; virtual desktop and web app support.

The previous Azure Migrate version (assessment-only for VMware) is deprecated—new projects/discoveries can no longer be created in it, though existing projects remain accessible. [11]

**Dependency analysis (Microsoft Learn, updated 2026-06-19):** Dependency analysis "identifies dependencies between discovered on-premises running in VMware, Hyper-V, physical servers or servers running on other public clouds." It provides: reviewing network dependencies and grouping inter-dependent servers into applications, identifying servers that must be migrated together, and helping avoid surprise outages after migration by ensuring nothing is left behind. Two options exist: [12]

- **Agentless dependency analysis** — Generally available for VMware VMs, Hyper-V VMs, physical servers, and servers in other public clouds. Supported in both Azure Public Cloud and Azure Government. This is the recommended approach. Captures TCP network connection data from enabled servers without installing agents. Connections between source server/process and destination server/process/port are logically grouped into dependencies. Data can be visualized in a map view or exported as CSV. The Azure Migrate appliance polls TCP connection data every 5 minutes, gathering process names with active connections, application names running those processes, and destination ports. Gathered data is processed on the appliance and sent to Azure Migrate every 6 hours.
- **Agent-based dependency analysis** — Supported only in the classic view (not the new experience), using the Service Map solution in Azure Monitor. Requires installing agents on each source server. Supported in public cloud but NOT supported in Azure Government. The classic view is scheduled for deprecation by the end of 2026; no new servers can be onboarded for agent-based analysis.

**Azure Migrate appliance for VMware** helps with discovery, assessment, software inventory, application dependency analysis, and migration. [13]

#### 1.2 Azure Migrate Application and Code Assessment (AppCAT)

The Azure Migrate application and code assessment is a developer-focused feature for analyzing ASP.NET and ASP.NET Core applications to plan re-platforming to Azure PaaS environments. Available as both a Visual Studio 2022 extension and a .NET command-line SDK tool (`dotnet-appcat`); it scans source code, configuration, and binaries to identify issues that need to be addressed before migrating to Azure App Service, AKS, or Azure Container Apps. A Java version also exists. It complements Azure Migrate's existing discovery/assessment features (Data Migration Assistant, App Service Migration Assistant). [14]

- Issues are categorized into four severities: Mandatory (e.g., Windows authentication needing to be changed to Azure AD), Optional (e.g., moving settings from web.config to Azure App Configuration/Key Vault), Potential (e.g., SQL Server connectivity depending on whether the database is accessible from Azure), and Information.
- Each incident includes a unitless story point estimate for relative effort comparison. Reports can be exported as HTML, CSV, or JSON.
- Example walkthrough analyzing the eShop "Northern Mountains" sample (github.com/dotnet/eshop) produced 41 incidents across nine issue types in 16 projects: 8 mandatory, 8 optional, 25 potential. Key findings included RabbitMQ usage (mandatory – 8 incidents), database usage (8 incidents), connection strings (6 incidents), hardcoded URLs (5 incidents), caching/Redis usage (5 incidents), HTTP usage (4 incidents), local file usage (1 incident, marked N/A), and static content (3 optional incidents).
- CLI tool is installed via `dotnet tool install -g dotnet-appcat` and run with the `appcat` command (e.g., `appcat analyze solution.sln`). Supports non-interactive mode for scripting: `appcat analyze eShopLegacyMVC.csproj -s HTML -r OutputPath --code --non-interactive`. The solution must build without errors when using the CLI.
- Future roadmap: GitHub Copilot Chat integration, ability to specify multiple Azure target environments (e.g., Windows App Service vs. AKS with Linux containers, already available in the Java version), and binary output analysis. Documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/migrate/appcat/overview. [14]

#### 1.3 Azure Database Migration Service (DMS)

**Azure Database Migration Service (classic) pricing (Microsoft):** A fully managed service designed for operational database and data warehouse migrations. [16]

- **Standard Tier:** Supports offline (also called "one-time") migrations only. Designed for most small- to medium-sized business workloads. Available in 1-, 2-, and 4-vCore options. **FREE** to customers at all vCore levels.
- **Premium Tier:** Supports offline AND online (continuous) migrations for business-critical workloads requiring minimal downtime. Designed for large or business-critical workloads with faster migration speeds. 4-vCore option priced at $/hour (specific rate not shown on page). **Free for 6 months (183 days)** from the DMS service creation date before charges begin.
- **Savings plan for databases:** Flexible spend-based pricing with a One-Year Discount of **35%** on price per vCore. Customers commit to a fixed hourly spend for one year and receive lower prices across eligible Azure database services.
- DMS (classic) services can be used for up to 1 year from the date of service creation. Customers can create up to **10 DMS (classic) services per subscription**; additional services require a support ticket.

**Third-party cost reference for DMS (migrationcost.com, 2026):** [17]

- Standard tier: FREE for offline migrations of databases up to 1 TB.
- Premium tier: ~$0.37/vCore-hour (4 vCore) or $0.55/vCore-hour (8 vCore); supports online migrations with minimal downtime.
- A typical SQL Server to Azure SQL MI migration using premium 4 vCore tier for two weeks costs roughly $1,250 per database.
- Microsoft is phasing to a new "Azure Database Migration Service (modern)" generation with a different pricing model.

#### 1.4 Azure Site Recovery (ASR) for Migration Replication

**Official Azure Site Recovery pricing (Microsoft):** ASR is billed based on the number of instances protected. Every instance is FREE for the first 31 days of protection. After 31 days, charges apply per instance protected (both for recovery to customer-owned sites and to Azure). ASR between Azure regions is charged at the same rate as ASR to Azure. Billing is calculated using the average daily number of protected instances over a monthly period (e.g., protecting 20 instances for half a month and none for the other half results in an average of 10 protected instances). The 31-day free period applies to every new instance, regardless of how long a customer has been using the service. Even during the free period, customers may incur charges for Azure Storage, storage transactions, data transfer, and compute charges for recovered VMs. Azure Hybrid Benefit allows up to 40% or more savings using Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance. Test recoveries are limited to brief DR testing within one week every 90 days. [20]

- Licensing requirements by recovery site type: On-Premises (fully licensed servers or end-customer licenses via Disaster Recovery Software Assurance benefit); Service Provider (licensed via SPLA – Services Provider License Agreement); Azure (Disaster Recovery Software Assurance benefit applies, changed in January 2015 Product Use Rights; Azure Hybrid Benefit can be leveraged).
- Azure Site Recovery replication for SQL Server is covered under the Software Assurance Disaster Recovery benefit.
- Azure does not support persistent MAC addresses, so MAC-based license models cannot be used for migration/DR.

**Third-party ASR cost reference (migrationcost.com, 2026):** [17]

- ASR charges $25 per protected instance per month after a 31-day free trial per instance.
- Standard rate: $25/month for replication to Azure and Azure-to-Azure DR. On-premise DR use case: $54/month.
- A 100-server migration with a 3-month replication window costs approximately $7,500 in ASR fees.
- Third-party alternatives like Carbonite Migrate cost $400–$800 per server one-time, making ASR meaningfully cheaper.

**ASR cost breakdown (Critical Cloud, June 7, 2026):** ASR is a pay-as-you-go disaster recovery service with no upfront hardware or software costs, but it accumulates four separate cost components continuously once protection is enabled: [18]

1. **Licence fees per protected instance** – Billed hourly per protected VM or physical server, with a 31-day free trial per new instance. Rates vary by workload type (Azure-to-Azure, VMware/Hyper-V to Azure, physical server to Azure).
2. **Cache storage** – Requires a General Purpose v2 storage account in the source region. Costs depend on the storage SKU and data volume; high-I/O workloads (databases, transaction processing) can incur significant costs.
3. **Target storage** – Replicated data lands on Managed Disks in the target recovery region, paid continuously regardless of whether failover occurs. "For a 1 TB Premium SSD protecting a production database VM, you are paying for a 1 TB Premium SSD in the recovery region at full price, from the moment protection is enabled. Multiply this across a large number of protected VMs and it becomes the largest single cost component." Optimization: use Standard SSD or Standard HDD where RTO allows.
4. **Network charges for replication traffic** – Initial replication incurs a one-time egress charge for full disk copy; ongoing delta replication charges standard inter-region transfer rates. Optimization: schedule replication during off-peak hours (e.g., 20:00–06:00 GMT).

Compute costs during failover: Replication itself incurs no compute costs, but failed-over VMs (test or actual) run at standard VM compute rates. "Test failovers should be temporary: run the test, validate recovery, and clean up. A test failover left running for a week at VM rates for ten protected VMs is an avoidable cost that surprises teams who run tests but forget to tear them down." ASR's minimum RPO is ~5 minutes for VMware workloads with typical recovery points every 15-30 minutes for Azure-to-Azure, making it cost-competitive for workloads with RPO requirements in the 15-minute to 1-hour range. Zerto supports continuous data protection with near-zero RPO (sub-second), which ASR cannot match. [18]

**ASR vs. traditional DR (Infrassist, November 14, 2025):** [19]

- **Traditional DR costs:** Upfront hardware for mid-size enterprises (500-2,000 employees): $150K-300K. Monthly costs: colocation ($2,000-5,000), network ($500-1,500), maintenance contracts ($2,000-4,500, roughly 18-22% of hardware cost/year). Hardware refresh cycles every 3-5 years. Five-year reality check for 50 VMs: $200K hardware + $480K operations + $100K mid-cycle refresh = $780,000 total (~$13,000/month). ~20% of SMEs cite affordability as primary barrier to DR adoption.
- **Azure Site Recovery costs (50-VM environment):** ASR licenses: 50 VMs × $31 = $1,550/month; test failover compute: 10 VMs × $120 = $1,200/month; storage (LRS): 15TB × $19/TB = $285/month; replication bandwidth: 2TB × $87/TB = $174/month; Azure Backup add-on: 15TB × $10/TB = $150/month. Total Azure: $3,359/month; complete monthly cost with services: $5,259. Savings of 56-65% versus traditional DR ($12K-15K monthly).
- **Side-by-side:** Upfront cost: $150K-300K (traditional) vs. $0 (Azure). Monthly cost: $12K-18K vs. $3K-5K. RTO: 2-8 hours vs. 15 minutes. RPO: 1-4 hours vs. 15-30 minutes. Testing: production disruption risk vs. isolated, zero impact.
- **Client case study (Virginia manufacturing firm):** Traditional quote: $200,000 upfront + $3,000/month (new Nimble array $120K, replication software $25K, secondary site $35K, implementation $20K). Azure implementation: 12 production VMs migrated over 4-6 weeks using Azure Migrate; 4TB initial sync over 50Mbps (~72 hours); successful test failover on first try. Results after 6 months: $200K avoided, new monthly DR cost $4,200, five-year savings of $456,000, RTO dropped from 4+ hours to 15 minutes, RPO improved from 8 hours to 30 minutes.
- Implementation: 4-6 weeks typical (2 weeks assessment, 2 weeks configuration/sync, 2 weeks testing). Bandwidth: ~5Mbps per VM needed; Azure Data Box available for slow connections; ongoing replication needs only 1-2Mbps per VM.

#### 1.5 Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and Azure App Service for Re-platforming

**AKS overview (CloudThat, October 26, 2023):** AKS is "an advanced, managed container orchestration platform offered by Microsoft Azure... a pivotal solution to streamline containerized applications' deployment, scaling, and management." Fully managed service (Azure handles cluster maintenance, updates, and scaling); seamless integration with Azure services (Azure Active Directory, Azure Monitor, Azure DevOps); horizontal scaling capabilities; robust security measures including identity/access management, network policies, and compliance certifications; multi-region support for enhanced availability and disaster recovery. Key features: automated updates and patches, horizontal pod autoscaling, Azure Monitor and Azure Log Analytics integration, Azure Key Vault integration for secrets management, Azure DevOps integration for CI/CD pipelines, managed node pools, RBAC. AKS pricing is pay-as-you-go depending on node count/size, storage, and network usage. [46]

**AKS is free (Microsoft Azure Blog):** "AKS is free. You only pay for the VMs that add value to your business. Unlike other cloud providers who charge an hourly rate for the management infrastructure, with AKS you will pay nothing for the management of your Kubernetes cluster, ever." Features an Azure-hosted control plane, automated upgrades, self-healing, easy scaling, and a simple user experience. Azure Container Registry (ACR) managed SKUs became GA with three new sizes; ACR geo-replication preview allows managing a single registry replicated across any number of regions, with image pushes/pulls routing to the closest registry. [50]

**AKS Community Call June 2026 (US & Europe) highlights:** [49]

- **AKS Automatic updates:** In AKS Standard, customer owns system pool end-to-end. In AKS Automatic, AKS now owns the system layer—provisioning, right-sizing, scaling, and security isolation for system components. New pod readiness SLA: guarantees pods ready within 5 minutes at 99.9th percentile for all automatic clusters (default)—"First of its kind for managed Kubernetes—most services only offer control plane uptime SLAs." AKS now eats the cost of system nodes (minimum 3 less VMs customers pay for) — default operating model for all new AKS Automatic clusters as of early June 2026. No migration path to adopt managed system node pools on existing automatic clusters without recreating; Windows nodes not supported with managed system node pools. AKS Automatic is "absolutely recommended for production clusters... it's actually designed for production. Things like redundancy and all the best practices to make sure things are up and running are already there." Migration: easy to go from Automatic to Standard (minor API call), harder to go from Standard to Automatic.
- **Roadmap GA:** Gateway API support on AKS is GA—the replacement for Ingress. NGINX Ingress project has been deprecated; AKS extended support until fall 2026 (September or November), after which no security patches will be provided. Customers should migrate using options like the app routing add-on or App Gateway for Containers (AGC). Windows Server 2025 support is GA.
- **Public previews:** AKS on bare metal — new offering that removes hypervisor layer for edge scenarios, running AKS directly on bare metal (one-node clusters in public preview), built on Azure Local small form factor stack.
- **AKS Cost Analysis add-on (GA):** Allows cost allocation by cluster, namespace, and Azure assets from Azure portal. New features: open-source self-managed cost export sample (daily CSV to blob storage with breakdowns beyond namespace—deployments, services, labels, jobs; multiple export formats including raw usage, amortized file, and FOCUS spec format for multi-cloud comparison). A managed scheduled export feature is targeting Q4 2026. AKS Pricing Calculator (TCO estimator): New "cloud-native apps on Kubernetes" template provides a configurable baseline estimate for running a production AKS environment, including attached services (Azure Monitor, Defender, ACR, Azure Policy, etc.). Supports reserved instances, savings plans, and discounts. Azure Monitor dashboards with Grafana (GA): pre-built AKS dashboards free with every cluster regardless of tier. GPU observability (public preview): GPU metrics exporter installed by default on managed GPU node pools.
- First "Kube-n-Tell" session covered a financial services company dealing with AKS cluster sprawl.

**Windows containers on AKS migration solutions (Microsoft Docs):** Microsoft has collaborated with leading partners for migrating and modernizing applications to Windows containers: [48]

- **Azure Migrate:** Blog detailing the process of migrating ASP.NET web apps to Windows containers on AKS, covering initial discovery, TCO comparison, cloud readiness assessment, and containerization.
- **CAST:** Provides a detailed guide using CAST Highlight to identify containerization blockers and offers remediation strategies, enhancing migration with insights into application code, architecture, and third-party compliance.
- **UnifyCloud:** Introduces its CloudAtlas platform, an end-to-end migration tool for streamlining modernization of .NET applications to Windows containers on AKS.

**Azure Spring Apps retirement (Microsoft Learn, last updated 2025-10-31):** All Azure Spring Apps plans (Basic, Standard, Enterprise) entered a three-year retirement period on March 17, 2025, and will be retired on March 31, 2028. Microsoft and Broadcom recommend **Azure Container Apps** and **Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)** as the primary replacement services. Azure Container Apps is a fully managed, serverless container service with enhanced Java features. AKS is a managed container orchestration service using Kubernetes with automated updates, monitoring, and scaling. Alternative options include Azure App Service (PaaS) and Tanzu Platform Spring Essentials on Azure Container Apps. Azure Container Apps offers both a consumption model (per-second billing) and a dedicated model with single tenancy, specialized hardware, and more predictable pricing. [47]

#### 1.6 Partner Solutions and Modernization Tooling

**VIAcode (Microsoft-specialized partner with specializations in "Infrastructure & Database Migration" and "Migrating Enterprise Applications to Microsoft Azure"):** Lift-and-shift migration uses a 4-step process: (1) Pre-Migration Assessment using VIAcode's free Azure assessment, (2) Migration Planning with timeline and milestones, (3) Executing the Migration using Azure Migrate and Azure Site Recovery with minimal downtime and data backups, and (4) Post-Migration Optimization with performance monitoring, cost optimization, and security assessments. Large data migrations are handled via Azure Data Box and Azure Data Migration Service. #### 1.7 Migration Strategy Frameworks (6 Rs, 7 Rs)

**The 6 Rs for Azure (Apps4Rent, published July 31, 2026):** Framework originated from Gartner and was popularized across the industry. Six strategies ordered from least to most transformation: Rehost (lift and shift to Azure VMs with no changes), Replatform (move with targeted upgrades to managed services), Refactor/Rearchitect (restructure applications to be cloud-native), Repurchase (replace with SaaS products), Retire (decommission unused workloads), and Retain (keep on-premises for now). [3]

- Rehosting involves discovery/dependency mapping, right-sizing via Azure Migrate, replication/test failover, and wave-based cutover. Best for deadline-driven moves, datacenter exits, or vendor-constrained apps. Azure Hybrid Benefit allows applying existing Windows Server/SQL Server licenses to reduce VM costs.
- Replatforming swaps components for managed services without code rewrites (e.g., SQL Server on VM to Azure SQL Managed Instance, IIS web apps to Azure App Service, file servers to Azure Files, or apps to containers). It delivers the best return per engineering hour.
- Practical rule: "rehost by default when the calendar is the constraint, replatform by default when operations are the constraint." A hybrid pattern (rehost app servers, replatform databases) is often optimal.
- Refactoring is justified only for core business applications with real scaling/deployment needs; Microsoft's guidance is to modernize during migration only when the team has the skills and time, otherwise defer. A plan marking half the portfolio as "refactor" is usually wrong.
- Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework uses 8 strategies (adds rebuild and splits refactor into refactor, rearchitect, and rebuild; renames repurchase to replace), but the underlying per-workload decisions are identical.
- 5-step migration process: (1) inventory everything with Azure Migrate discovery, (2) eliminate retire/repurchase candidates first, (3) assign an R per workload scored on business value and technical fitness, (4) prepare the foundation via Azure landing zone, and (5) migrate in dependency-complete waves with post-migration optimization.
- Common mistakes: blanket rehosting or refactoring, one-to-one sizing, ignoring licensing strategy (Hybrid Benefit, reserved instances), migrating dependencies apart, and having no day-2 plan. Key quote: "there is no single correct way to move to the cloud, only a correct way to move each workload."

**The 7 Rs (CloudifyOps/Medium):** The framework evolved from Gartner's original 5 Rs to AWS's 6 Rs, and now includes a 7th strategy called Relocate. [2]

1. **Rehost (Lift and Shift)** — Fastest route; move infrastructure to cloud with minimal changes. Example: financial services firm migrating 200 VMs to AWS EC2 ahead of data centre lease expiry.
2. **Replatform (Lift and Reshape)** — Targeted cloud optimizations without redesigning core architecture. Example: migrating on-premises PostgreSQL to Amazon Aurora.
3. **Refactor/Re-Architect** — Cloud-native rebuild with microservices, stateless architecture, managed services, and CI/CD. Example: logistics platform achieving 10x deployment velocity and 99.99% uptime on Amazon EKS.
4. **Repurchase (Drop and Shop)** — Replace legacy apps with SaaS alternatives (Salesforce for CRM, Workday for HR, ServiceNow for ITSM).
5. **Retire** — Decommission systems no longer needed. Example: healthcare organization retiring 30 underused applications.
6. **Retain (Revisit Later)** — Keep applications on-premises when compliance constraints or risk outweigh near-term benefits, particularly for government/classified data.
7. **Relocate (Hypervisor Lift, the 7th R)** — Move entire VMware virtualization estates to cloud-hosted environments (VMware Cloud on AWS, Azure VMware Solution) without changing hypervisor, applications, or tooling. "Think of Rehost as 'move the VM'; Relocate as 'move the data centre virtually.'" Example: insurance company migrating 400 VMs with zero changes and zero retraining.

Four-step framework for choosing strategies: (1) portfolio discovery and assessment, (2) score each application across business criticality, technical complexity, compliance requirements, and cloud/AI readiness, (3) map applications to the 7 Rs, and (4) plan and execute in waves. Claims of industrialized, AI-driven migration platforms: accelerated timelines by 30–50%, reduced modernization rework by 25–40%, and reduced planning effort by 40–60% for refactoring. Four-stage legacy-to-AI-ready journey: Stabilize (Rehost/Relocate), Optimise (Replatform/Repurchase), Modernize (Refactor), and AI-Enable. Key takeaways: Rehost/Relocate are best for speed and low disruption; Refactor delivers maximum long-term value; Replatform balances effort and benefit; most enterprises use all seven strategies. [2]

**The 7 Rs (IBM Think, published 13 October 2025 by Stephanie Susnjara and Ian Smalley):** The framework evolved from the initial 5 R's (rehost, refactor, revise, rebuild, replace) introduced by Gartner in 2010. AWS expanded it to 6 R's in 2016 by adding "Retire," then added "Retain" in 2017 to complete the 7 R's. Today most enterprises use hybrid and multicloud strategies. Global cloud market was valued at USD 752.44 million in 2024 and projected to grow to USD 2,390.19 billion by 2030. Hybrid cloud migration can achieve 2.5 times more value than single public cloud (per IBM IBV report "Mastering Hybrid Cloud"). Approximately 58% of global decision-makers report cloud skills remain a considerable challenge (IBM IBV 2023 report). Cloud providers offer tools like AWS Application Migration Service, IBM Cloud migration services, and Azure Migrate. Plans should include success criteria, rollback procedures, data migration planning, and stakeholder coordination. Governance and cost management frameworks (resource tagging, budget alerts, regular cost reviews) should be established before migration begins. [4]

The article includes a detailed comparison table covering use-cases, pros, and cons of each strategy. Key considerations: Retire is cheapest but risks incompatibility with interconnected stacks; Relocate is quickest but limits cloud-native capabilities; Refactor is best for high-usability complex applications but requires extensive planning, training, and monitoring. [5]

### DIMENSION 3: DOWNTIME AND BUSINESS CONTINUITY RISKS

#### 3.1 Availability Zones

**Azure availability zones (official Microsoft page):** Azure availability zones are "physically and logically separated datacenters within each Azure region, each with independent power, network, and cooling." They provide **99.99% uptime SLA for virtual machines**. Support multisite active-active scaling, meet compliance/regulatory needs, and improve RTOs/RPOs. Each region connects at least three physically distinct datacenters, evaluated against more than 30 viability criteria and risk factors. **Latency between availability zones is maintained at less than two milliseconds.** Zone-redundant services automatically achieve resiliency without complex architecture. Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) provides holistic resiliency. Data traversing within or between regions is encrypted. Services fall into three categories: zonal, zone-redundant, and non-regional services. Availability zones are available in every country where Azure operates a region. Customer quotes include NAB (Steve Day, Executive General Manager Infrastructure): "Trust and resilience are critical for the financial services industry to meet both the regulatory requirements of APRA and customer expectations..." and Adobe (Mitch Nelson): "Availability zones give us the combination of low latency and high availability that we need to meet customer requirements... The physical separation of availability zones builds an extra layer of redundancy." [38]

**K21Academy AZ-900 study material:** Azure regions: 54 Azure regions across 140 countries with 3 availability zones per supported region. Not all regions support availability zones (e.g., Central US, East US 2, West US 2, West Europe, France Central, North Europe, Southeast Asia do support them). Availability zones are physically separate datacenters with independent power, cooling, and networking. Zonal services deploy to a self-selected zone; zone-redundant services replicate automatically across zones (e.g., data duplicated across three zones); always-available services are resilient to zone and region-wide failures. Availability zones are connected by high-performance networks with less than 2ms round-trip latency. Availability zones protect from whole datacenter failures; availability sets protect from hardware failures within a datacenter. Availability zones are included with Azure subscription (though inter-region travel may incur fees). [40]

#### 3.2 Paired Regions and Multi-Region Architectures

**Microsoft Well-Architected Framework design guide (regions and availability zones):** Defines active-active vs. active-passive architectures, asynchronous vs. synchronous replication, availability zones (separate groups of datacenters within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking), zonal (pinned) deployments (resources pinned to a specific availability zone), zone-redundant deployments (resources spread across multiple availability zones with Microsoft managing failover), and multi-region deployments. [36]

Four deployment approaches:
1. **Locally Redundant Deployments:** Single region without zone specification. Lowest cost, low reliability (subject to datacenter outages), acceptable performance, high operational efficiency.
2. **Zonal (Pinned) Deployments:** Resources pinned to specific availability zones. High performance (low latency), high cost when deployed across multiple zones, low operational efficiency (customer responsible for data replication, failover, and traffic distribution).
3. **Zone-Redundant Deployments:** Resources spread across multiple availability zones with synchronous replication managed by Microsoft. High reliability, moderate cost, high operational efficiency (automatic failover). "Recommended starting point for many production workloads."
4. **Multi-Region Deployments:** Resources deployed across multiple Azure regions. Highest reliability (resilient to full region outages), high cost, low operational efficiency. Uses either asynchronous replication (high performance, possible data loss) or synchronous replication (very high reliability, low performance due to cross-region latency).

Key recommendations: "For many production workloads, a zone-redundant deployment provides the best balance of trade-offs. You can extend this approach with asynchronous data backup to another region. If you aren't sure which approach to select, start with this type of deployment." Mission-critical workloads should use BOTH multiple availability zones AND multiple regions. Consider RTO and RPO when implementing backup strategies. Risks: hardware outages (high likelihood), datacenter outages (medium likelihood), and region outages (low likelihood). [36]

**Modern Azure Resilience with Mark Russinovich (Microsoft Tech Community, April 6, 2026, updated April 28, 2026):** [37]

- Four primary resilience architecture patterns: (1) In-region High Availability with Availability Zones, (2) Regional Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BCDR) using paired regions, (3) Non-paired region BCDR, and (4) Multi-region active/active designs.
- Historical context: Azure launched regions in pairs (2010, rebranded 2014) to align with enterprise BCDR practices, offering familiar primary/secondary failover patterns, regulatory support, turnkey GRS replication, and platform-level update sequencing. **However, since 2020, new regions are typically designed with multiple availability zones and no paired region.**
- Availability Zones (introduced in 2018) are physically isolated data center groups with independent power, cooling, and networking, enabling platform-managed zone redundancy.
- **"Region pairs should be viewed as an architectural choice rather than a rule."** With matured Safe Deployment Practices (SDP), paired regions are no longer the sole mechanism for managing correlated change risk. Customers can now use non-paired regions or mixes to optimize for data residency, regulatory boundaries, latency, and differentiated recovery objectives.
- Distinguish HA (near-zero downtime, minimal data loss) from DR (defined recovery time and acceptable data loss).
- Use Azure Site Recovery (ASR) for near-continuous replication and orchestrated failover to any region of choice, and Azure Backup for policy-based data protection.
- Regional parity is never guaranteed even between paired regions (differences in SKUs, scale limits, capacity, cost, and operational maturity must be accounted for).
- AZs combined with geo-redundant services can provide equivalent or better protection for workloads that used 1+1 paired regions mainly for datacenter-failure protection, with less complexity and cost.
- Future: Resiliency agent in Azure Copilot (preview) that identifies missing resiliency coverage and provides automated remediation guidance; unified "Resiliency in Azure" experience.

**K21Academy paired regions:** Each Azure region is paired with another region in the same geography at least 300 miles away (e.g., West US with East US, Southeast Asia with East Asia) to enable replication and reduce interruption risks. Azure updates are rolled out to paired regions one at a time. Benefits of paired regions: physical separation between datacenters, region recovery during outages, automatic platform-provided replication (e.g., Geo-Redundant Storage), data residency/compliance benefits, and sequential system updates. There are 160+ Azure datacenters worldwide. [40]

#### 5.6 Azure Dedicated HSM, Managed HSM, and Customer-Managed Keys

**Azure Key Vault Managed HSM (Microsoft Learn via docs.azure.cn, last updated 2026-06-22):** "Azure Key Vault and Azure Key Vault Managed HSM are designed, deployed, and operated so that Microsoft and its agents are precluded from accessing, using, or extracting any data that's stored in the service, including cryptographic keys." Encryption at rest is a key technical measure for data control and compliance, covering standards like HIPAA and FIPS 140-2/3. [42]

- **Encryption solutions:** Azure platform encryption (platform-managed, host-level encryption); Customer-managed keys (CMK) — customer creates, rotates, and manages key encryption keys (KEK) lifecycle; Azure Key Vault Standard (software keys, FIPS 140-2 Level 1); Azure Key Vault Premium (FIPS 140 validated HSM-protected keys); Azure Key Vault Managed HSM (fully managed, single-tenant, customer-controlled, **FIPS 140-3 Level 3** HSM-protected keys); BYOK (bring your own key) support for importing HSM-protected keys from on-premises HSMs.
- **Managed HSM vs. Standard/Premium:** single-tenant (vs. multitenant), customer-controlled root of trust (vs. Microsoft), FIPS 140-3 Level 3 compliance.
- **Physical controls:** HSM devices are tamper-resistant, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated, covered in hardened epoxy and metal casing, housed in geographically dispersed datacenters compliant with ISO/IEC 27001:2013 and NIST SP 800-53. Physical access controls include fences, dead-bolt doors, thermal alarms, cameras, biometrics, background checks, 24x7 security personnel.
- **Technical controls:** Confidentiality via Intel SGX enclaves; security domain (encrypted blob with HSM backup, user credentials, signing key, data encryption key) that Microsoft personnel cannot recover; access controls via control plane (Azure RBAC) and data plane (Managed HSM local RBAC); TLS 1.2/1.3 encryption in transit; firewall configuration; private endpoints on the Microsoft backbone network; monitoring via Azure Monitor; BYOK.
- **Administrative controls:** Data defense commitment (challenging government requests), contractual obligations via Azure Trust Center, cross-region replication, disaster recovery (Site Recovery, Azure Backup, business continuity program), MSRC integration with 24/7 security response, regulatory compliance built-in initiatives, audit reports, Red Team/Blue Team exercises.

**Azure Cloud HSM overview (Microsoft Learn):** Azure Cloud HSM is "a highly available, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated single-tenant service that complies with industry standards. Azure Cloud HSM grants customers complete administrative authority over their hardware security modules (HSMs)." [44]

- Customers retain administrative control over their HSMs with secure, direct, end-to-end encrypted access over a private, dedicated link from their virtual network, while Microsoft handles high availability, patching, and maintenance.
- Each HSM cluster consists of three HSM nodes with automatic key and policy synchronization across nodes. Supports load balancing of cryptographic operations and periodic backups.
- **Data residency:** Cloud HSM does not store or process customer data outside the region in which the customer deploys the HSM instance.
- **Single-tenant isolation:** Each HSM instance is dedicated to a single customer with a separate customer-specific security domain that cryptographically isolates it.
- **Compliance:** FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated by NIST; eIDAS support (Austrian scheme for qualified electronic signatures and seals); PCI and PCI 3DS validated HSMs with Attestation of Compliance available in Microsoft Service Trust Center.
- **Use cases:** PKCS#11, OpenSSL, JCA, JCE, CNG, and key storage provider (KSP); Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS); SSL/TLS offloading (Apache, NGINX, F5 BIG-IP); TDE (Microsoft SQL Server or Oracle); certificate storage; document, file, and code signing.
- **Best fit:** Migrating on-premises applications to Azure VMs, migrating from Azure Dedicated HSM or AWS Cloud HSM, applications requiring PKCS#11, and shrink-wrapped software (Apache, NGINX, F5 BIG-IP, SQL Server/Oracle TDE, AD CS).
- **Not a fit:** Azure Cloud HSM is IaaS-only and does not integrate with PaaS or SaaS Azure services. Not appropriate for Microsoft cloud services requiring customer-managed key encryption (e.g., Azure Information Protection, Azure Disk Encryption, Azure Data Lake Storage, Azure Storage, Microsoft Purview Customer Key) — those should use Azure Key Vault Managed HSM.
- **Physical security:** Restricted access datacenter areas with physical access controls and video surveillance. Physical and logical tamper detection triggers key deletion (zeroization). Protects against brute-force attacks by locking out cryptography officers (COs) and cryptography users (CUs) after failed access attempts. No scheduled maintenance windows.

**Azure Dedicated HSM (UK G-Cloud 14 listing via SOFTCAT PLC):** Described as managing hardware security modules in the cloud, enabling deployment of API gateways alongside APIs hosted in Azure. ISO/IEC 27001 certified (accredited by Schellman & Company, original registration Nov 29, 2011; version 13 dated Nov 28, 2023); CSA STAR Level 2 Attestation (2013); PCI DSS (accredited by Coalfire, March 15, 2021); Cyber Essentials and Cyber Essentials Plus; BS7858:2019 staff security clearance; up to Developed Vetting (DV) government clearance. Data locations: United Kingdom, EEA, and other locations; user control over data storage locations. Encryption: TLS 1.2+, IPsec/TLS VPN, MACsec for data between datacentres; Azure Key Vault, Disk Encryption, Storage Service Encryption. Resilience: availability zones with independent power/cooling/networking, round-trip latency <2ms. Authentication: 2-factor authentication, public key auth, identity federation, VPN, username/password; Just-in-Time access restrictions for Microsoft engineers. [43]

**FIPS 140 (Azure Compliance, Microsoft Learn):** FIPS 140 is a US government standard defining minimum security requirements for cryptographic modules. Testing is maintained by the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), a joint effort between NIST and Canada's Communications Security Establishment. FIPS 140 covers 11 security areas, with modules rated security levels 1-4. Latest version FIPS 140-3 references ISO/IEC 19790:2012. Key transition: FIPS 140-2 modules remain active until 21 September 2026 when they move to the historical list. [45]

- Microsoft has validated cryptographic modules since 2001 and certifies modules with each Windows release. Through the Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle (SDL), all Azure services use FIPS 140 approved algorithms.
- Azure Key Vault supports two resource types: Vaults (multi-tenant HSMs with FIPS 140 Level 2 validation) and Managed HSMs (single-tenant, FIPS 140 Level 3 validated, supporting AES-128 and AES-256 symmetric keys).
- "FIPS 140 validated" means CMVP certification of a module; "FIPS 140 compliant" is an industry term for products relying on validated modules. Applications and cloud services are NOT validated through FIPS 140 (only cryptographic modules are). Microsoft does not enforce FIPS Mode by default in Azure due to hyper scale performance requirements.
- FedRAMP requires FIPS 140 validation via NIST SP 800-53 SC-13 control.

- **Per-workload decision-making is critical:** "there is no single correct way to move to the cloud, only a correct way to move each workload." [3] "The right migration is the one that uses the cheapest strategy that delivers what the business needs for that specific workload, not the most ambitious strategy applied across the board." [8]
- **For deadline-driven finance migrations (e.g., data center lease expiry):** Rehost/lift-and-shift is fastest and lowest risk. Example: financial services firm migrating 200 VMs ahead of data centre lease expiry. [2]
- **For operations-constrained environments:** Replatform by default; hybrid pattern (rehost app servers, replatform databases) is often optimal. [3]
- **Refactoring is justified only for core business applications with real scaling/deployment needs**; Microsoft's guidance is to modernize during migration only when the team has the skills and time, otherwise defer. [3]
- **Lift-and-shift opens the door to further modernization:** "Once in Azure, businesses can begin taking advantage of cloud-native services like Azure SQL Database or Azure App Service to enhance their applications over time." [1]
- **Azure-specific advantages for finance:** Azure is best for Microsoft-centric infrastructure, hybrid cloud, .NET modernization, and regulated industries (Azure Migrate, Site Recovery, AKS, Functions, Cosmos DB). [6]
- **Cost trade-off example (YouTube/Hi-Tech Institution, March 11, 2026):** Lift & Shift: lower upfront cost (~$30k/year maintenance due to legacy system inefficiencies) but higher ongoing costs. Re-architecture: higher upfront cost but reduces ongoing expenses to ~$10k/year with optimized modern infrastructure. Short-term savings vs. long-term value trade-off over 5+ years. Lift & Shift best for urgent/fast deployments (2-3 months) and short-term needs; Re-architecture best for long-term growth, high availability, and handling increased traffic. 5-step organizational decision process: (1) audit current systems, (2) set clear goals (e.g., reduce IT costs by 20-30%), (3) compare options against goals, (4) pilot with a low-risk component, (5) choose based on pilot results. [7]
- **NetApp rehost/refactor/replatform:** Rehost (lift and shift) drops the application into the cloud as-is; a critical step is ensuring the application still has access to the same documents and data once in the cloud (e.g., Microsoft Azure Files allows cloud VMs to mount file shares identical to on-premise environments, making lift and shift possible). Refactor modifies existing software or a large chunk of the code base to take advantage of cloud features; most time-consuming and resource-intensive but can provide the highest return on investment long-term. Replatform is the middle ground—similar to rehosting but with some modification to take advantage of new cloud infrastructure. [9]

**Reasons to migrate to Google Cloud:** digital transformation with latest technology, scalable resources without physical hardware investment, advanced analytics and ML services, and cost savings through pay-as-you-go pricing (shifting from CAPEX to OPEX).

**The 6 Steps to Google Cloud Migration** (based on the official Google Cloud Migration Guide):
1. **Assessing and Discovering Workloads** - Create a thorough inventory of existing IT assets, identify applications/data/services, determine GCP compatibility, categorize workloads by complexity/criticality/cloud readiness, and estimate costs.
2. **Building a Foundation in Google Cloud** - Set up a scalable/secure cloud environment aligned with organizational structure and compliance, create projects for teams/applications, implement access controls, configure network settings, and establish logging/monitoring frameworks.
3. **Transferring Large Datasets** - Use Google Cloud's Storage Transfer Service for automated data movement (supports scheduling and security), or Transfer Appliance (a high-capacity server shipped to the customer's location) for extremely large datasets where network constraints make online transfers impractical.
4. **Deploying the Workloads** - Transfer applications/services and configure them, conduct thorough testing, monitor workloads post-deployment using Google Cloud's monitoring tools to track usage and optimize resource allocation.
5. **Migrating to Automated, Containerized Deployments** - Leverage Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to automate deployment/scaling/management; containers encapsulate code/config/dependencies; use CI/CD pipelines for automatic build, test, and deployment.
6. **Optimizing the New Environment** - Use Google Cloud's operations suite to monitor performance, identify underutilized/overprovisioned resources, implement auto scaling, use managed services, and leverage serverless computing options.

**Free Migration Tools from Google Cloud:**
- **Migrate to Virtual Machines** (formerly Migrate for Compute Engine): Automates moving VMs from VMware vSphere, Microsoft Hyper-V, or physical servers; optimizes VMs for performance and cost.
- **Migrate to Containers**: Moves applications from traditional/virtualized environments into containerized deployments using GKE.
- **Database Migration Service (DMS)**: Fully managed service supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server with automated replication, validation, and synchronization with minimal downtime.
- **BigQuery Data Transfer Service**: Automates data movement from SaaS apps (e.g., Google Ads) and external sources (e.g., Amazon S3) into BigQuery with scheduled transfers and automatic schema detection.

**Expert Tips (from Lanir Shacham, CEO of Faddom):**
1. Leverage pre-migration assessments to gauge workload compatibility.
2. Prioritize network optimization using Cloud VPN or Interconnect.
3. Automate repetitive tasks with Deployment Manager and CI/CD pipelines.
4. Adopt a phased migration approach starting with non-critical systems.
5. Invest in staff training on Google Cloud services.

**Best Practices for GCP Migration:**
- **Establish a Rollback Strategy**: Document each phase, take snapshots/backups before migrations, test rollback procedures, and automate rollback triggers.
- **Plan for Gradual Rollouts**: Migrate small groups in phases, use traffic splitting/versioning to redirect portions of user traffic gradually.
- **Prepare Dev and Ops Teams**: Maintain communication channels, provide training and resources on GCP technologies.
- **Define How to Retire the Source Environment**: Verify data integrity, test all applications, confirm backup/DR mechanisms in GCP, and obtain formal stakeholder approval before decommissioning.
- **Streamline Deployment**: Establish CI/CD pipelines, adopt infrastructure-as-code (IaC), and containerize workloads for uniform environments.

**Faddom Promotion:** The article concludes by promoting Faddom's application dependency mapping tool, which is agentless, requires no credentials, starts at $10K/year, maps entire environments in real-time (24/7), and allows one person to map a whole data center in an hour. 1. **Rehost (lift and shift):** Minimal modification; fastest and easiest; ideal when workload works as-is; but doesn't leverage cloud features.
2. **Replatform (lift and optimize):** Optimizes workloads for cloud (e.g., microservices, GKE containers); more work and testing required than rehost.
3. **Refactor (move and improve):** Modifies workloads to take advantage of cloud capabilities (performance, features, cost, UX); takes longer and requires new skills.
4. **Re-architect (continue to modernize):** Changes how code functions (e.g., monolithic to microservices); more complex, riskier, and requires extensive testing.
5. **Rebuild (remove and replace/rip and replace):** Completely redesigns and rewrites the app; removes technical debt but takes longest and requires new toolchains.
6. **Repurchase:** Moves from purchased on-premises workload to cloud-hosted SaaS equivalent (e.g., Google Workspace); potentially easier but more expensive with fewer granular controls.

**Google Cloud Adoption Framework:** A maturity assessment tool evaluating four themes (Learn, Lead, Scale, Secure) across three phases (Tactical, Strategic, Transformational) to gauge organizational cloud readiness.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical blog post by Nawaz Dhandala (founder of OneUptime) published February 17, 2026, providing a complete walkthrough for migrating petabytes of on-premises data to Google Cloud Storage (GCS) using Google Transfer Appliance. The article argues that for datasets requiring more than a week to transfer over a network, physically shipping data via Transfer Appliance is the most practical and cost-effective option.

KEY FACTS:
- Network transfer is impractical for petabyte-scale data: a 1 PB transfer over a dedicated 10 Gbps connection takes ~10 days at full bandwidth (realistically longer), and 500 TB over a 1 Gbps connection at 80% utilization takes ~58 days.
- Transfer Appliance comes in two sizes: TA40 (40 TB usable) and TA300 (300 TB usable); multiple appliances can be used in parallel for petabyte-scale migrations.

STEP-BY-STEP PROCESS (7 steps):
1. Plan the migration: calculate data volume, count files (small files under 1KB transfer slower), check for files exceeding the 5 TB max size limit, and create destination GCS buckets (e.g., using gcloud storage buckets create with appropriate storage classes like STANDARD and NEARLINE).
2. Order the appliance through Google Cloud Console, select size, provide shipping details, and prepare the data center (network ports of 10/40/100 GbE, power, physical space, staff access).
3. Connect and configure the appliance: it gets an IP via DHCP or static IP, is accessed via CLI, supports NFS/SMB/SCP/SFTP file share modes, and presents as an NFS mount point.
4. Load data using rsync or cp, running multiple parallel transfers for maximum throughput (e.g., using GNU parallel with -j 8); tune NFS options (rsize=1048576, wsize=1048576) and consider tar archiving for many small files.
5. Verify data with checksums (md5sum comparisons), unmount the appliance, and run "ta finalize" which encrypts data at rest using AES-256 with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK); enter the returned passcode in Google's return instructions form.
6. Monitor ingestion in Cloud Console, with email notifications from Google and optional Pub/Sub notifications (e.g., OBJECT_FINALIZE event type).
7. Validate migrated data by comparing file counts and spot-checking checksums between source and destination.

COST CONSIDERATIONS:
- Transfer Appliance pricing includes an appliance fee (per use), onsite usage fee (fixed days included, then per weekday), shipping costs, and operations costs (Class A/B requests); no Transfer Service fee is incurred for physical ingest.
- Comparison example: network transfer of 500 TB costs ~$3,400 in Interconnect fees (10 Gbps at ~$1,700/month for ~2 months) plus engineering time, vs. Transfer Appliance using 2x TA300 units completed in ~10 days.
- For 1 PB migration: order 4x TA300 appliances, load 250 TB each in parallel, complete in 2-3 weeks versus months over the network.

COMMON PITFALLS:
- Not testing with a small transfer first
- Slow source storage (test read speeds before the appliance arrives)
- Millions of small files under 1 KB (archive into tar bundles first)
- Not planning the GCS bucket structure in advance (reorganizing petabytes after ingestion is expensive)

The article concludes: "if your data takes weeks to transfer over the network, ship it instead." The post is part of the OneUptime blog, which promotes OneUptime as an open-source observability platform combining infrastructure monitoring, incident management, status pages, and APM.
</summary>

1. **What SUDs Are:** Automatic price reductions applied to specific GCP Compute Engine resources when servers run for a significant portion of a billing month. No contract or manual activation required. Maximum blended savings of ~30% if a VM runs the full month.

2. **How SUD Calculation Works (Tiered System, ~730-hour month):**
   - 0–25% of month (0–182 hrs): Standard on-demand rate, no discount
   - 25–50% (~183–365 hrs): 20% discount on hours in that block
   - 50–75% (~366–547 hrs): 40% discount
   - 75–100% (~548–730 hrs): 60% discount
   - Blended maximum: up to 30% total savings

3. **Eligibility:**
   - Eligible: N1, N2, N2D, certain custom machine types, sole-tenant nodes
   - NOT eligible: E2, C2/C3, A2, Cloud SQL, Spot/Preemptible VMs
   - GKE nodes ARE eligible if using eligible machine families (e.g., N2)

4. **Common Traps:**
   - Reseller/invoiced accounts may not pass SUDs through (one Reddit user reported losing $3K+ in unapplied SUDs)
   - Short-lived daily jobs (e.g., 90 min/day ≈ 45 hrs/month) never hit the 182-hour threshold
   - Discount calculated per project and region (cannot be shared across projects)

5. **Tracking SUDs:** Google Cloud Console → Billing → Cost Breakdown → Monthly credits section shows SUD line items. Zero means ineligible machine types or insufficient runtime.

6. **Maximization Strategy:** Use eligible N2 machines for 24/7 baseline workloads (SUDs auto-apply), and use Spot/Preemptible VMs (up to 91% discount) for batch/temporary workloads.

7. **SUD vs. CUD Comparison:**
   - SUD: No contract, automatic, flexible, max ~30% savings, best for unpredictable usage
   - CUD: 1-3 year contract, manual purchase, max up to 70% savings, best for stable 24/7 operations
   - Resource-Based CUDs: Commit to specific hardware quantity in specific region (highest discount, zero flexibility)
   - Spend-Based CUDs: Commit to dollar amount per hour across eligible services (flexible, slightly lower discount)
   - CUDs can be combined with Reservations to secure both price and hardware availability
   - Software license commitments available separately for SUSE/RHEL

8. **Break-Even Example:** A $0.10/hr server (730 hrs = $73/month baseline):
   - With SUD (30% blended): ~$51.10/month
   - With 3-year CUD (55% discount): $32.85/month — but CUD becomes a sunk cost if workload volatility causes underutilization

9. **Key FAQs:** Custom machine types remain eligible; resizing mid-month resets the discount calculation; 30% is only a blended maximum at 100% uptime (a half-month server yields only ~10% effective savings); Spot/Preemptible VMs don't qualify.

The article positions Costimizer as an automated FinOps agent that connects to GCP to identify SUD-qualifying resources and determine optimal transition points to CUDs.

This is an opinion piece by Antonio Lagrotteria (Engineering Manager, Full-Stack Architect, AWS Community Builder) published on Medium, discussing Google Cloud Platform's (GCP) January 2024 announcement that it will eliminate egress/outbound data transfer fees for customers leaving their platform. The author argues that while this appears philanthropic, it's likely a strategic business move, and he explores both sides of the egress cost debate.

**GCP's Motivation (Author's Theories):**
1. Steal market share from AWS and Azure (GCP is a distant third cloud vendor)
2. Anticipate future regulations on egress costs
3. Trigger reactions from other cloud providers and customers

**What Are Egress Costs:** Fees charged by cloud providers when data is transferred out of their network, including intra/extra-region, availability zone, public internet traffic, downloading files, accessing storage/compute, and hybrid (on-prem/cloud) API consumption. These costs can add up significantly for businesses with substantial data transfer needs.

**Reasons to KEEP Egress Costs:**
1. Sustainable cloud provider infrastructure maintenance (revenue funds ongoing development)
2. Natural customer lock-in strategy (prevents easy departure)
3. Educates customers on well-architected, cloud-native designs (discourages inefficient network use)

**Reasons to REMOVE/Reduce Egress Costs:**
1. Free flow of data — fosters innovation and collaboration
2. Earn customer trust — costs are complex to calculate (e.g., AWS Cost Explorer for EC2 and VPC Flow logs is not intuitive), and removing them creates fairness and transparency
3. Data-driven decisions in hybrid setups — costs discourage moving large datasets, limiting analytics and insights, particularly in large enterprises with migration constraints

**Conclusion:** The author hopes this GCP announcement triggers a response from other major cloud providers to seriously reconsider their egress transfer cost strategies, potentially using it as an opportunity to become the undisputed leader in cloud computing.
</summary>

"Google Cloud Provider (GCP) announced in January 2024 that they are removing any egress/outbound costs for any customer leaving their platform."

--- SOURCE 1: Part-14: Google Compute Engine (GCE) – Live Migration & Availability Policy Explained 🚀 - DEV Community ---
URL: https://dev.to/latchudevops/part-14-google-compute-engine-gce-live-migration-availability-policy-explained-a6m

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is Part-14 of a GCP learning series by Latchu@DevOps, explaining Google Compute Engine (GCE) Live Migration and Availability Policies.

**Key topics covered:**

1. **Division of maintenance responsibilities**: Users manage VM instance-level updates (OS patches, configuration management) using VM Manager (Patch Management, OS Configuration Policies), while GCP teams handle host-level hardware and software updates for Compute Engine hosts.

2. **Live Migration**: Allows VM instances to keep running even when the underlying host system undergoes maintenance or upgrades. It covers hardware/infrastructure upgrades, power grid or network maintenance, and regular system patching. Live Migration = zero downtime during GCP maintenance.

3. **How Live Migration works**: When a host machine is scheduled for maintenance, running VMs are automatically migrated to another host in the same zone, with VM settings and metadata unchanged and no manual intervention required. It is supported for VMs with local SSDs but NOT supported for GPUs, Spot VMs, and Preemptible VMs.

4. **Availability Policy settings** (configured at VM creation):
   - **On Host Maintenance**: "Migrate VM Instance" (recommended, best for availability) vs. "Terminate VM Instance" (VM stops during host maintenance)
   - **Automatic Restart**: "ON" (recommended, VM restarts automatically after crashes) vs. "OFF" (VM stays stopped until manually started)

5. **Best practices**: Always enable Live Migration unless workloads don't support it, keep Automatic Restart ON for production workloads, and use VM Manager for guest OS updates while relying on GCP for host maintenance.

**Core message**: Users manage the VMs, GCP manages the hosts, and Live Migration bridges the gap to ensure seamless VM operation during Google's backend upgrades or infrastructure events, maximizing uptime and workload resilience with minimal manual intervention.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Live Migration = Zero Downtime During GCP Maintenance", "Supported: VMs with local SSDs. Not Supported: GPUs, Spot VMs, and Preemptible VMs", "Migrate VM Instance (Recommended) → VM is live migrated to another host (Best option for availability)", "You manage the VMs, GCP manages the hosts, and Live Migration bridges the gap!", "Always enable Live Migration (Migrate VM Instance) unless you have workloads that don't support it. Keep Automatic Restart ON for production workloads."
