## 2. COST MODELING

### 2.1 AWS TCO Analysis and Cloud Economics

**CloudZero — "Guide To Calculating TCO On AWS And Tools To Help"** (published September 27, 2025; updated July 31, 2026): Defines AWS TCO as the sum of all costs associated with migrating, hosting, running, and maintaining applications, workloads, and data on AWS, typically calculated over 3-5 years. 5-step process: (1) Calculate existing infrastructure cost (equipment, datacenter, software, payroll, maintenance, security, upgrades); (2) Consider opportunity costs and hidden costs (downtime, idle capacity, facility renovations); (3) Calculate AWS migration costs across three phases: assessment/discovery, mobilization, and migration (the most costly phase); (4) Calculate monthly AWS charges based on services used, resource consumption models (On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans), and purchase method; (5) Compare AWS TCO vs. on-premises TCO. Pitfalls that increase AWS TCO: over-provisioning resources, lack of automated scaling, poor cost monitoring, underutilizing spot instances, ignoring reserved instances/savings plans, not optimizing reserved capacity, inefficient storage management, ignoring software license costs, and overlooking security/compliance requirements. [31]

**Hykell — "AWS performance SLA"**: Organizations can reduce costs by 30-50% by tiering services based on business impact rather than pursuing uniform high availability. Multi-region active-active architectures can increase costs 3-5x. Multi-AZ deployments double compute costs and introduce data transfer fees. [32]

### 2.2 AWS Data Transfer and Egress Pricing

**DigitalOcean — "Understanding AWS's Egress Costs"**: AWS charges $0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB of outbound data to the public internet, dropping to $0.085 per GB for the next 40 TB, $0.07 per GB for the next 100 TB, and $0.05 per GB beyond 150 TB. Applies to both EC2 and S3. Inbound (ingress) is free for most services. AWS charges $0.02 per GB for data transferred between different AWS regions. S3 data transfer out to the internet ranges from $0.05 to $0.09 per GB depending on volume. CloudFront CDN charges regional data transfer out fees of at least $0.02 per GB and up to $0.114 per GB for certain regions. AWS egress pricing can be more than five times as expensive as DigitalOcean's flat $0.01 per GiB. A Forrester TEI report cites a 186% ROI over three years for DigitalOcean customers. Cost examples: small business with 5 TB outbound ($460.80) plus 2 TB inter-regional ($40.96) totaling ~$501.76; larger deployment with 100 TB outbound ($7,987.20) plus 50 TB inter-regional ($1,024) totaling ~$9,011.20. (Pricing data accurate as of August 2023.) [33]

**nOps — "AWS Egress Costs & How to Avoid Them"** (published June 7, 2026): Public internet: ~$0.09/GB for first 10 TB/month with tiered discounts; first 1 GB/month free. Between AZs: ~$0.01/GB per direction (even within same region). Between regions: ~$0.02–$0.09/GB, never free. NAT Gateways: charged per hour AND per GB. **2025 Pricing Changes**: (1) Free Tier increased from 1 GB to 100 GB/month (excludes China and GovCloud); (2) Egress fee waivers for legitimate, planned, AWS-approved cloud migrations off AWS. Hidden costs: cross-service API calls, VPC Peering and Transit Gateway (per-GB + data processing fees), Interface Endpoints/PrivateLink (per-hour and per-GB), load balancer to backend traffic, logging/monitoring/telemetry pipelines. Comparison (2025): AWS 100 GB/month free tier, $0.09/GB starting rate, charges cross-AZ traffic, waives fees for migration off AWS; GCP 5 GB/month free tier, $0.12/GB starting rate, free same-zone traffic; Azure 5 GB/month free tier, $0.087–$0.09/GB starting rate, free intra-region traffic. Lightsail includes 1–7 TB free egress monthly depending on plan, then $0.09/GB. [34]

**Forrester — "Amazon AWS Joins Google Cloud In Removing Egress Costs"**: AWS announced removal of egress fees when migrating data to another cloud provider or on-premises, following Google Cloud's January announcement. Unlike Google, AWS doesn't require customers to fully exit or close their accounts, but AWS does require a **60-day exit, full removal of all data and workloads**, and warns repeated migration requests will face "additional scrutiny." Both AWS and Google messaging imply one-way movements. AWS has provided 100 GB of free data egress per month since 2021 (except GovCloud and China). Later the same day, Microsoft Azure also announced removal of its data transfer fees when canceling/deleting an Azure subscription. [35]

**Cloudflare — "What is AWS data transfer pricing?"**: Amazon S3 free transfers: first 100 GB per month transferred out to the Internet (aggregated across all AWS services and Regions except China and GovCloud); data transferred between S3 buckets in the same Region; data transferred from S3 to AWS services within the same Region; data transferred out to Amazon CloudFront. S3 pricing example (US West-Northern California): first 10 TB/month at $0.09/GB; next 40 TB/month at $0.09/GB; next 100 TB/month at $0.07/GB; greater than 150 TB/month at $0.05/GB. US customers typically pay $0.02/GB for transferring data from S3 to a different AWS availability zone. More than half of C-level executives and DevOps professionals cite significant or unexpected cloud spending as their biggest challenge. [36]

**AWS Cost and Usage Report — "Understanding data transfer charges"**: Five categories: (1) Within-region transfers (UsageType `Region-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes`; charged for both inbound and outbound, two line items per transfer); (2) Between-region transfers (only the outgoing source region line item is charged; e.g., `USE2-APS3-AWS-Out-Bytes`); (3) Data transfer out to internet (`Region-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes`); (4) Direct Connect traffic (public virtual interfaces: `DataXfer-In`/`DataXfer-Out`; private/transit: `DataXfer-In:dc.3`/`DataXfer-Out:dc.3`); (5) S3 Transfer Acceleration and CloudFront traffic (CloudFront uses `Region-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes` or `-OBytes` with product code `AmazonCloudFront`). [37]

### 2.3 Microsoft SQL Server and Windows Licensing on AWS

**AWS Prescriptive Guidance — "Understand SQL Server licensing"**: Three AWS licensing categories: (1) License included (pay-as-you-go); (2) BYOL with Microsoft License Mobility for products like SQL Server with Software Assurance (SA) — can bring to shared or dedicated tenancy; (3) BYOL without license mobility (e.g., Windows Server), which requires dedicated options. **Cost data — monthly on-demand costs for c5.xlarge running 24/7**: Windows Server + SQL Server Enterprise = $1,353/month; Windows Server + SQL Server Standard = $609/month; Windows Server only = $259/month; Compute only/Linux = $127/month. Optimization strategies:
- Perpetual Windows Server licenses purchased before 10/1/2019 (or true-ups under Enterprise Agreements signed before that date) can be deployed on Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts.
- Physical-level licensing on dedicated hosts (e.g., 48 licenses for 48 cores/96 vCPUs on an R5 dedicated host with Datacenter/Enterprise editions) can save up to 50% on SQL Server licensing vs. vCPU-based shared tenancy.
- SQL Server consolidation: two 2-vCPU instances into one 4-vCPU instance can reduce licensing by 50% (SQL Server requires minimum four core licenses per instance).
- Downgrading SQL Server Enterprise to Standard can significantly reduce costs. TDE is available in Standard since SQL Server 2019; failover clustering with FSx for Windows File Server is an alternative to Always On availability groups.
- SQL Server Developer edition (free) in non-production environments for SQL Server 2016 and later.
- **Optimize CPU feature**: disabling hyperthreading or turning off CPUs — r5.4xlarge with 16 vCPUs reduced to 8 active vCPUs (50% license savings); r5.12xlarge with 48 vCPUs reduced to 8 (83% savings).
- References AWS Optimization and Licensing Assessment (AWS OLA) and right-sizing. [27]

**WintelGuy.com — "MS SQL 2025 Ent Licensing Calculator"**: SQL Server Enterprise requires a minimum of four core licenses for each physical processor when licensing by physical core and a minimum of four core licenses per each VM when licensing by virtual CPU. Virtual CPU (VM) licensing is ONLY available under subscription licenses or licenses with active SA. Cloud hosting: SQL Server Enterprise core licenses with License Mobility through SA can be used on dedicated hosted services from Listed Providers (Alibaba, Amazon, Google, Microsoft). Unlimited virtualization rights are NOT available on Listed Providers' dedicated hosted services, except Azure. [28]

**AWS Pricing Calculator docs — "Generating estimates for Windows Servers and SQL Servers on EC2"**: Supported licensing/tenancy combinations: License Included (LI) for both Windows and SQL (Shared tenancy); LI Windows + BYOL SQL (Shared or Dedicated Hosts); BYOL for both (Dedicated Hosts only). BYOL Windows + LI SQL is not supported. Key factors: whether licenses were purchased before/after October 1, 2019, and whether the user has active Software Assurance for SQL Server. CPU optimization allows BYOL customers to specify custom vCPU counts (e.g., x1e.4xlarge with 4-14 optimized vCPUs) at no price difference. SQL passive nodes with Software Assurance (SQL 2014+) don't require licensing. Default pricing model: Standard Reserved Instances; terms 1 or 3 years; payment options Full upfront (best discount), Partial upfront, No upfront (default). [29]

**AWS Pricing Calculator docs — "Generating estimates for Windows Servers and SQL Servers on EC2 Dedicated Hosts"**: Supported: Windows LI + SQL LI (Shared tenancy), Windows LI + SQL BYOL (Shared tenancy or Dedicated Hosts), Windows BYOL + SQL BYOL (Dedicated Hosts). "The licensing options include AWS provided licenses with License Included (LI) offerings. They also include your existing licenses with Bring Your Own License (BYOL) offerings for optimal cost savings." "The default value is `Standard Reserved Instances`. ### 2.4 Oracle Licensing on AWS

**Cintra — "Oracle BYOL vs AWS Licensing"** (published 02 Dec 2024): **License Included (LI)**: AWS includes the Oracle Database license with RDS, bundled into the hourly price; only available for Oracle Standard Edition One and Two (restricted to SE2 per AWS Service Terms section 10.3.1); cannot host third-party services. **BYOL**: required for all Oracle editions other than SE1/SE2, and for all editions on Amazon EC2. Under Oracle's Cloud Licensing Policy, **two AWS vCPUs equal one Oracle license**. RDS BYOL example: 160 physical cores/320 vCPUs with cloud factor 0.5 = 160 Oracle licenses. EC2: r7i Shared Tenancy (160 cores/320 vCPUs, factor 0.5 = 160 licenses); r7iz.metal-16xl (160 cores/320 vCPUs, factor 0.5 = 80 licenses); r7iz dedicated hosts (192 cores/384 vCPUs, factor 0.5 = 96 licenses). Three common mistakes: overlooking Oracle support policies, neglecting license compliance management, assuming immunity from Oracle audits (using Oracle on AWS RDS can be a significant audit trigger). Hourly licensing is exclusively available on Amazon RDS. [38]

**MigrationCost.com — "Oracle Database to AWS Migration Cost (2026)"**: **Core licensing rule**: In January 2017, Oracle introduced a 2:1 vCPU conversion ratio for AWS EC2 (and Azure VM) compute — two AWS vCPUs require one Oracle Processor licence. This effectively doubles Oracle licence costs on EC2 BYOL vs. on-premise. The 2:1 rule does NOT apply to RDS for Oracle (due to a separate AWS-Oracle agreement) or OCI. Four destination paths: (1) RDS for Oracle SE2 with License Included: +10 to +25% run-rate vs on-prem; (2) RDS for Oracle EE with BYOL (no 2:1 penalty): -10 to +10% run-rate; (3) Oracle on EC2 BYOL Dedicated Hosts (2:1 penalty): +15 to +40% on licence; (4) Aurora PostgreSQL via SCT (no Oracle licence): -60 to -80% on database total cost. For any workload above 4 vCPUs, RDS for Oracle BYOL is cheaper than EC2 BYOL. Exceptions requiring EC2: RAC, specific Data Guard configs, Database Vault, Advanced Security Option. Aurora PostgreSQL via SCT: SCT automates 70-90% of schema conversion; remaining 10-30% of PL/SQL requires manual conversion. Migration takes 1-4 weeks for SCT analysis, 4-16 weeks for PL/SQL conversion, plus 4-12 weeks for app-side changes. Total migration cost per database: $60K-$300K. Oracle EE with SULS costs $47,500 per processor licence plus 22% annual support ($58K/year fully loaded). A 16-vCPU Oracle EE workload costs ~$465K/year in licensing vs $35K-$60K/year on Aurora. Break-even on $150K migration is typically 4-8 months. Worked 10-database scenario (12 months): net totals Low $868K, Typical $1.888M, High $4.21M. Terminating Oracle licences post-migration saves ~22% of purchase price annually in SULS; terminating 8 EE processor licences saves ~$102K/year permanently. Single database under 1 TB costs $20K-$80K to migrate; larger (5-50 TB) cost $80K-$400K each. RDS migrations of a single database under 5 TB take 4-12 weeks; Aurora migrations take 12-36 weeks. Large estates of 20+ databases run 12-36 months. [39]

**House of Brick — "Oracle Database Licensing for AWS Migrations"**: Oracle's Cloud Policy counts vCPUs rather than physical cores; the core factor table does not apply. Rules: two vCPUs count as one Oracle processor license with multi-threading enabled; one vCPU equals one license with multi-threading disabled; for Standard Editions, four or fewer vCPUs count as one socket license (rounding up in increments of four); max 16 vCPUs for Standard Edition, max 8 vCPUs for SE1 and SE2. Alternatively, traditional core-based licensing can be used with AWS Dedicated Hosts or Bare Metal servers. **Multi-AZ and Cross-Region Replicas**: every active Multi-AZ or Cross-Region replica requires its own Oracle license (double the vCPUs for BYOL counting). Cross-Region automated backups do not require licensing until activated. **Multitenant**: more than three pluggable databases in a container database requires licensing the Multitenant option. **DR and Backups**: DR environments with Oracle software must be fully licensed; Oracle contract allows offsite backup testing four times per year with a maximum calendar days per test; GoldenGate is separately licensed (source and target) with 1-year term licenses available at 20% of perpetual license cost; Data Guard must be fully licensed on both sides. **Container Licensing**: any EC2 instance with a container running Oracle software must be licensed. Comparative table: on-premises 160 physical cores, core factor 0.5 = 80 licenses for VMware on x86; Amazon RDS BYOL 160 vCPUs = 160 licenses; Amazon EC2 shared tenancy = 160 licenses vs. bare metal = 80 licenses vs. dedicated hosts = 96 licenses. [40]

**Redress — "OCI vs AWS for Oracle: Two Conversion Rules"** (published September 8, 2025; updated July 29, 2026): Oracle's Authorized Cloud Environment policy covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, but NOT OCI. On authorized clouds: two vCPUs count as one Processor license (with hyperthreading enabled); the 0.5 x86 core factor does NOT apply, effectively doubling license counts; SE2 limited to instances up to 8 vCPUs. On OCI: one Processor license maps to two OCPUs. Worked example (16 physical cores): Data center = 8 Processor licenses; AWS/Azure/Google = 16 Processor licenses (no core factor); OCI = 8 Processor licenses. Gap: 8 licenses ≈ $380,000 at list price, plus 22% annual support. Hyperthreading: turning it off does NOT reduce license counts on authorized clouds. **Real Application Clusters is NOT available on authorized clouds** (only on OCI, Exadata Cloud at Customer, or Oracle-operated multicloud services). Amazon RDS for Oracle license-included only covers SE2; EE requires BYOL on RDS. About 6 in 10 platform comparisons built in 2024-2025 found the license count was the largest line in the five-year model. [41]

**AWS RDS for Oracle Pricing page**: License Included supports SE2 only (AWS has licensed Oracle software); BYOL supports SE2 and EE (requires appropriate Oracle Database license with Software Update License & Support). On-Demand: per hour, one-second increments with 10-minute minimum; Single-AZ and Multi-AZ. Reserved Instances: 1- or 3-year terms; No Upfront, Partial Upfront, All Upfront; size flexibility under BYOL; cannot be modified after purchase. T3 instances run in Unlimited mode; CPU credits charged at $0.075 per vCPU-Hour (same across all regions, not covered by Reserved Instances). Storage: General Purpose SSD 20 GiB to 64 TiB; Provisioned IOPS SSD 1,000–256,000 IOPS and 100 GiB to 64 TiB; Magnetic 20 GiB to 3 TiB (backward compatibility only); up to 3 additional volumes, max 256 TiB total (gp3 and io2). For Multi-AZ, write I/O doubles due to synchronous replication. **Zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift**: 50 GB export ($0.01/GB) + 50 GB resynchronization ($0.01/GB) + 5 GB CDC transfer ($2.00/GB) = $11.00 total in US East (N. Virginia) over 30 days. Data transfer: 100 GB free data transfer "out" per month (aggregate across all AWS services except China and GovCloud); all data transfers "in" are free. Eligible discounts: promotional credits, AWS MAP investment, and Database Savings Plans (1-year term). [42]

## 3. DOWNTIME AND BUSINESS CONTINUITY RISKS

### 3.1 AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS)

**AWS DRS Pricing page**: Flat hourly fee of **$0.028 per source server per hour** (flat rate regardless of disk count, storage size, number of drill/recovery launches, or AWS Region). No upfront costs, minimum fees, or resources to manage. Pricing includes continuous data replication, test launches, recovery launches, and point-in-time recovery. Additional charges: replicating source servers consumes EBS storage and EC2 compute billed separately. **Pricing Example #1 (100 on-premises servers, 200 disks/30TB, 3.3% daily change rate, 730 hours)**: AWS DRS charge = 100 servers × $0.028/hour × 730 hours = $2,044.00; EBS volumes $1,425.00 (50% gp3 at $0.08/GB-month = $1,200; 50% sc1 at $0.015/GB-month = $225); EBS snapshots (default 7-day retention) $1,846.50 ($0.05/GB-month); EC2 Replication Servers $1,053.54 (14 t3.small at $0.0208/hour + 3 m5.2xlarge at $0.384/hour); **TOTAL MONTHLY COST: $6,389.03** (US-East N. Virginia, On-Demand). **Pricing Example #2 (8-hour DR drill launching 100 recovery instances)**: EBS volumes $28.49; EC2 instances $94.46; **TOTAL: $122.94**. Technical notes: one equally sized EBS "staging disk" per source disk; Replication Servers are low-cost t3.small EC2 instances by default, each handling up to 15 staging disks; costs for fully provisioned recovery servers incurred only during drills and recovery. [43]

**AWS Storage Blog — "Optimize costs and speed up replication with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery"**: AWS DRS offers RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes. Cost structure: $0.028/hour service cost per source server; staging disk costs; snapshot data (PIT schedules: every 10 min for last hour, hourly for 24 hours, daily for 7 days — configurable from 1-365 days); replication servers (one t3.small EC2 at $0.0236/hour per 15 source volumes); conversion servers (less than $0.05 per launched recovery instance); target failover EC2 instances (e.g., $0.1699/hour for t3a.xlarge). Optimization example: optimizing a 75 TB provisioned fleet (30 TB in use) down to 36 TB reduces initial sync time from 6.944 days to 3.333 days and monthly cost from $9,356 to $4,703.45 (US East/N. Virginia, July 18, 2022). AWS DRS is a sound choice for Pilot Light DR strategies. [44]

**AWS DRS Concepts documentation**: **RTO**: typically 5–20 minutes, highly dependent on OS boot time — Linux servers typically boot within 5 minutes; Windows typically within 20 minutes. **RPO**: continuous block-level replication enabling crash-consistent RPO in the sub-second range. In-memory application data is not replicated until written to source volumes. **PIT Snapshots**: crash-consistent recovery points from EBS Snapshots. Default retention: 1 PIT per 10 minutes for the prior hour, 1 per hour for prior 24 hours, 1 per day for prior 7 days. Only the "Day" retention limit is configurable (1–365 days). "Use most recent data" attempts to create an on-demand PIT Snapshot representing a sub-second RPO, waiting up to 10 minutes. [45]

**Substack — "AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)"**: Fully managed service powered by CloudEndure. Features: continuous data replication with low RPO and options for synchronous/asynchronous replication; automated failover and recovery with automatic DNS updates; pay-per-use pricing eliminating idle standby infrastructure; EC2-based recovery, cross-region recovery, on-demand recovery drills; real-time monitoring via Amazon CloudWatch; encryption (in-transit and at-rest) and compliance support (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). 2025 updates include: enhanced automated recovery workflows with application-specific recovery sequencing; integration with AWS Backup; expanded region availability (Africa/Cape Town, Asia Pacific/Jakarta and Kuala Lumpur, South America/São Paulo); FIPS 140-2 certified encryption, deeper IAM role-based access control, Amazon GuardDuty monitoring; support for tens of thousands of VMs; DR support for containers on ECS/EKS/Fargate and serverless on Lambda; advanced analytics with automated risk assessment via CloudWatch and QuickSight; improved live DR drill testing; new planning tools including visual DR Planner and cost estimator; integration with Veeam and Commvault; enhanced regulatory compliance support (GDPR, HIPAA, SOC). Limitations: compatibility constraints with some legacy systems, recovery window variability, network bandwidth/latency bottlenecks for large data transfers, learning curve. [46]

### 3.2 DR Strategies: Multi-AZ, Multi-Region, Active-Passive vs Active-Active

**N2W — "AWS Disaster Recovery: 4 Strategies"** (updated 2026): Four DR strategies: (1) **Backup and Restore** — most cost-effective (AWS Backup); highest RTO/RPO (hours); (2) **Pilot Light** — critical core elements always running, non-essential off until needed; recovery in minutes; (3) **Warm Standby** — scaled-down but always-on environment that can quickly scale up; near-instant recovery; (4) **Multi-Site (Hot Standby)** — identical live environment running concurrently; near-zero RTO/RPO but highest cost. Bonus: Multi-AZ and Multi-Region. **Major AWS US-East-1 regional outage in late 2025 lasted ~15 hours due to a DNS resolution failure in the Region's control plane**, taking down workloads across all Availability Zones simultaneously. Organizations that stayed online were running active-active or active-passive across multiple Regions. Key lesson: treat the Region as a failure domain. [47]

**AWS Architecture Blog — "Disaster Recovery (DR) Architecture on AWS, Part I: Strategies for Recovery in the Cloud"**: Defines disaster as "any event that prevents a workload or system from fulfilling its business objectives in its primary location." RTO and RPO are the two primary objectives; lower numbers cost more. Multi-AZ protects against localized disruptions; Multi-Region protects against events impacting multiple data centers. Four strategies (highest to lowest RTO/RPO): Backup and restore; Pilot light (critical data live, e.g., Aurora global database replicating to read-only cluster; compute idle/shut off); Warm standby (live data plus minimum deployment at reduced capacity, e.g., one EC2 instance per tier); Multi-site active/active (two or more Regions actively accept requests with data replicated, e.g., DynamoDB global tables). Even with replication, backups are still necessary to protect against data deletion/corruption. [48]

**AWS Whitepaper — "Disaster recovery options in the cloud"**: Four strategies. **Backup and Restore**: use IaC (CloudFormation or AWS CDK); services include EBS snapshots, DynamoDB backups, RDS/Aurora snapshots, EFS, Redshift, Neptune, DocumentDB, FSx; AWS Backup centralizes and supports cross-Region/account copying; S3 object versioning and CRR. **Pilot Light**: core infrastructure (databases, object storage) always on; application servers loaded but deprovisioned until failover; continuous cross-region async replication services include S3 Replication, RDS read replicas, Aurora global databases, DynamoDB global tables, DocumentDB global clusters, ElastiCache Global Datastore. **"With Amazon Aurora global database, if your primary Region suffers a performance degradation or outage, you can promote one of the secondary regions to take read/write responsibilities in less than one minute even in the event of a complete regional outage."** AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery implements the Pilot Light strategy using block-level replication. Traffic management via Route 53 (ARC recommended for data plane failover), AWS Global Accelerator, or CloudFront. **Warm Standby**: scaled-down but fully functional copy in another Region; can handle traffic immediately at reduced capacity without additional action (unlike pilot light which requires "turning on" servers); uses EC2 Auto Scaling to scale out; note: Auto Scaling is a control plane operation and lowers resiliency. **Multi-site Active/Active**: workload runs simultaneously in multiple Regions; write strategies: "write global" (single Region handles all writes, promoted on failure), "write local" (closest Region, e.g., DynamoDB global tables with last-writer-wins reconciliation), "write partitioned" (partitioned by key, e.g., bi-directional S3 replication). **"For maximum resiliency, you should use only data plane operations as part of your failover operation. This is because the data planes typically have higher availability design goals than the control planes."** AWS Resilience Hub validates RTO/RPO targets. [49]

**AWS Compute Blog — "Building resilient multi-Region Serverless applications on AWS"**: **Active-Passive**: one Region "Active" handles all production traffic; other Regions "Passive" replicating data and configurations, with readiness levels: Hot Standby (fully deployed), Warm Standby (partially deployed), Pilot Light (minimal core infrastructure). AWS serverless pay-for-value pricing means organizations pay primarily for data replication rather than idle compute. Lambda provisioned concurrency keeps functions warm for failover but incurs costs regardless. **Active-Active**: multiple Regions actively serve traffic concurrently; highest availability but expensive; requires rigorous engineering for data synchronization, conflict resolution, retry mechanisms/circuit breakers; each Region must handle full application load if another fails. The demo uses CloudWatch alarms and a manual approval process — "automated failover is not recommended" for critical applications. Route 53 health check configuration: 10-second request interval with failure threshold of 2. Chaos engineering tools: chaos-lambda-extension and AWS Fault Injection Service (AWS FIS). Cross-Region observability requires monitoring Region A's resources from Region B; CloudWatch enables cross-account and cross-Region monitoring. [50]

**AWS Architecture Blog — "Disaster Recovery Solutions with AWS managed services, Part 3: Multi-Site Active/Passive"**: "Multi-Site Active/Passive" (warm standby) is best for business-critical workloads with higher availability requirements. Seven components demonstrated with a payment transaction processing application: (1) Amazon Route 53 health-checked routing policies (active/passive failover); (2) Amazon EKS control plane (regional, single-tenant); (3) EKS data plane using EC2 Auto Scaling groups with one node in secondary Region that scales up on failover; Velero with Portworx manages persistent volume snapshots stored in S3 (replicated cross-Region via S3 CRR); (4) Amazon OpenSearch Service cross-cluster replication (active-passive follower/leader model; available on Elasticsearch 7.10 or OpenSearch 1.1+); (5) Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL cross-Region read replicas (can be promoted to standalone source servers); (6) Amazon ElastiCache Global Datastore (fully managed cross-Region replication with automatic async replication); (7) Amazon Redshift A/A approach with data flowing via SNS and S3, Lambda functions distributing to both Regions, SQS queues with Extended Client Library. [51]

**AWS Architecture Blog — "Disaster Recovery (DR) Architecture on AWS, Part IV: Multi-Site Active/Active"**: Offers the lowest RTO/RPO but higher cost and complexity. Traffic routing: Route 53 geolocation routing (deterministic, keeps user data in specific Regions, controls write routing) or latency routing. Read/write patterns: **Read-local/write-local** (DynamoDB global tables replicate within a second; "last writer wins" reconciliation); **Read-local/write-global** (one global write Region; uses DynamoDB global tables with write redirection, or Aurora global database with write forwarding over AWS network <1 second replication latency, or ElastiCache Global Datastore); **Read-local/write-partitioned** (each record assigned a "home Region" by first write or partition key; writes route back to home Region). Failover: Route 53 DNS record updates (with appropriately low TTL) or AWS Global Accelerator (non-DNS, static IPs, traffic dials/weights). [52]

## 4. PERFORMANCE AND SCALABILITY POST-MIGRATION

### 4.1 Performance Characteristics by Migration Approach

- **Lift-and-shift (Rehost)**: moves applications to AWS without changes, "without having to make any changes to the applications, their architecture, or the migrated servers" [6, 9]; delivers ~30% cost savings even without cloud optimizations (GE Oil & Gas) [1, 5]; performance is generally preserved since applications run natively on EC2, but elastic scaling requires follow-on optimization (right-sizing, RI commitments, phased modernization roadmap) [5].
- **Replatforming**: minor optimizations without changing core architecture (e.g., SQL Server to Amazon RDS, containerizing with App2Container, AWS Graviton processors) [2, 3, 4].
- **Re-architecture**: enables cloud-native features — elastic scaling, serverless, microservices [1, 2]. AWS Prescriptive Guidance: "Refactor is not recommended for large migrations because it involves modernizing the application during the migration" — instead rehost/relocate/replatform first and modernize after [3].

### 4.2 Scalability Capabilities (Auto Scaling, Serverless)

**Spacelift — "Scaling AWS Infrastructure: Auto Scaling & Other Services"**: Vertical scaling (upgrading EC2 instance type or RDS class) is limited by max capacity, may require downtime, best for monolithic/single-node apps. Horizontal scaling (Auto Scaling EC2 instances, adding Aurora replicas) is theoretically unlimited, no downtime, ideal for distributed/stateless apps. **AWS Auto Scaling** automatically increases/decreases compute resources based on demand (e.g., if web server memory usage exceeds 90%, a new instance is added; removed once usage drops below threshold). Supports scheduled scaling. ALB divides load between EC2 instances or Lambda functions. RDS Multi-AZ places a standby database in another AZ. RDS Read Replicas enhance read performance, auto-synced in real time (available in Aurora and RDS for MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server). Amazon Aurora offers high availability and performance at global scale. Event-driven architecture with SQS and Lambda; Lambda scales by default creating more function instances based on incoming event volume. [57]

**AWS Auto Scaling docs — "Predictive scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling"**: Predictive scaling analyzes historical load data to detect daily/weekly patterns and forecasts future capacity needs so EC2 Auto Scaling can proactively increase capacity. Well suited for: cyclical traffic; recurring on-and-off workload patterns (batch processing, testing, periodic data analysis); applications that take a long time to initialize causing latency impact during scale-out events. Benefits: faster scaling by launching capacity in advance of forecasted load, and potential cost savings by avoiding over-provisioning. [58]

**AWS Architecture Blog — "Let's Architect! Serverless architecture on AWS"**: Half of new applications built by Amazon use AWS Lambda (Andy Jassy, 2020 re:Invent keynote). Topics include event-driven architecture with Amazon EventBridge, serverless patterns (Lambda Power Tuning for memory configuration), transforming rather than transporting data, orchestrating workflows with Step Functions. [59]

**AWS HPC Blog — "A serverless architecture for high performance financial modelling"**: **RenaissanceRe** (one of the world's leading reinsurance companies; 2021: $8B gross premiums, ~$18B capital under management) migrated its high-performance financial modelling system from an on-premises cluster (Python web server + Celery cluster of 9 servers with 512GB RAM and 48 CPU cores each, RabbitMQ, Redis, SAN) to a "serverless first" AWS architecture. Portfolio rollup executes Monte-Carlo risk models across 7,000+ deals, processing ~45TB of data and producing 600GB of raw analytic output per run (~5 runs per day); real-time deal analytics requires thousands of runs per day. New architecture: AWS Step Functions as execution planner building a DAG of deal dependencies stored in Amazon ElastiCache for Redis; Amazon Kinesis "Job" stream; AWS Lambda for high-priority real-time deal analytics; **AWS Fargate for bulk portfolio rollup computations — up to 3,000 containers running in parallel during a full run**; Amazon S3 as computational data lake; Amazon SQS for standard priority jobs; Amazon EventBridge for error handling (failed jobs resubmitted up to three times). S3 key-partitioning supports 100GiB/s data transfer rates on ~20GiB of input data split across 15-20k files. [60]

**AWS Whitepaper — "Microservices on serverless technologies"**: AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate integrated with API Gateway enable fully serverless applications that greatly decrease operational complexity. As of April 7, 2023, AWS Lambda functions can progressively stream response payloads back to clients, significantly improving time to first byte. Amazon Aurora Serverless is an on-demand, auto-scaling database. [61]

**AWS re:Post — "Building a Serverless Architecture on AWS"**: Serverless provides automatic scaling, high availability, and pay-as-you-go pricing. Key services: Lambda, API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB, Step Functions, SNS & SQS. [62]

**Relevant Software — "Microservices on AWS"**: Microservices architecture market projected to grow from $5.31 billion in 2023 to ~$21.61 billion by 2030 (CAGR 18.66%). AWS holds 32% of the global cloud infrastructure market. [63]

### 4.3 Latency Considerations for Financial Trading Workloads

**AWS Industries Blog — "Rethinking the low latency trade value proposition using AWS Local Zones"**: At re:Invent 2021, NASDAQ announced partnership with AWS to transform Capital Markets and migrate its North American markets to the cloud. AWS launched Local Zones in New York, Chicago, Kansas City, and Minneapolis (September 2021), enabling low-latency trading workloads with exchange access requirements as low as **1 millisecond**. Proof Trading's institutional equities execution platform on AWS achieves latency of **~50μs between AWS servers within the same availability zone and ~400μs across availability zones**. Recommended architecture: latency-sensitive execution components in Local Zones (close to exchanges); high-performance supporting systems (strategy development, capital management) in resilient Availability Zones. [64]

**AWS Web3 Blog — "Optimize tick-to-trade latency for digital assets exchanges and trading platforms on AWS (Part 2)"**: Five-tier hierarchy of latency impacts, ordered by impact: Placement & Region (100ms), Network Path Engineering (2ms), Instance & Bare Metal selection (200µs), OS Tuning & Kernel Bypass (50µs), Application Tuning (5µs). **Placement decisions have approximately 20,000x more latency impact than application tuning.** "No amount of cache-line alignment or lock-free queue tuning recovers the milliseconds you lose by deploying in the wrong Region or routing traffic through an unnecessary network hop." Market maker trading hot-path: (1) Market Data Ingestion (kernel bypass DPDK with PTP timestamping); (2) Packet Processing & Normalization (single-threaded parsing with huge pages and busy polling); (3) Signal Generation (all-in-memory state, NUMA-aware); (4) Risk Assessment (in-memory deterministic checks, async logging to NVMe); (5) Order Construction & Transmission (kernel bypass send with wire timestamping, direct NIC access, placement close to matching engine). Benchmark tool: github.com/aws-samples/trading-latency-benchmark. Optimization layers: Placement (same Region and AZ as exchange gateway; AWS Direct Connect for hybrid); Network Path (avoid ELB, Transit Gateway, NAT, or inspection appliances; use VPC Peering; shared Cluster Placement Groups; "EC2 hunting"); Instance Selection (largest instance size for full-slot exclusive access; bare metal .metal guarantees single tenancy — benchmark results show metal instances provide 6-14% p50 improvement and 15-29% p99.9 improvement over full-slot instances, e.g., m8azn: 17.7µs vs 18.9µs p50; m5zn: 20.3µs vs 23.6µs p50; C7i 24xl: 20.3µs vs 21.7µs p50); Time Synchronization (Amazon Time Sync Service, free, hardware timestamps require physical NIC traversal); Networking (network-optimized instances m6in, c6in, m8azn reduce tail latency up to 85% at p99.9, increase single-flow bandwidth 5x; use latest ENA driver; ENA Express is rarely right for HFT — increases CPU overhead and inflates p50; conventional ENA with DPDK, XDP zero-copy, or SR-IOV preferred); Storage (instance store offers sub-millisecond latency but ephemeral; EBS io2 Block Express competitive for persistent); OS Tuning (Linux kernels 6.1+ deliver lower latency; Ubuntu with kernel 6.12+ preferred, followed by Rocky Linux and RHEL; tail latency improved almost universally after tuning, max latency dropped 27% even where p50 barely changed on m8azn.metal; Intel c7i and AMD m5zn benefit most at 28-36% p50 improvement; Graviton c8g offers exceptional consistency — 21.4µs p50, 23.4µs p99.9 — with minimal tuning). [65]

**AWS for Financial Services LinkedIn — AWS Outposts racks**: New next-generation AWS Outposts racks bring the latest x86-powered EC2 instances to data centers with **40% better performance and simplified networking**. Promoted for Capital Markets companies to build ultra-resilient, ultra-low latency market infrastructure meeting fair trading and equal access requirements, handle data residency requirements, and enhance operational efficiency through consistent APIs across cloud and on-premises environments. [66]

SOC 2 compliance is mostly about organizational controls; auditors look at how infrastructure is provisioned and changed — using IaC (e.g., Terraform) with compliance controls embedded early makes demonstrating compliance easier. AICPA Trust Services Criteria (CC1-CC9) are in AWS Artifact's SOC 2 report; everything else (access reviews, change management, incident response, vendor management) is the customer's responsibility. Recommended services: AWS Audit Manager, AWS Config, AWS CloudTrail, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS IAM, AWS Security Hub, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS KMS, VPC/security groups/Network ACLs, AWS Backup. SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria categories: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy. [73]

### 5.4 Security Hub, AWS Config, Control Tower, Audit Manager, KMS

**AWS Security Hub — "Standards reference for CSPM"**: Eight supported standards: (1) AWS Foundational Security Best Practices; (2) AI Security Best Practices (network isolation, encryption, VPC placement, AWS KMS key usage); (3) AWS Resource Tagging; (4) CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark; (5) NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5; (6) NIST SP 800-171 Revision 2; (7) PCI DSS; (8) Service-managed standard, AWS Control Tower. "Security Hub CSPM standards and controls don't guarantee compliance with any regulatory frameworks or audits. Instead, they provide a way to evaluate and monitor the state of your AWS accounts and resources." If consolidated control findings are enabled, a single finding is generated per control even across multiple standards. [74]

**AWS User Guide for Federally Regulated Financial Institutions in Canada** (October 2025 edition): AWS operates two Regions in Canada — Canada (Central) in Montreal and Canada West (Calgary) — each with three Availability Zones. AWS compliance certifications relevant to FRFIs: CCCS Medium Cloud Security Profile (150 services assessed as of November 2023) and Protected B High Value Assets (PBHVA) assessment (149 services); ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, ISO 9001; PCI DSS Level 1; SOC 1, SOC 2, SOC 3. **AWS Artifact provides access to 2,600+ security controls and compliance documents.** OSFI Guidelines coverage: B-10 (Third-Party Risk Management, effective May 1, 2024), B-13 (Technology and Cyber Risk Management, effective January 1, 2024), E-21 (Operational Risk Management and Resilience, published August 22, 2024; full adherence by September 1, 2026; testing for all critical operations by September 1, 2027). AWS recommends the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF), AWS Well-Architected Framework (six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability), Financial Services Industry Lens, and NIST Cybersecurity Framework alignment whitepaper. Shared responsibility: for IaaS like EC2, customers handle the guest OS, patches, and security group configuration; for abstracted services like S3 and DynamoDB, customers manage data, encryption, asset classification, and IAM permissions. [75]

**AWS Compliance / re:Post on SOC 2**: AWS Artifact is a no-cost, self-service portal for on-demand access to AWS compliance reports. [67, 73]

**Packt video — "AWS Data Security: Regulated Industries and AWS Compliance Programs"**: Strongly regulated industries include financial services, healthcare, and public sector. AWS compliance does not automatically make a customer's deployment compliant; customers may need to enhance the platform with intrusion detection/prevention systems, specific configurations, web application firewalls, or specific data encryption. AWS provides artifacts (certificates, audit reports, documentation) accessible via the AWS Management Console under the Security section, under NDA. [76]

### 5.5 Data Residency, GDPR, and Financial Services Guidance

- **AWS Compliance page**: GDPR is among the 143 supported standards. AWS gives customers ownership and control over their customer content, with tools determining where content is stored. [67]
- **AWS Compliance Programs**: the AWS European Sovereign Cloud is a new independent cloud entirely within the EU designed for digital sovereignty. [68]
- **SOC Compliance page**: the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (GA January 2026) has its own SOC 2 report covering independent EU corporate structures, EU-resident personnel, and strict residency requirements. [71]
- **AWS for Financial Services LinkedIn (AWS Outposts)**: Outposts racks handle data residency requirements and consistent APIs across cloud and on-premises, for Capital Markets companies. [66]
- **Canada FRFI Guide**: Canadian customers can store data within Canada (Montreal and Calgary Regions). [75]
- **AWS "What is a Cloud Migration Strategy?"** notes security and compliance requirements as a key consideration (conduct security assessments and establish governance frameworks). [2]
- **AWS Web3 Blog** (latency): AWS Direct Connect for hybrid scenarios; placement decisions dominate latency. [65]

### 5.6 AWS Artifact

- AWS Artifact is a no-cost, self-service portal for on-demand access to AWS compliance reports (auditor-issued reports, certifications, accreditations, third-party attestations). [67]
- SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports are available via AWS Artifact (NDA required for SOC 1/SOC 2; SOC 3 publicly available); the SOC Continued Operations Letter (Bridge Letter/COL) is updated monthly in AWS Artifact. [71]
- PCI DSS certification is accessible through AWS Artifact, including the PCI DSS AOC, AWS Responsibility Summary, and the OSCAL-format report package. [69]
- AWS Artifact provides access to 2,600+ security controls and compliance documents (Canada FRFI guide). [75]

### 5.7 KMS Encryption and Security Features of Migration Tools

- AWS MGN: data encrypted in transit via TLS 1.2, transferred directly from source servers to the user's VPC; encrypted at rest via Amazon EBS encryption. [9]
- AWS DRS: encryption in-transit and at-rest; FIPS 140-2 certified encryption (2025 updates); compliance support for HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR, SOC. [46]
- AWS re:Post SOC 2 guidance: AWS KMS for encryption is a recommended service. [73]
- AWS Security Hub AI Security Best Practices covers AWS KMS key usage. [74]

## 6. ADDITIONAL FINANCE-SPECIFIC AND CROSS-CUTTING FINDINGS

### 6.1 Financial Services Cloud Adoption Context

- NASDAQ is partnering with AWS to transform Capital Markets and migrate its North American markets to the cloud (announced re:Invent 2021). [64]
- AWS Outposts racks are promoted for Capital Markets companies to build ultra-resilient, ultra-low latency market infrastructure that meets fair trading and equal access requirements, handles data residency, and provides consistent APIs across cloud and on-premises. [66]
- RenaissanceRe (reinsurance, $8B gross premiums, ~$18B capital under management) migrated high-performance financial modelling to serverless AWS architecture with up to 3,000 parallel Fargate containers. [60]
- AWS Canada FRFI guide provides compliance mapping for OSFI-regulated institutions. [75]
- Cloudtech notes 71% of U.S. companies identify digital assets as determining M&A deal success; Klamath Health Partnership achieved 77% infrastructure cost reduction (HIPAA-compliant EHR). [5]

### 6.2 Key Statistics and Data Points

- GE Oil & Gas saved roughly 30% of costs by rehosting without cloud optimizations. [1, 5]
- Up to 10-20% of an enterprise IT portfolio can be retired. [1]
- Applications with CPU/memory consumption below 5% can be retired immediately; 5-20% may qualify if no inbound requests over 90 days. [2, 3]
- AWS DMS has migrated more than 1.5 million databases. [5]
- On-premises server utilization averages only 12-18%; more than 30% of servers run at under 10% utilization. [5]
- IT infrastructure staff become 47% more efficient; application development teams 35% more productive after AWS migration. [5]
- ~75% of organizations fall behind cloud migration schedules; 38% delayed by more than one quarter (McKinsey). [5]
- ~58% of global decision-makers report cloud skills as a considerable challenge (IBM IBV 2023). [4]
- Hybrid cloud migration can realize 2.5x more value than single public cloud platforms (IBM IBV). [4]
- Global cloud market valued at USD 752.44 million in 2024, projected USD 2,390.19 billion by 2030. [4]
- Microservices architecture market: $5.31 billion (2023) to ~$21.61 billion by 2030 (CAGR 18.66%); AWS holds 32% of global cloud infrastructure market. [63]
- Half of new applications built by Amazon use AWS Lambda (2020). [59]
- AWS publishes over 300 separate SLAs. [32]
- AWS supports 143 security standards and compliance certifications. [67]
- AWS Artifact provides access to 2,600+ security controls and compliance documents. [75]
- A major AWS US-East-1 regional outage in late 2025 lasted ~15 hours due to DNS resolution failure in the Region's control plane. [47]

### 6.3 AWS Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) and Other Programs

- The AWS Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) provides tools, training, partner expertise, and investment based on AWS's experience migrating thousands of enterprise customers. [2]
- RDS for Oracle pricing is eligible for AWS MAP investment and Database Savings Plans. [42]
- CloudZero lists AWS MAP support among TCO tools. [31]

### 6.4 AWS Migration Hub Status Change (Critical Note)

- **AWS Migration Hub is no longer open to new customers as of November 7, 2025. For capabilities similar to AWS Migration Hub, explore AWS Transform.** Migration Hub Orchestrator itself remains available and is offered at no additional cost — users only pay for AWS resources they provision for migrations. [12]

# Azure Cloud Migration Strategies for Enterprise Finance Applications: Comprehensive Research Findings

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

1. **Tavily Search 1:** "Azure Migrate lift-and-shift re-platform re-architecture migration strategy enterprise finance" and "Azure cloud migration strategies lift-and-shift vs re-platform vs re-architect enterprise applications" — yielded 10 sources on migration strategy frameworks (7 Rs, 6 Rs, lift-and-shift vs. re-architect comparisons).

2. **Tavily Search 2:** "Azure Hybrid Benefit pricing Windows Server SQL Server migration TCO calculator" and "Azure Database Migration Service SQL Server managed instance migration pricing" — yielded 10 sources on Azure Migrate, Site Recovery, and Database Migration Service tooling/pricing.

3. **Tavily Search 3:** "Azure Hybrid Benefit SQL Server Windows Server free extended security updates 2008 2012 licensing portability pricing" and "Azure compliance PCI DSS SOC 2 GDPR financial services data residency Microsoft Purview Defender for Cloud Azure Policy Dedicated HSM" — yielded 10 sources on licensing, ESUs, and compliance.

4. **Tavily Search 4:** "Azure availability zones paired regions active-active active-passive multi-region architecture disaster recovery financial services" and "Azure SQL Managed Instance performance elastic pool autoscaling VM series M-series Esv4 finance high performance" — yielded 10 sources on DR architecture, VM series, and SQL performance.

5. **Tavily Search 5:** "Azure SQL Managed Instance performance autoscaling high availability finance workload VM series M-series Esv4 Fsv2 pricing 2026" and "Azure regions paired regions availability zones active-active active-passive multi-region architecture financial services SLA" — yielded 10 sources on SQL MI limits, availability zones, and multi-region support.

6. **Tavily Search 6:** "Azure reserved instances savings plan pricing compute Azure savings plan discount VM pricing 2026", "Azure data transfer egress pricing outbound bandwidth 2026 per GB", and "Azure Trust Center Microsoft Purview data residency Defender for Cloud Azure Dedicated HSM customer managed keys documentation" — yielded 10 sources on VM sizing, SQL pricing models, and compliance.

7. **Tavily Search 7:** "Azure Dedicated HSM customer-managed keys FIPS 140-2 Microsoft Purview data governance Azure Trust Center Service Trust Portal" and "Azure Kubernetes Service AKS Azure App Service re-platforming migration containerization tools enterprise finance modernization" — yielded 10 sources on HSM/Key Vault/Service Trust Portal and AKS/App Service modernization.

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### DIMENSION 1: TOOLING AND SERVICES

#### 1.1 Azure Migrate — Discovery, Assessment, Dependency Analysis

**Azure Migrate product overview (Microsoft):** Azure Migrate is described as a comprehensive cloud migration tool designed to help organizations streamline their path to the cloud through assessment, migration, and modernization. Key capabilities include: seeing the IT estate clearly, deciding faster with guided options, migrating and modernizing servers/databases/web apps, and optimizing performance, cost, and management. Azure Migrate embeds security and compliance, offers cost optimization through Azure Accelerate, and supports modernization of workloads to Azure App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service, and other Azure services. The product page highlights customer stories from Fortune Brands, Solv, and Syensqo, and its FAQ covers the difference between Azure Migrate and Azure Site Recovery. [15]

**Azure Migrate release history (What's New, Microsoft Learn, page last updated June 22, 2026):** Azure Migrate "helps you discover, assess, and migrate on-premises servers, apps, and data to the Azure cloud platform." Notable features by date: [11]

- **May 2026 (Public preview):** Automatic discovery of applications by grouping workloads discovered through the Collector, Appliance, or CSV import, using server naming patterns, inferred environments, and server roles.
- **April 2026 (Public preview):** Reserved tags to enrich data with business context (environment: Prod, Dev, Test, UAT; migration intent: Migrate, Retain, Retire), which influence assessments, SKU calculations, pricing, and migration planning. MongoDB assessments with readiness, right-sizing recommendations, and cost estimates for Azure Document DB or MongoDB on Azure VMs.
- **March 2026 (Public preview):** Reports feature for executive-level migration/modernization insights (including security and business case insights), tailored to strategies like PaaS (AI-ready), Azure Virtual Machines, or Azure VMware Solution (AVS). General Availability of Gen2 VM migration to Trusted Launch Azure VMs (UEFI-based Secure Boot and vTPM). Azure Copilot migration agent for conversational VMware migration planning. Security insights expanded to cover Web apps and Databases (not just Servers and Software).
- **November 2025:** Three new built-in RBAC roles: Azure Migrate Owner (end-to-end), Azure Migrate Decide & Plan Expert, and Azure Migrate Execute Expert, enabling least-privilege access. Windows Server redeployment to Azure using Infrastructure as Code (IaC) templates (public preview). GitHub Copilot assessment for code insights in web app assessments targeting AKS or Azure App Service. Arc-based discovery for assessing Arc-enabled on-premises servers and SQL instances without new infrastructure. Wave Planning for structured large-scale migrations with waves, sequencing, visualization, tracking, and monitoring.
- **October 2025:** Integrated Security insights (public preview) with dashboard, auto-detection of unsupported OS/software, pending updates, CVEs, and recommendations for Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Azure Update Manager. Software inventory enhancements: review software across all servers, sanitized/classified categories, support status, vulnerabilities, potential Azure targets, and scoping/filtering. Dependency visualization across multiple servers with intuitive navigation, node interaction, filtering by netstat data, per-server view, and high-affinity server grouping.
- **September 2025:** PostgreSQL discovery and assessment (public preview) for migration to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, with configuration-based assessment, cost estimation, and readiness categorization. General Availability of ZRS (Zone-Redundant Storage) Disks migration support.
- **July 2025:** SSH authentication for Linux servers in VMware and Hyper-V appliance stacks (GA).
- **June 2025:** End-to-end migration of Gen2 VMs to Trusted Launch VMs (public preview) for all migration scenarios; Sustainability insights in Business Case for emissions estimation and ESG goal support.
- **May 2025:** Premium SSD v2 disk support (GA); Ultra Disk migration support (public preview); ZRS Disk migration (public preview); upgraded agent-based migration stack (GA); application awareness features including inventory view across tiers, tags, enhanced dependency analysis, application assessment, and Action Center.
- **February 2025:** MySQL discovery and assessment (public preview).
- **November 2024:** AVS cost assessments with AV64 host type and Azure NetApp Files; Enterprise Linux (RHEL/SLES) migration via Azure Hybrid Benefit; business case creation for Azure Arc onboarding.
- **October 2024:** RVTools XLSX import reads storage data from vPartition and vMemory sheets.
- **April 2024:** Movere service retired (March 1, 2024); SAP discovery and assessment; Java (Tomcat) web app assessment for App Service and AKS.
- **March 2024:** Spring Boot app discovery/assessment via Kubernetes appliance.
- **February 2024:** Azure Hybrid Benefit savings for Enterprise Linux subscriptions.
- **December 2023:** Cost savings from Azure management services in business cases.

Connections between source server/process and destination server/process/port are logically grouped into dependencies. Data can be visualized in a map view or exported as CSV. The Azure Migrate appliance polls TCP connection data every 5 minutes, gathering process names with active connections, application names running those processes, and destination ports. Gathered data is processed on the appliance and sent to Azure Migrate every 6 hours.
- **Agent-based dependency analysis** — Supported only in the classic view (not the new experience), using the Service Map solution in Azure Monitor. Requires installing agents on each source server. Supported in public cloud but NOT supported in Azure Government. The classic view is scheduled for deprecation by the end of 2026; no new servers can be onboarded for agent-based analysis.

#### 1.2 Azure Migrate Application and Code Assessment (AppCAT)

The Azure Migrate application and code assessment is a developer-focused feature for analyzing ASP.NET and ASP.NET Core applications to plan re-platforming to Azure PaaS environments. Available as both a Visual Studio 2022 extension and a .NET command-line SDK tool (`dotnet-appcat`); it scans source code, configuration, and binaries to identify issues that need to be addressed before migrating to Azure App Service, AKS, or Azure Container Apps. A Java version also exists. It complements Azure Migrate's existing discovery/assessment features (Data Migration Assistant, App Service Migration Assistant). [14]

- Issues are categorized into four severities: Mandatory (e.g., Windows authentication needing to be changed to Azure AD), Optional (e.g., moving settings from web.config to Azure App Configuration/Key Vault), Potential (e.g., SQL Server connectivity depending on whether the database is accessible from Azure), and Information.
- Each incident includes a unitless story point estimate for relative effort comparison. Reports can be exported as HTML, CSV, or JSON.
- Example walkthrough analyzing the eShop "Northern Mountains" sample (github.com/dotnet/eshop) produced 41 incidents across nine issue types in 16 projects: 8 mandatory, 8 optional, 25 potential. Key findings included RabbitMQ usage (mandatory – 8 incidents), database usage (8 incidents), connection strings (6 incidents), hardcoded URLs (5 incidents), caching/Redis usage (5 incidents), HTTP usage (4 incidents), local file usage (1 incident, marked N/A), and static content (3 optional incidents).
- CLI tool is installed via `dotnet tool install -g dotnet-appcat` and run with the `appcat` command (e.g., `appcat analyze solution.sln`). Supports non-interactive mode for scripting: `appcat analyze eShopLegacyMVC.csproj -s HTML -r OutputPath --code --non-interactive`. The solution must build without errors when using the CLI.
- Future roadmap: GitHub Copilot Chat integration, ability to specify multiple Azure target environments (e.g., Windows App Service vs. AKS with Linux containers, already available in the Java version), and binary output analysis. Documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/migrate/appcat/overview. [14]

#### 1.4 Azure Site Recovery (ASR) for Migration Replication

**Official Azure Site Recovery pricing (Microsoft):** ASR is billed based on the number of instances protected. Every instance is FREE for the first 31 days of protection. After 31 days, charges apply per instance protected (both for recovery to customer-owned sites and to Azure). ASR between Azure regions is charged at the same rate as ASR to Azure. Billing is calculated using the average daily number of protected instances over a monthly period (e.g., protecting 20 instances for half a month and none for the other half results in an average of 10 protected instances). The 31-day free period applies to every new instance, regardless of how long a customer has been using the service. Even during the free period, customers may incur charges for Azure Storage, storage transactions, data transfer, and compute charges for recovered VMs. Azure Hybrid Benefit allows up to 40% or more savings using Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance. Test recoveries are limited to brief DR testing within one week every 90 days. [20]

- Licensing requirements by recovery site type: On-Premises (fully licensed servers or end-customer licenses via Disaster Recovery Software Assurance benefit); Service Provider (licensed via SPLA – Services Provider License Agreement); Azure (Disaster Recovery Software Assurance benefit applies, changed in January 2015 Product Use Rights; Azure Hybrid Benefit can be leveraged).
- Azure Site Recovery replication for SQL Server is covered under the Software Assurance Disaster Recovery benefit.
- Azure does not support persistent MAC addresses, so MAC-based license models cannot be used for migration/DR.

**Third-party ASR cost reference (migrationcost.com, 2026):** [17]

- ASR charges $25 per protected instance per month after a 31-day free trial per instance.
- Standard rate: $25/month for replication to Azure and Azure-to-Azure DR. On-premise DR use case: $54/month.
- A 100-server migration with a 3-month replication window costs approximately $7,500 in ASR fees.
- Third-party alternatives like Carbonite Migrate cost $400–$800 per server one-time, making ASR meaningfully cheaper.

**ASR cost breakdown (Critical Cloud, June 7, 2026):** ASR is a pay-as-you-go disaster recovery service with no upfront hardware or software costs, but it accumulates four separate cost components continuously once protection is enabled: [18]

1. **Licence fees per protected instance** – Billed hourly per protected VM or physical server, with a 31-day free trial per new instance. Rates vary by workload type (Azure-to-Azure, VMware/Hyper-V to Azure, physical server to Azure).
2. **Cache storage** – Requires a General Purpose v2 storage account in the source region. Costs depend on the storage SKU and data volume; high-I/O workloads (databases, transaction processing) can incur significant costs.
3. **Target storage** – Replicated data lands on Managed Disks in the target recovery region, paid continuously regardless of whether failover occurs. "For a 1 TB Premium SSD protecting a production database VM, you are paying for a 1 TB Premium SSD in the recovery region at full price, from the moment protection is enabled. Multiply this across a large number of protected VMs and it becomes the largest single cost component." Optimization: use Standard SSD or Standard HDD where RTO allows.
4. **Network charges for replication traffic** – Initial replication incurs a one-time egress charge for full disk copy; ongoing delta replication charges standard inter-region transfer rates. Optimization: schedule replication during off-peak hours (e.g., 20:00–06:00 GMT).

Compute costs during failover: Replication itself incurs no compute costs, but failed-over VMs (test or actual) run at standard VM compute rates. "Test failovers should be temporary: run the test, validate recovery, and clean up. A test failover left running for a week at VM rates for ten protected VMs is an avoidable cost that surprises teams who run tests but forget to tear them down." ASR's minimum RPO is ~5 minutes for VMware workloads with typical recovery points every 15-30 minutes for Azure-to-Azure, making it cost-competitive for workloads with RPO requirements in the 15-minute to 1-hour range. Zerto supports continuous data protection with near-zero RPO (sub-second), which ASR cannot match. [18]

**ASR vs. traditional DR (Infrassist, November 14, 2025):** [19]

- **Traditional DR costs:** Upfront hardware for mid-size enterprises (500-2,000 employees): $150K-300K. Monthly costs: colocation ($2,000-5,000), network ($500-1,500), maintenance contracts ($2,000-4,500, roughly 18-22% of hardware cost/year). Hardware refresh cycles every 3-5 years. Five-year reality check for 50 VMs: $200K hardware + $480K operations + $100K mid-cycle refresh = $780,000 total (~$13,000/month). ~20% of SMEs cite affordability as primary barrier to DR adoption.
- **Azure Site Recovery costs (50-VM environment):** ASR licenses: 50 VMs × $31 = $1,550/month; test failover compute: 10 VMs × $120 = $1,200/month; storage (LRS): 15TB × $19/TB = $285/month; replication bandwidth: 2TB × $87/TB = $174/month; Azure Backup add-on: 15TB × $10/TB = $150/month. Total Azure: $3,359/month; complete monthly cost with services: $5,259. Savings of 56-65% versus traditional DR ($12K-15K monthly).
- **Side-by-side:** Upfront cost: $150K-300K (traditional) vs. $0 (Azure). Monthly cost: $12K-18K vs. $3K-5K. RTO: 2-8 hours vs. 15 minutes. RPO: 1-4 hours vs. 15-30 minutes. Testing: production disruption risk vs. isolated, zero impact.
- **Client case study (Virginia manufacturing firm):** Traditional quote: $200,000 upfront + $3,000/month (new Nimble array $120K, replication software $25K, secondary site $35K, implementation $20K). Azure implementation: 12 production VMs migrated over 4-6 weeks using Azure Migrate; 4TB initial sync over 50Mbps (~72 hours); successful test failover on first try. Results after 6 months: $200K avoided, new monthly DR cost $4,200, five-year savings of $456,000, RTO dropped from 4+ hours to 15 minutes, RPO improved from 8 hours to 30 minutes.
- Implementation: 4-6 weeks typical (2 weeks assessment, 2 weeks configuration/sync, 2 weeks testing). Bandwidth: ~5Mbps per VM needed; Azure Data Box available for slow connections; ongoing replication needs only 1-2Mbps per VM.

#### 1.7 Migration Strategy Frameworks (6 Rs, 7 Rs)

**The 6 Rs for Azure (Apps4Rent, published July 31, 2026):** Framework originated from Gartner and was popularized across the industry. Six strategies ordered from least to most transformation: Rehost (lift and shift to Azure VMs with no changes), Replatform (move with targeted upgrades to managed services), Refactor/Rearchitect (restructure applications to be cloud-native), Repurchase (replace with SaaS products), Retire (decommission unused workloads), and Retain (keep on-premises for now). [3]

- Rehosting involves discovery/dependency mapping, right-sizing via Azure Migrate, replication/test failover, and wave-based cutover. Best for deadline-driven moves, datacenter exits, or vendor-constrained apps. Azure Hybrid Benefit allows applying existing Windows Server/SQL Server licenses to reduce VM costs.
- Replatforming swaps components for managed services without code rewrites (e.g., SQL Server on VM to Azure SQL Managed Instance, IIS web apps to Azure App Service, file servers to Azure Files, or apps to containers). It delivers the best return per engineering hour.
- Practical rule: "rehost by default when the calendar is the constraint, replatform by default when operations are the constraint." A hybrid pattern (rehost app servers, replatform databases) is often optimal.
- Refactoring is justified only for core business applications with real scaling/deployment needs; Microsoft's guidance is to modernize during migration only when the team has the skills and time, otherwise defer. A plan marking half the portfolio as "refactor" is usually wrong.
- Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework uses 8 strategies (adds rebuild and splits refactor into refactor, rearchitect, and rebuild; renames repurchase to replace), but the underlying per-workload decisions are identical.
- 5-step migration process: (1) inventory everything with Azure Migrate discovery, (2) eliminate retire/repurchase candidates first, (3) assign an R per workload scored on business value and technical fitness, (4) prepare the foundation via Azure landing zone, and (5) migrate in dependency-complete waves with post-migration optimization.
- Common mistakes: blanket rehosting or refactoring, one-to-one sizing, ignoring licensing strategy (Hybrid Benefit, reserved instances), migrating dependencies apart, and having no day-2 plan. Key quote: "there is no single correct way to move to the cloud, only a correct way to move each workload."

**The 7 Rs (CloudifyOps/Medium):** The framework evolved from Gartner's original 5 Rs to AWS's 6 Rs, and now includes a 7th strategy called Relocate. [2]

1. **Rehost (Lift and Shift)** — Fastest route; move infrastructure to cloud with minimal changes. Example: financial services firm migrating 200 VMs to AWS EC2 ahead of data centre lease expiry.
2. **Replatform (Lift and Reshape)** — Targeted cloud optimizations without redesigning core architecture. Example: migrating on-premises PostgreSQL to Amazon Aurora.
3. **Refactor/Re-Architect** — Cloud-native rebuild with microservices, stateless architecture, managed services, and CI/CD. Example: logistics platform achieving 10x deployment velocity and 99.99% uptime on Amazon EKS.
4. **Repurchase (Drop and Shop)** — Replace legacy apps with SaaS alternatives (Salesforce for CRM, Workday for HR, ServiceNow for ITSM).
5. **Retire** — Decommission systems no longer needed. Example: healthcare organization retiring 30 underused applications.
6. **Retain (Revisit Later)** — Keep applications on-premises when compliance constraints or risk outweigh near-term benefits, particularly for government/classified data.
7. **Relocate (Hypervisor Lift, the 7th R)** — Move entire VMware virtualization estates to cloud-hosted environments (VMware Cloud on AWS, Azure VMware Solution) without changing hypervisor, applications, or tooling. "Think of Rehost as 'move the VM'; Relocate as 'move the data centre virtually.'" Example: insurance company migrating 400 VMs with zero changes and zero retraining.

Four-step framework for choosing strategies: (1) portfolio discovery and assessment, (2) score each application across business criticality, technical complexity, compliance requirements, and cloud/AI readiness, (3) map applications to the 7 Rs, and (4) plan and execute in waves. Claims of industrialized, AI-driven migration platforms: accelerated timelines by 30–50%, reduced modernization rework by 25–40%, and reduced planning effort by 40–60% for refactoring. Four-stage legacy-to-AI-ready journey: Stabilize (Rehost/Relocate), Optimise (Replatform/Repurchase), Modernize (Refactor), and AI-Enable. Key takeaways: Rehost/Relocate are best for speed and low disruption; Refactor delivers maximum long-term value; Replatform balances effort and benefit; most enterprises use all seven strategies. [2]

**The 7 Rs (IBM Think, published 13 October 2025 by Stephanie Susnjara and Ian Smalley):** The framework evolved from the initial 5 R's (rehost, refactor, revise, rebuild, replace) introduced by Gartner in 2010. AWS expanded it to 6 R's in 2016 by adding "Retire," then added "Retain" in 2017 to complete the 7 R's. Today most enterprises use hybrid and multicloud strategies. Global cloud market was valued at USD 752.44 million in 2024 and projected to grow to USD 2,390.19 billion by 2030. Hybrid cloud migration can achieve 2.5 times more value than single public cloud (per IBM IBV report "Mastering Hybrid Cloud"). Approximately 58% of global decision-makers report cloud skills remain a considerable challenge (IBM IBV 2023 report). Cloud providers offer tools like AWS Application Migration Service, IBM Cloud migration services, and Azure Migrate. Plans should include success criteria, rollback procedures, data migration planning, and stakeholder coordination. Governance and cost management frameworks (resource tagging, budget alerts, regular cost reviews) should be established before migration begins. [4]

**The 7 Rs (NetApp, by Sudip Sengupta):** Gartner first introduced the 5 Rs model; AWS expanded to 6 Rs by adding "Retire," then introduced the 7 Rs by adding "Retain." The article includes a detailed comparison table covering use-cases, pros, and cons of each strategy. Key considerations: Retire is cheapest but risks incompatibility with interconnected stacks; Relocate is quickest but limits cloud-native capabilities; Refactor is best for high-usability complex applications but requires extensive planning, training, and monitoring. [5]

**Lift-and-shift vs. re-architect cost comparison (The Competenza, June 25, 2026, by Nishant Agrawal):** [6]

- **Lift and Shift cost range:** $40,000–$150,000+ (small business apps $40K-75K, mid-sized enterprise $75K-120K, large enterprise workloads $120K-150K+).
- **Re-architecting cost range:** $200,000–$600,000+ (small modernization $200K-300K, mid-sized $300K-500K, large complex systems $600K+).
- Lift and shift: faster migration (weeks vs. months), lower upfront cost, but higher long-term operating costs and limited cloud-native capability. Re-architect: slower, higher initial investment, but superior long-term ROI, scalability, performance, security, and AI-readiness.
- Azure is best for Microsoft-centric infrastructure, hybrid cloud, .NET modernization, and regulated industries (Azure Migrate, Site Recovery, AKS, Functions, Cosmos DB).
- Recommended hybrid approach for most enterprises: move stable workloads quickly via lift and shift while re-architecting mission-critical applications.
- Security considerations: Lift and shift risks include legacy security gaps, excessive user permissions, poor cloud configurations (misconfigured storage buckets, firewalls, unsecured APIs), limited cloud-native security features. Re-architecting enables zero-trust access, encryption, automated checks, microservices isolation, and DevSecOps.

**Sequentur cost/effort data for SMBs:** [8]

- Lift-and-shift: $3,000-$15,000 per single Windows Server migration; often costs slightly MORE per year than on-prem due to ongoing cloud bills with no operational changes; 1-4 weeks per workload.
- Re-platform: 30-80% more project effort than lift-and-shift; $10,000-$40,000 for SQL workloads; operational savings recoup the higher one-time cost in 12-24 months; 4-16 weeks per workload.
- Re-architect: 5-20 times the cost of lift-and-shift; typically $150,000-$750,000 for a line-of-business app at a 40-person business; 6-24 months timeline.
- Typical full SMB migration combining multiple strategies lands in the 3-to-9-month range.
- Core thesis: "The right migration is the one that uses the cheapest strategy that delivers what the business needs for that specific workload, not the most ambitious strategy applied across the board."
- Per-workload decision tree: (1) does anyone use it? No → Retire; (2) should it be in cloud at all? No → Retain; (3) does a mature SaaS exist? Yes → Repurchase; (4) critical, 5+ years, architecturally limited? Yes → Re-architect; (5) can it run on managed service? Yes → Re-platform; (6) default → Lift-and-shift.

**Gartner's assessment factors (vFunction):** Gartner recommends evaluating six factors: Business fit, Business value, Agility, Cost, Complexity, and Risk. IDG/Foundry research: "Application/legacy system modernization has risen in importance to become a top priority for CIOs in 2022." vFunction cautions that lift and shift "genuinely does not modernize anything" and can simply move technical debt to the cloud. Additional strategies covered: Encapsulation (making application features accessible as APIs without modernizing the underlying system), Rewrite, and Replace. [10]

**Lift-and-shift to Azure (VIAcode):** Lift-and-shift (also known as rehosting) involves "transferring applications and their data from an on-premises environment to the public cloud—in this case, Microsoft Azure—without requiring changes to the code or architecture." Ideal for businesses needing fast cloud migration—particularly those running legacy systems like SQL Server applications and SSIS packages. Azure-specific advantages include immediate cost savings (eliminating physical hardware overhead, Azure Hybrid Benefit, reserved instances), enhanced security and compliance (Azure Security Center, GDPR/HIPAA compliance), faster time-to-cloud, and a pathway to cloud-native services like Azure SQL Database and Azure App Service for continued modernization. "Using tools like Azure Migrate and Azure Site Recovery, the migration begins. Critical workloads are migrated with minimal downtime, and data backups are performed to ensure that no data is lost in the process." [1]
